title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
text: A starving chef must eat 10,000 bites (his order), but the restaurant only serves 10,000 per day. Ordering everything at once sends the price soaring — that’s market impact. Waiting too long and the pizza gets cold — that’s timing risk. The solution: an algorithm that intelligently splits the orders to eat without being noticed, neither too fast nor too late.

Waiting too long and the pizza gets cold — that’s timing risk. The solution: an algorithm that intelligently splits the orders to eat without being noticed, neither too fast nor too late.

title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Large orders move prices to their own disadvantage → splitting is mandatory.
Fundamental trade-off: market impact (cost of speed) ↔︎ timing risk (cost of waiting).
9 algorithms exist, each optimising this trade-off differently.
We choose the algo via the efficient frontier (cost/risk space) and \(\lambda\) (risk aversion).
Dominant cost: timing risk = 40% — not commissions.

title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
Oral explanation
Intuition




Temporary impact
Price perturbation that dissipates after the trade.
Spring: compressed then released.


Permanent impact
Price rise that persists — the market has received a signal.
The market has “understood” the intention.


TWAP
Equal slices in time.
Timer every 15 min.


VWAP
Follow the historical intraday volume profile.
Swim with yesterday’s current.


POV
\(w_i = \alpha \cdot v_i\): proportional to actual volume.
Stick to today’s market pace.


MI
Dark pools + hidden orders, quasi-zero impact.
Secret queue without a sign.


IS
Minimises gap between decision price and execution price.
Pay as close as possible to the decision instant.


AS (AIM/PIM)
Adaptive IS: accelerates according to trend hypothesis.
IS with a directional thermostat.


MC
Targets the closing price.
Wanting to pay the official evening price.


LIQ
Trades if and only if liquidity + price are favourable.
Only opening your wallet in good conditions.


Efficient frontier
Algorithms minimising cost for each risk level.
Pareto frontier of trading.


\(\lambda\)
Tangent slope to the frontier = cost/risk ratio.
Slider between expensive safety and cheap risk.

title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

Large order → market impact → need for splitting
Splitting → trade-off impact ↔︎ timing risk → efficient frontier
Investor profile → \(\lambda\) → tangency point = optimal algo
↑ cost ↓ risk : MC → IS → AS → POV → PI → VWAP → LIQ → MI ↓ cost ↑ risk
TWAP → off frontier (simple but inefficient)
Historical volume → VWAP; actual volume → POV; dark pools → MI; price vs benchmark → PI / AS

title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
text:
📐 Essential Formulas








Formula
Meaning
To remember




\(\text{VWAP} = \dfrac{\sum p_i v_i}{\sum v_i}\)
Volume-weighted average price.
Large transactions weigh more.


\(n = \dfrac{t_1-t_0}{\Delta t}+1\;;\;w_i=\dfrac{w}{n}\)
TWAP: number of slices and uniform size.
Equal division in time.


\(w_i = \alpha \cdot v_i\)
POV: size proportional to observed volume.
\(\alpha \in [1\%,20\%]\).


\(\tilde{\alpha} = \dfrac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\)
POV: self-participation correction.
\(\alpha=5\%\Rightarrow\tilde{\alpha}=5.3\%\).


\(\lambda = \dfrac{\text{cost}}{\text{risk}}\)
Risk aversion.
Large \(\lambda\) → safe and expensive algo (MC, IS).

title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

TWAP predictable → front-running possible; off frontier → do not choose by default.
VWAP ≠ guaranteed price: follows estimated volume, not price.
POV self-impact: correct with \(\tilde{\alpha}\) if \(\alpha\) is high.
MI: low completion rate → dark pool without counterparty = unexecuted order.
MC double trap: too early = timing risk; too late = high impact.
AIM vs PIM: AIM accelerates if prices are favourable (mean-reversion); PIM accelerates if prices are unfavourable (persistent trend).
Portfolio trading: entrusting the full list to the broker → information leakage risk.

title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: Difference between temporary and permanent impact?
Short answer: Temporary = reversible perturbation (price comes back). Permanent = informational signal retained durably by the market.

Q: Why is TWAP suboptimal?
Short answer: Predictable (front-running) and off the efficient frontier: same risk, higher cost than alternatives.

Q: Difference VWAP vs POV?
Short answer: VWAP follows a historical volume profile; POV reacts to real-time observed volume — more adaptive, but still predictable.

Q: How do we use \(\lambda\) to choose an algorithm?
Short answer: \(\lambda\) is the slope of a line from the origin in cost/risk space. The tangency point with the efficient frontier gives the optimal algorithm.

Q: Difference AIM / PIM in AS?
Short answer: AIM: aggressive when prices are favourable (mean-reversion hypothesis). PIM: aggressive when prices are unfavourable (persistent trend hypothesis).

Q: What is the dominant transaction cost?
Short answer: Timing risk (40%), far ahead of market impact (6%) and commissions (1%).

Q: Main risk of outsourced portfolio trading?
Short answer: Confidentiality: sharing the full portfolio composition with a broker exposes it to exploitation of that information.

title: Algorithmic Execution — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

Impact = temporary (reversible) + permanent (signal).
Key trade-off: market impact ↔︎ timing risk.
Frontier: \(MC \to IS \to AS \to POV \to PI \to VWAP \to LIQ \to MI\).
TWAP off frontier (simple ≠ optimal).
\(\lambda = \text{cost}/\text{risk}\) → tangent → optimal algo.
POV: correct \(\alpha\) if large (\(\tilde{\alpha} = \alpha/(1-\alpha)\)).
MI: dark pools → low impact, low completion, often hybrid.
AIM = mean-reversion; PIM = persistent trend.
Dominant cost: timing risk = 40%.
Portfolio trading: simultaneous orders + confidentiality to protect.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
This chapter explores the structure of financial markets and their empirical properties. Two major questions run through it:

Are markets efficient — that is, do they correctly reflect all available information?
Do financial prices behave like simple random walks, or do they present recognizable structures?

To answer these, we examine trading venues, available instruments, traded volumes, and finally the stylised facts (stylised facts) — that is, the empirical regularities universally observed on financial markets.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
This chapter explores the structure of financial markets and their empirical properties. Two major questions run through it:

Are markets efficient — that is, do they correctly reflect all available information?
Do financial prices behave like simple random walks, or do they present recognizable structures?

To answer these, we examine trading venues, available instruments, traded volumes, and finally the stylised facts (stylised facts) — that is, the empirical regularities universally observed on financial markets.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Market Evolution

Increasing Volatility over the Long Term
The observation of the S&P 500 from 1950 to 2012 illustrates a profound transformation of financial markets. Until the 1970s, markets exhibited relatively calm and regular movements.
From the 1980s onwards, several phenomena amplified volatility:

The progressive deregulation of financial markets
The development of electronic trading (electronic trading)
The globalization of capital flows
The appearance of new complex financial instruments (derivatives)







TipIntuition



Moving averages over 1, 2 and 3 years smooth short-term fluctuations and make it possible to visualize underlying trends. We observe that S&P 500 growth accelerated from the 1980s onwards, accompanied by much more marked volatility.








NoteKey Takeaway



The volatility of financial markets is not stationary: it tends to increase with the complexification of financial systems and the rise of algorithmic trading.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
section: Efficient Market Hypothesis (Efficient Market Hypothesis — EMH)
text:
Efficient Market Hypothesis (Efficient Market Hypothesis — EMH)

Definition and Origin
The Efficient Market Hypothesis (Efficient Market Hypothesis, EMH) is a fundamental theory of modern finance, proposed by Eugene Fama in 1960 and rewarded with the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2013.
It rests on the central idea that financial asset prices reflect at all times all available information. Consequently:

Investor behaviors are rational on average
It is impossible to beat the market systematically
The price is always at its fair value (fair value)
It is impossible to buy undervalued or overvalued assets in a durable way







TipIntuition



If prices instantly incorporate all information, then any abnormal profit opportunity is instantly eliminated by arbitrageurs. The market functions like an information processing machine.




The Three Forms of EMH
EMH is articulated in three forms according to the extent of information integrated in prices:

Weak Form (Weak Form)
The weak form states that prices reflect all information contained in past prices.
Implications:

Technical analysis (technical analysis) is ineffective — studying historical charts does not generate abnormal returns
The future of prices is determined solely by external information (exogenous information)
The price follows a random process (random walk) — without new information, there is no predictable trend
The market is not necessarily in equilibrium at every instant







WarningPractical Consequence



If the weak form is true, trading strategies based on moving averages, Bollinger bands, support and resistance levels have no systematic added value. Any mechanical rule derived from past prices is doomed to long-term inefficiency.




Semi-Strong Form (Semi-Strong Form)
The semi-strong form states that prices reflect all publicly available information, and this instantly as soon as it is published.
This includes:

Company earnings announcements
Central bank decisions
Published macroeconomic data
Press releases and analyst analyses







TipIntuition



If the semi-strong form is valid, it is useless to read financial newspapers for investment decisions: by the time you read a piece of information, it is already integrated into the price.




Strong Form (Strong Form)
The strong form is the most demanding: it states that prices reflect all information, whether public or private (insider information).






ImportantRadical Implication



If the strong form is true, even insiders (insiders) — persons with confidential information about a company — cannot realize abnormal profits. This is the least empirically accepted form, and it directly contradicts the very existence of laws against insider trading.





Criticisms of EMH
EMH is widely criticized, including in its weakest form. Markets present numerous signs of irrationality:

Persistent Overvaluation
Equity markets (equity) can remain overvalued relative to economic fundamentals (fundamentals) for long periods. The internet bubble (1997–2000) is the most striking illustration.


The Case of Great Investors
The durable outperformance of managers like George Soros or Warren Buffett is difficult to explain by statistical chance alone. If markets were perfectly efficient, these exceptional performances over several decades would have a negligible probability.






TipIntuition



If you flip a coin 1 000 times and always get heads, do you think it’s luck? The durable outperformance of certain investors suggests that there are exploitable inefficiencies.




Herding Behaviour (Herding Behaviour)
Herding behaviour (herding behaviour) describes the tendency of investors to imitate the decisions of others rather than analyze fundamentals. This phenomenon amplifies market movements and creates collective inefficiencies.


Algorithmic Trading (Algorithmic Trading)
The rise of algorithmic trading (algorithmic trading, algo trading) has profoundly modified the microstructure of markets. Automatic algorithms react to signals in milliseconds, sometimes amplifying irrational movements rather than correcting them.


Speculative Bubbles (Speculative Bubbles)
Speculative bubbles (speculative bubbles) constitute perhaps the strongest criticism of EMH: assets remain systematically mispriced for months or years before a brutal return to reality.



Example — The Bitcoin Bubble (Bitcoin Bubble)
The 2013 Bitcoin bubble is a paradigmatic example of irrational market behavior.
Between January 2013 and December 2013:

The Bitcoin price went from a few dollars to over 1 000 USD
Daily transactions exploded, indicating strong speculation
The rise was accompanied by massive media interest — a classic signal of market euphoria
The correction was then brutal and prolonged







WarningLesson from the Bitcoin Bubble



The correlation between price and transaction volume indicates that the rise was fueled by speculation and the FOMO phenomenon (Fear Of Missing Out) rather than by fundamental valuation. This type of dynamic is incompatible with EMH.




Example — The Flash Crash of May 6, 2010
The Flash Crash (Flash Crash) of May 6, 2010 is one of the most studied events in modern market history.
In a few minutes, the Dow Jones fell by nearly 998 points (−9.2 %) before recovering almost all of its losses in the same session.
Characteristics of the event:

The fall occurred between 2:30 PM and 3:00 PM New York time
Prices of certain stocks temporarily reached absurd levels (a few cents or several thousand dollars)
Several US exchanges (NASDAQ, NYSE, ARCA, BATS…) recorded similar movements simultaneously
High-frequency trading algorithms (High Frequency Trading, HFT) played a central role in the amplification







ImportantImplications for EMH



A collapse of 9 % without new fundamental information, followed by an immediate recovery, is incompatible with an efficient market. It reveals the fragilities introduced by automation and high-frequency trading in the microstructure of markets.




A Final Word — The 2013 Nobel Paradox
In 2013, the Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded jointly to Eugene Fama (defender of EMH), Lars Peter Hansen and Robert Shiller (critic of EMH and theorist of speculative bubbles).
As journalist Christophe Boucher noted in Le Monde:

Economics remains the only discipline where two people can share the same Nobel Prize by telling completely opposite things.







NoteKey Takeaway



There is no consensus on the efficiency of financial markets. EMH remains a useful but imperfect reference framework. The empirical reality of markets contains elements both compatible and incompatible with this hypothesis.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Where Do We Exchange?

Regulated Markets (Regulated Markets / Exchanges)
Regulated markets (exchanges) are official trading venues, subject to strict regulation.
Examples:

NYSE — New York Stock Exchange (US equities)
LSE — London Stock Exchange (UK equities)
CME — Chicago Mercantile Exchange (commodity futures)
SIX — SIX Swiss Exchange (Swiss equities)

Characteristics:

It is a centralized physical or electronic venue
Regulation is strict: quotation rules, surveillance, transparency
There is a clearing process (clearing process) by a clearing house (clearing house)
Electronic trading (electronic trading) is growing strongly, but floor trading (floor trading) partially persists







NoteKey Takeaway — Clearing



The clearing house acts as central counterparty (Central Counterparty, CCP) for each transaction. It guarantees that even if a counterparty defaults, the other will receive its payment. This mechanism considerably reduces counterparty risk (counterparty risk).


Brokers (brokers) like Interactive Brokers allow access to several trading venues simultaneously from a single interface.


Over The Counter Markets (Over The Counter — OTC)
OTC markets (Over The Counter) are decentralized markets where transactions are carried out directly between parties, without going through a central exchange.
Examples:

Oanda (forex broker)
Bond markets
Complex derivatives markets

Characteristics:

Less formal operation and more flexible regulation
Presence of market makers (market makers) who propose bid and ask prices (bid/ask quotes)
Lack of transparency : prices are not necessarily publicly disseminated
Not necessarily a physical venue — everything happens by phone or electronically







WarningOTC Risk



OTC markets are riskier because they do not benefit from the protection offered by a clearing house. In case of counterparty default, fund recovery can be difficult.




Market Maker vs Broker
It is important to distinguish two types of financial intermediaries:



Role
Market Maker (Market Maker)
Broker (Broker)




Example
Oanda
Dukascopy


Risk taking
✅ Yes — holds inventory
❌ No — no inventory


Remuneration
Bid/ask spread
Commission


Function
Ensures liquidity
Executes orders









TipIntuition — Market Maker



A market maker earns its living from the spread: it buys at a price slightly below the market price and resells slightly above. In return, it takes the risk of holding positions in inventory. The more liquid the market, the tighter the spread.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Financial Assets

Equities (Equity)
Equities (equity, stocks, shares) represent a participation in the capital of a company.
Main characteristics:

The holder becomes a shareholder (shareholder) and co-owner of the company
Dividends (dividends) are paid periodically (if the company decides so)
The shareholder bears the residual risk: in case of bankruptcy, shareholders are reimbursed last







TipIntuition



Holding a share is betting on the future growth of a company. The return comes both from capital gain (capital gain) on the share price and from distributed dividends.




Bonds (Bonds)
Bonds (bonds) are debt securities: the investor lends money to an issuer who commits to repay it with interest.
Characteristics:

Can be issued by States (sovereign bonds, treasuries) or companies (corporate bonds)
The price of a bond is a function of its maturity (maturity) and the coupon payment schedule (coupon schedule)
Less risky than equities in general (creditors are reimbursed before shareholders)







NoteKey Takeaway — Price / Rate Relationship



The price of a bond moves in inverse direction to the interest rate: if rates rise, existing bonds (at lower fixed rates) lose value. This relationship is fundamental in bond management.




Commodities (Commodities)
Commodities (commodities) include physical products such as:

Agricultural : wheat (wheat), corn (corn), coffee, sugar, etc.
Energy : oil (oil), natural gas (natural gas)
Metals : gold (gold), silver (silver), copper (copper)

Financial particularity:

Commodities are generally not traded directly on financial markets
Futures contracts (futures) are used to gain exposure to these assets without having to take physical delivery
The role of storage and transportation costs is central in valuation







WarningPhysical Delivery — Warning



An investor who buys an oil futures and forgets to close or roll over (roll over) their position before expiration may find themselves obliged to take delivery of barrels of oil! This is why expiration date management is crucial on commodity markets.




Currencies (Currencies / Foreign Exchange — FX)
Currencies (currencies) constitute a market in its own right, the foreign exchange market (Forex, FX market).
Fundamental characteristics:

Currencies are always quoted in pairs : EUR/USD, USD/CHF, GBP/USD, etc.
There is an interest rate differential (interest rate differential) between the two currencies of a pair
This differential generates a carry return (carry) or a carry cost depending on the position taken







ImportantCurrencies — Backbone of Markets



Currencies are the backbone (backbone) of financial markets. Any international investment implies a currency conversion, exposing the investor to foreign exchange risk (FX risk).

5 000 billion dollars per day means that the foreign exchange market exchanges in a single day a sum exceeding the annual GDP of many countries. No government can durably control this market.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Main Instruments

Overview
Financial markets offer a varied range of instruments allowing exposure to different assets in different forms. The choice of instrument depends on the investment horizon, the desired risk level, and any hedging need (hedging).


Spot Instrument (Spot)
The spot instrument (spot) designates the asset itself, transacted and delivered immediately.
Examples:

A share bought on the stock exchange
An amount of dollars bought against euros
Note: a tonne of physical wheat is generally not quoted spot on financial markets







TipIntuition



Buying spot means buying the real asset, here and now. Delivery can however take a few business days (typically T+2 for equities).




Over-The-Counter Forward Contract (Forward)
A forward contract (forward contract) is an agreement between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a price fixed today, at a determined future date.
Characteristics:

Bilateral contract, negotiated over the counter (OTC)
Flexibility on amount, date and conditions
Implies a counterparty risk (no clearing house)



Standardized Futures Contract (Futures)
A futures contract (futures contract) is the standardized version of a forward, traded on an organized exchange with a clearing mechanism.
Differences from the forward:

Standardized contracts: amount, expiration date, underlying asset predefined
Traded on a regulated exchange (exchange)
Clearing house (clearing house) eliminates counterparty risk
Margin calls (margin calls) daily according to price evolution







WarningThe Roll Over — Watch the Expiration



Futures have an expiration date (expiry date). An investor who does not wish to take delivery of the underlying asset (typical for commodities!) must roll over (roll over) their position: close the contract near its expiration and open a new one on the next contract. This operation has a cost.








TipIntuition — Futures vs Forward



The futures is to the forward what a standardized apartment in a condominium is to a custom-built house: more liquidity and security (thanks to the clearing house), but less flexibility.




Option (Option)
An option (option) is a right (and not an obligation) to buy (call option) or to sell (put option) an asset at a predefined price (strike price), at or before a given date (expiry date).
Characteristics:

The option buyer pays a premium (premium) to acquire this right
The seller (writer) collects the premium and takes the obligation to deliver/buy if the option is exercised
The option can be exercised or not depending on the evolution of the underlying asset price







NoteKey Takeaway — Uses of Options



Options are used to:

Hedge (hedge) against adverse price movements
Speculate with leverage (leverage)
Generate income by selling options (premium collection strategies)





Index (Index)
An index (index) groups a set of assets into a representative basket (basket) of a market or a market segment.
Examples:

S&P 500 : the 500 largest US market capitalizations
Currency basket : basket of weighted currencies
CAC 40, DAX 40, SMI : European equity indices







TipIntuition



An index makes it possible to measure the overall performance of a market without being exposed to the specific risk of a single company. ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds) make it possible to replicate the performance of an index at lower cost.




And Many Other Derivatives…
Financial markets also offer a vast range of derivatives (derivatives):

Swaps (notably interest rate swaps and FX swaps)
CDO (Collateralized Debt Obligations)
Warrants, certificates, turbos, etc.

These instruments are often used both for hedging (hedging) and speculation.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Stylised Facts

Definition
Stylised facts (stylised facts) are robust empirical regularities observed on financial price and return time series, regardless of the market, frequency or period considered.
Their importance lies in the fact that they distinguish real markets from a simple random walk (random walk). A realistic financial model must reproduce these properties.
Main reference: Cont (2001, 2005), Empirical properties of asset returns.


Volatility Clustering (Volatility Clustering)
Volatility clustering (volatility clustering) is undoubtedly the best known stylised fact. It was formalized by Cont (2005).
Observation:

Large price variations tend to be followed by large variations (in one direction or another)
Small variations tend to be followed by small variations

This property implies that volatility is not constant over time — we speak of heteroskedasticity (heteroskedasticity).






NoteKey Takeaway — The GARCH Model



Heteroskedasticity is precisely what the GARCH model family (Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) models. The H in GARCH directly designates this phenomenon. These models are ubiquitous in quantitative finance for volatility modeling and forecasting.








TipIntuition



Volatility clustering reflects the fact that markets “get agitated” in episodes: crises and stress periods are characterized by ample and successive movements, while calm periods see small movements follow one another. The daily returns of BMW are a clear visual example of this.




Negative Short-Term Autocorrelation
At high frequency (high frequency), return series exhibit a negative autocorrelation (negative autocorrelation) at short time lags.
This phenomenon was documented by Cont (2001) on USD/Yen tick data from 1992 to 1994.
Observation:

At the first lag (lag 1), the autocorrelation of price variations is significantly negative
For subsequent lags, it returns close to zero







TipIntuition — Bid-Ask Bounce



This short-term negative autocorrelation is partly explained by the bid-ask bounce (bid-ask bounce): transactions alternate between the ask price (ask) and the bid price (bid), mechanically creating a positive/negative alternation in price variations.








WarningContrary to the Medium Term



At lower frequencies (daily, weekly), returns are close to absence of correlation — consistent with the weak form of EMH. It is at high frequency that deviations are visible.




Scaling Laws (Scaling Laws)
Scaling laws (scaling laws) describe how certain return statistics transform when changing the time scale.
Formulation:
\[\mathbb{E}[|r|] \sim \Delta t^{\alpha}\]
This relation indicates that the expected absolute return evolves as a power law of the time step \(\Delta t\), with exponent \(\alpha\).
Properties:

This law is observed over a wide range of time scales (from the second to several months)
It describes how to move from one temporal resolution to another
It constitutes a form of self-similarity (self-similarity) of financial markets







TipIntuition — Financial Fractals



Scaling laws recall the behavior of fractals: by zooming in or out on a financial price series, one finds similar statistical properties. This contrasts with the simple random walk where \(\alpha = 0.5\) exactly.




Fat-Tailed Distributions (Fat-Tailed Distributions)
Financial returns do not follow a normal (Gaussian) distribution — this is one of the most important stylised facts for risk management.
The empirical distributions of returns exhibit fat tails (fat tails, heavy tails):

The central peak (leptokurtosis) is higher and thinner than that of a Gaussian
The tails of the distribution contain much more probability than the Gaussian predicts







ImportantConsequence for Risk Management



Extreme events (crashes, flash crashes, crises) are much more frequent than the normal law predicts. A risk model based on normality will systematically underestimate extreme losses. This is precisely what contributed to the 2008 financial crisis (inadequate risk models).


The empirical distributions resemble Lévy distributions (Lévy distributions) or stable distributions (stable distributions), which have much fatter tails than the Gaussian.
Illustrative example:

The probability density of S&P 500 price variations every 30 minutes clearly shows a higher peak and fatter tails than the Gaussian distribution of same variance.



Other Important Stylised Facts
Beyond the four properties presented in detail, markets present other regularities:
Seasonality (seasonality):

Daily, weekly, monthly and annual seasonal patterns in volumes and volatility
Market activity is not uniform throughout the day

Asymmetry in equity markets (asymmetry in equity markets):

Equity markets tend to fall faster than they rise (negative skewness)
Corrections are often more brutal and faster than rises

Correlations between spread, volume and volatility:

Negative correlation between bid-ask spread and volume: the higher the volume, the tighter the spread (tight spread)
Positive correlation between volume and volatility: periods of high activity are also periods of high uncertainty







NoteKey Takeaway — Conclusion on Stylised Facts



The set of these stylised facts clearly shows that financial markets do not behave like simple random walks. They result from complex human interactions, herding behaviors, institutional constraints, and non-linear dynamics.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Market Seasonality

Equity Intraday Seasonality (Equity Daily Seasonality)
Equity markets exhibit a characteristic intraday seasonality, documented notably by Frijns (2006) on several exchanges (NYSE, NASDAQ, Paris Bourse).
The intraday profile of volatility or volume presents a characteristic U-shape (U-shape):

Peak at opening : strong activity and strong volatility from market opening
Calm in mid-day : reduced activity
Peak at closing : renewed activity before market close







TipIntuition — Why the U-Shape?



At opening, traders react to news accumulated overnight and adjust their positions. In mid-day, activity naturally reduces. At closing, traders must close their daily positions, creating a second activity peak.


This profile is robust across different stock markets, although its intensity varies according to local microstructures (quotation rules, hours, presence of a mid-day fixing).


FX Intraday Seasonality (FX Daily Seasonality)
The foreign exchange market presents a different intraday seasonality, dictated by session overlaps worldwide (Masry, 2011).
The FX market is open 24/7, 5 days a week. Activity follows the successive openings of the major financial centers:



Session

The major peak of activity occurs during the London–New York overlap (1:00 PM–5:00 PM GMT), which concentrates the majority of world exchanges.






NoteKey Takeaway — London-New York Overlap



The overlap session between London and New York is the period of greatest liquidity and often of greatest volatility on the foreign exchange market. It is during this window that most important economic indicators are published.



Weekly Seasonality and Influence of Sleep
In-depth research also shows a weekly seasonality (intraweek seasonality) on the FX market. Activity peaks repeat at regular intervals during the week, corresponding to the successive openings of sessions.
The influence of “sleeping hours” (sleeping hours by region) on market activity illustrates that markets are directly driven by the biological and social cycles of human traders.






TipIntuition



FX seasonality is a direct consequence of the fact that the foreign exchange market is global and decentralized. Activity follows the sun: it moves from Asia to Europe then to America as the hours pass.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Market Events

Classification — Endogenous vs Exogenous
Market events (market events) are disturbances that generate significant price movements. They fall into two major categories:





graph TD
    A["Market Events"] --> B["Endogenous\n(Endogenous)"]
    A --> C["Exogenous\n(Exogenous)"]
    B --> D["Liquidity crunch\n(Liquidity crunch)"]
    C --> E["Scheduled news\n(Scheduled news)"]
    C --> F["Unscheduled news\n(Unscheduled news)"]












NoteDefinitions — Endo/Exogenous




Endogenous (endogenous) : comes from the inside of the system — the cause arises from the market itself
Exogenous (exogenous) : comes from the outside — external information or shock impacts the market





Endogenous Events
Endogenous events result from the internal dynamics of the market, without identifiable external cause.
The main example is the liquidity crunch (liquidity crunch):

Numerous sellers find no buyers (or vice versa)
Prices collapse (or soar) not because of economic news, but because of an imbalance between supply and demand for liquidity
The Flash Crash of 2010 is an example of a partly endogenous event, amplified by trading algorithms



Exogenous Events — Scheduled News
Scheduled news (scheduled news) are economic publications whose date and time are announced in advance. They generate predictable volatility spikes.
Important examples:

Non-Farm Payrolls (NFP) : published every first Friday of the month at 8:30 AM EST (2:30 PM Swiss time) — measure of US employment excluding the agricultural sector. This is one of the most anticipated indicators and generates the strongest reaction on the foreign exchange market.
GDP (Gross Domestic Product, GDP) : quarterly publication of economic growth data by country
Consumption indices : consumer confidence, home sales, durable goods orders, etc.
Interest rate decisions by central banks (Fed, ECB, SNB…)







ImportantTrading the News — A Major Challenge



Scheduled news are known in advance, but their content is uncertain. Markets already anticipate an expected value (consensus). What matters is not the absolute published figure, but the deviation from expectations (surprise). A good figure below expectations can make a market fall.




Exogenous Events — Unscheduled News
Unscheduled news (unscheduled news) are, by definition, unpredictable. Their impact is generally more violent because markets cannot prepare for them.
Historical examples:

September 2011 : the Swiss National Bank (SNB) unilaterally sets a floor (floor) of 1.20 CHF for EUR/CHF, generating an immediate rise of several percent of the Swiss franc in a few seconds
September 11, 2001 terrorist attack in Manhattan: closure of US exchanges, global market collapse at reopening
Natural disasters, nuclear accidents, surprise political decisions…







WarningRisk Management in the Face of Unscheduled Events



Unscheduled events illustrate the limit of risk models: no model can anticipate a terrorist attack or a surprise central bank decision. Risk management must provide protection mechanisms against the unknown (tail risk hedging, black swan events).




Quantification of Market Events
Academic research, notably that of T. Bisig (2012), has sought to quantify and classify market events on high-frequency EUR/USD data.
The methodology consists in:

Measuring the magnitude (magnitude) of each event — that is, the extent of the price movement
Analyzing the temporal profile of the reaction — immediate or gradual
Superimposing magnitude and price around the time of the event

The graphs illustrate real events occurring on the EUR/USD pair between 2007 and 2009, showing that each major event leaves a characteristic footprint on high-frequency data.






TipIntuition — Utility of Quantification



Being able to automatically identify and quantify market events in high-frequency data makes it possible to clean data (for statistical models), estimate the impact of news, and potentially build event-driven trading strategies.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors
text:
Key Takeaways






NoteMarket Efficiency (EMH)




Fama’s theory (1960, Nobel 2013): prices reflect all available information
Three forms: weak (past prices), semi-strong (public information), strong (all information)
Widely criticized: speculative bubbles, Flash Crash, herding behaviors testify to real inefficiencies
No consensus : EMH remains a useful framework, not an absolute truth









NoteTrading Venues and Instruments




Regulated markets (exchanges) : centralized, strict surveillance, clearing house → less risky
OTC (Over The Counter) : decentralized, market makers, less transparent → riskier
Instruments: spot, forward, futures (standardized), options (right, not obligation), indices
The roll over of futures is crucial to avoid physical delivery









NoteVolumes




NYSE Euronext US : largest world exchange by volume (~6 900 Bn USD in 2013)
Forex : the largest market on the planet (~5 000 Bn USD/day)
EUR/USD : 25 % of world FX volume · ~3.6 M USD exchanged per second









NoteStylised Facts — Markets Are Not Random Walks




Volatility clustering : large variations follow large variations (→ GARCH)
Negative autocorrelation at short term / high frequency
Scaling laws : \(\mathbb{E}[|r|] \sim \Delta t^{\alpha}\)
Fat tails (fat tails) : extreme events are much more frequent than the normal law predicts
Seasonality : daily (U-shape for equities; sessions for FX), weekly, monthly









NoteMarket Events




Endogenous : born from the market itself (liquidity crunch)
Scheduled exogenous : NFP, GDP, interest rate decisions → anticipated volatility
Unscheduled exogenous : terrorist attacks, surprise central bank decisions → brutal and unpredictable impact
The quantification of events (Bisig, 2012) enables their systematic analysis on high-frequency data

title: Portfolio Construction — Review
text:
Fundamental Concepts
Portfolio: set of assets held simultaneously.
Diversification: combining low-correlation assets to reduce risk without sacrificing return → the only “free lunch” in finance.
MPT — Modern Portfolio Theory: Markowitz framework (1952), Nobel Prize 1990.



Asset Return and Risk







Measure
Formula




Historical expected return
\(E[R_i] = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} R_i(t)\)


Variance
\(\text{Var}(R_i) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(R_i(t) - E[R_i])^2\)


Volatility
\(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\text{Var}(R_i)}\)









WarningPitfall



Expected returns are more an art than a science — this is the most uncertain and most influential step.





Portfolio of \(N\) Assets
Weight constraint: \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i = 1\)







Measure
Formula




Return
\(R_p(t) = \sum_i w_i R_i(t)\)


Expected return
\(E[R_p] = \sum_i w_i E[R_i]\)


Variance (double sum)
\(\sigma_p^2 = \sum_i \sum_j w_i w_j \text{Cov}(R_i, R_j)\)


Variance (matrix form)
\(\sigma_p^2 = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{C}\, \mathbf{w}\)



Covariance: \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])]\)
Covariance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\): complete encoding of relationships between assets.






WarningPitfall — Sample Size



Minimum \(N^2/2\) observations to estimate \(\mathbf{C}\) reliably.





Correlation
\[
\rho_{ij} = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_i, R_j)}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \in [-1, +1]
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{Cov}(R_i, R_j) = \rho_{ij}\,\sigma_i\sigma_j
\]



Value of \(\rho\)
Interpretation




\(+1\)
Identical evolution — no diversification


\(0\)
Independence — partial diversification


\(-1\)
Opposite direction — maximum diversification






2-Asset Portfolio — Impact of \(\rho\)
\[
\sigma_P = \sqrt{w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2w_1 w_2 \rho_{12}\sigma_1\sigma_2}
\]
Example: \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 0.10\), \(w_1 = w_2 = 0.5\)



\(\rho_{12}\)
\(\sigma_P\)
Remark




\(+1\)
\(0.100\)
Weighted average — no gain


\(+0.5\)
\(0.087\)



\(0\)
\(0.071\)



\(-0.5\)
\(0.050\)



\(-1\)
\(0.000\)
Risk cancelled (ideal case)









WarningPitfall



If \(\sigma_1 \neq \sigma_2\), even with \(\rho = -1\) the risk is not zero: \(\sigma_P = |w_1\sigma_1 - w_2\sigma_2|\).





Efficient Frontier
Definition: set of portfolios that maximize \(E[R_p]\) for a given \(\sigma_P\) (or minimize \(\sigma_P\) for a given \(E[R_p]\)).
Dominance: portfolio A dominates C if same return and lower risk, or same risk and higher return.



Calculation Methods









Method
Principle
Advantages
Limitations




Monte-Carlo
Random draws of \(\mathbf{w}\)
Intuitive
Slow, inefficient, \(\nearrow\) with \(N\)


Closed-form (Lagrange)
Exact analytical solution
Exact, fast
Negative weights possible, no complex constraints


Numerical optimization
scipy.minimize
Flexible, constraints
Local optimum possible




Closed-form — Key Scalars
\[
a = \mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{1},\quad
b = \mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu},\quad
c = \boldsymbol{\mu}^T\mathbf{C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu},\quad
d = ac - b^2
\]
\[
\lambda_1 = \frac{c - b\mu_P}{d},\quad
\lambda_2 = \frac{a\mu_P - b}{d},\quad
\mathbf{w}^* = \mathbf{C}^{-1}(\lambda_1\mathbf{1} + \lambda_2\boldsymbol{\mu})
\]


Numerical Optimization — Problem
\[
\min_{\mathbf{w}}\;\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w} - q\,\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\mu}
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{w}=1,\quad 0\leq w_i\leq 1
\]

\(q = 0\) → minimum variance
\(q \to \infty\) → maximum return
Varying \(q\) traces the entire efficient frontier







WarningEffect of constraints



Weight constraints lower the efficient frontier and reduce the attainable risk region.






Risk-Free Asset & CML
Risk-Free Asset: short-term sovereign bond, \(\sigma_{rf} = 0\), \(\rho_{rf,P} = 0\).
Combination risk-free asset (\(w_{rf}\)) + portfolio \(P_0\):



Measure
Formula




Return
\(E[R_{P_1}] = w_{rf}\,r + (1-w_{rf})\,E[R_{P_0}]\)


Risk
\(\sigma_{P_1} = (1-w_{rf})\,\sigma_{P_0}\)



→ Linear relationship in \((\sigma_P, E[R_p])\) space.
CML (Capital Market Line): tangent line to the efficient frontier passing through \(r\).

On the CML → optimal
Below → suboptimal
Beyond the tangency point → leverage (borrowing)

Relations between concepts





flowchart LR
    A[Assets\nE[Ri], σi] --> B[Covariance\nMatrix C]
    B --> C[Portfolio\nVariance\nwᵀCw]
    A --> D[Expected\nReturn\nΣwi·E[Ri]]
    C --> E[Efficient\nFrontier]
    D --> E
    E --> F[CML + Risk-\nFree Asset r]
    F --> G[Optimal\nPortfolio]









Pitfalls & Critical Points

Expected returns: difficult to estimate, very influential on the final result
Correlations in crisis: tend towards \(+1\) → diversification reduced at the worst moment
Sample size: too short → covariance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) unreliable
Negative weights (closed-form): imply short selling, often unrealistic
Constraints: always reduce the efficient frontier (less freedom = less efficiency)
\(\rho = -1\): theoretical, almost nonexistent in practice

text:
Algorithms — Quick Reference Cards

TWAP

Equal slices in time, independent of price and volume
✅ Simple · ❌ Predictable · ❌ Ignores the market
Variants: +noise on time/sizes · aggressive (start) or passive (end) profile



VWAP

Follows historical intraday volume profile
Buying below VWAP = good execution
❌ Total volume known only at end of day → uses historical data
❌ Price not guaranteed · ❌ No real-time reaction



POV

Size proportional to observed actual volume
Typical \(\alpha\): 1 % (small) to 20 % (large)
Similar to VWAP but dynamic · Always predictable



MI

Uses dark pools (opaque markets) + hidden orders
Risk: low completion rate
Often hybrid: 20 % via public VWAP/POV + remainder in dark pool



IS

Minimizes: execution price − decision price
Arbitrage: market impact ↔︎ timing risk
Favors execution early in session · Inputs: volatility, risk aversion



AS








Type

Assumption

Aggressive if prices favorable

Adapts activity according to current price / benchmark gap

text:
Pricing — Binomial Tree
1-step structure :

\(S_0 \cdot u\) (up) with probability \(p\)
\(S_0 \cdot d\) (down) with probability \(1-p\), \(u = 1/d\)

Hedge delta :
\[\Delta = \frac{f_u - f_d}{S_0 u - S_0 d}\]
Risk-Neutral Probability :
\[p = \frac{e^{rT} - d}{u - d}\]
Option price :
\[\boxed{f = e^{-rT}\left[p \cdot f_u + (1-p) \cdot f_d\right]}\]
Calibration :
\[u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \quad d = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{T}}\]






WarningComplexity



\(n\) steps → \(2^n\) paths. At 30 steps : \(\approx 10^9\) paths → memory intensive.

\[d_1 = \frac{\ln(S_0/K) + (r + \sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \quad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}\]

title: The Limit-Order Book — Oral Review
text: Imagine a giant flea market: thousands of sellers stick post-its on a board (“I sell at €50”), buyers add theirs (“I buy at max €48”). No one is matched yet. Then someone shouts: “I buy now!” — boom, the cheapest seller’s post-it disappears. That’s the LOB. And the juicy detail: 75% of the post-its are torn off before ever being used. The OTC market maker, meanwhile, is the junk dealer who buys and resells himself — convenient, but he keeps the difference (the spread) and takes the risk of ending up with unsold stock.

title: The Limit-Order Book — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Problem: organise millions of simultaneous exchanges in a transparent and fair way.
Two models: OTC (via market maker, spread = remuneration, inventory risk) vs. LOB (centralised book, direct participants).
Fundamental trade-off: limit order (better price, not guaranteed) ↔︎ market order (guaranteed execution, less favourable price).
LOB dynamics: 3 cases depending on the price position relative to bid/ask.
Statistical reality: 70–80% cancellations, concave price impact, fat-tailed distributions.
Physical modelling: a minimalist model (Maslov) reproduces the key statistical properties of real markets.

title: The Limit-Order Book — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
One-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




LOB \(\mathcal{L}(t)\)
Set of submitted, unexecuted and uncancelled orders at time \(t\)
The “order book” on hold


Bid \(b(t)\)
Maximum price among all active buy orders
The highest bidder on the buy side


Ask \(a(t)\)
Minimum price among all active sell orders
The lowest asker on the sell side


Spread \(s(t)\)
Ask − bid gap, always \(\geq 0\)
No-deal zone: no crossing possible


Mid-price \(m(t)\)
Average of bid and ask, proxy of the “true price”
Neutral reference point


Relative price \(\delta^x\)
Distance of an order to the best price on its side
\(\delta^x = 0\) = at best; \(\delta^x > 0\) = less aggressive


Depth \(N^b, N^a\)
Total volume available at each relative price level
Measures liquidity at each rung of the book


Limit order
Not immediately executable → enters the LOB and waits
“I want, but only at this price”


Market order
Executed immediately at the best available price
“I want now, regardless of the exact price”


Tick \(\pi\)
Smallest possible price gap between two consecutive orders
Minimum granularity of the book


Hurst exponent \(H\)
Measures the long-term memory of a time series
\(H < 0{,}5\) = mean-reverting; \(H = 0{,}5\) = random walk


Market impact
LOB modification caused by an order, potentially permanent
A large order leaves a lasting “footprint”

title: The Limit-Order Book — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

Order submitted → compared to bid/ask → Market order if \(p_x \geq a(t)\), Limit order otherwise
Limit order below bid → LOB unchanged
Limit order inside spread → bid \(\uparrow\) (or ask \(\downarrow\)) → spread reduced
Market order → consumes depth → price impact concave in \(|w|\)
Impact normalised by market cap → Master Curve (Lillo et al.) → universal power law
LOB → 70–80% of orders cancelled before execution
Maslov model (homogeneous) → \(H \approx 1/4\), non-Gaussian, volatility clustering
Heterogeneity → ABM (Agent-Based Models)

title: The Limit-Order Book — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

\(s(t) \geq 0\) always — if ask < bid, there would have been immediate matching.
Limit order ≠ guaranteed execution → opportunity risk (the market may never come back to the desired price).
Doubling \(|w|\) does not double the impact — impact is concave, not linear.
\(H \approx 1/4\) in Maslov → anti-persistent (mean-reverting), not trending (\(H > 0{,}5\)).
Dark pool opacity ≠ guaranteed efficiency (scandals and regulatory fines documented).
Maslov = homogeneous traders → does not reproduce heterogeneity → requires ABM.
The Master Curve is universal after normalisation by market capitalisation — not raw.

title: The Limit-Order Book — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is the difference between OTC and LOB?
Short answer: In OTC, you trade with a market maker who is remunerated via the spread and bears inventory risk. In LOB, you trade with other participants via a centralised and automatic book.

Q: Why is the spread always positive?
Short answer: If ask < bid, there would be immediate matching. By definition, the remaining orders in the LOB cannot cross.

Q: When does a limit order inside the spread modify the bid?
Short answer: When \(b(t) < p_x < a(t)\) for a buy: this order becomes the new bid, reducing the spread.

Q: Why use a market order rather than a limit order?
Short answer: To guarantee execution when speed matters more than price — for example during a strong trend or to close a position quickly.

Q: What does a concave market impact concretely imply?
Short answer: Splitting a large order into small pieces costs less than a single massive order — this is the basis of optimal execution algorithms (VWAP, TWAP, etc.).

Q: What is \(H\) in Maslov and what does it mean?
Short answer: \(H \approx 1/4 < 0{,}5\) → anti-persistence: a rise tends to be followed by a fall (mean-reverting), unlike a random walk (\(H = 0{,}5\)).

Q: Why are 70–80% of orders cancelled?
Short answer: Price exploration, continuous algorithmic adjustments, changes of intention — the majority of limit orders never find a counterparty at the desired price.

Q: What is the Master Curve of Lillo et al.?
Short answer: By normalising market impact by market capitalisation, we obtain a universal curve (power law) valid for all assets — regardless of their size or sector.

Q: What are the three priority rules and how do they differ?
Short answer: Price-Time (FIFO at equality) favours early orders; Prorata (\(w / \sum w\)) favours large orders by proportional allocation; Price-Size serves the largest order first at equal price.

Q: What is the difference between an iceberg order and a dark pool?
Short answer: Iceberg = partially hidden size in a visible LOB. Dark pool = fully opaque LOB, no order visible before execution.

LOB = set of active orders (submitted, unexecuted, uncancelled).
Spread \(s = a - b \geq 0\) always; mid-price \(m = (a+b)/2\).

Priorities: Price-Time (FIFO) / Prorata / Price-Size.

Master Curve = universal power law after normalisation by market capitalisation.

title: Agent-Based Models — Review
text:
Minority Game — Key Formulas
Strategy selection (Softmax / Boltzmann):
\[P(s_j^t) = \frac{\exp(\lambda\, U_{s_j}(t))}{\sum_{k=1}^{S} \exp(\lambda\, U_{s_k}(t))}\]

\(\lambda \to \infty\) → highest-score strategy (deterministic)

Aggregate attendance:
\[A(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i^{\mu(t),\, s_i}\]
Utility update (Virtual Score):
\[U_{i,s}(t+1) = U_{i,s}(t) - a_{i,s}^{\mu(t)} \cdot \frac{A(t)}{\beta}\]

\(\beta \in \{1,\, N,\, 2^M\}\) — normalization factor
Score increases if the strategy was in the minority

Predictability:
\[H = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{\mu=0}^{2^M-1} \langle A|\mu \rangle^2\]
Price / returns:
\[r(t) = \frac{A(t)}{\lambda}, \qquad P(t) = P(t-1)\cdot\exp\!\left(\frac{A(t)}{\gamma}\right)\]

title: Returns and Time Value of Money — Oral Review
text:
You invest 1 000 CHF in January. In December, you have 1 100 CHF. Great! But your friend says he earned “10 % per month” — should you believe him? And your bank advertises “10 % annual, compounded daily” — how much is that, exactly?
This chapter answers a single obsession: how to measure, compare and compound monetary gains over time — without getting trapped by numbers that seem simple but aren’t. The golden rule: we don’t sum, we multiply (for simple returns) — and we take the log to make life easier.

A return measures a relative price variation — always in %.
Simple returns over multiple periods compound (multiplication), they do not sum.
Logarithmic (continuous) returns are additive over time — but not across assets in a portfolio.
Money has a time value: 1 CHF today is worth more than 1 CHF tomorrow.
The more frequent the compounding, the higher the future value — the limit being continuous compounding (\(e^{rn}\)).
The continuous rate \(r\) is always lower than the corresponding simple rate \(R\).
Investing abroad exposes to FX risk on top of the asset’s risk.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Summing simple returns: \(20\% + 16.7\% + 14.3\% = 50.9\%\) ≠ \(60\%\) — always compound.
Asymmetry of simple returns: \(+20\%\) then \(-20\%\) does not bring back to the initial price (\(100 \to 120 \to 96\)).
Annualization by multiplication: \(R_a \neq 12 \times R_m\) — use \((1+R_m)^{12}-1\).
Confusing \(r\) and \(R\): \(r = \ln(1+R) < R\) — the continuous rate is always smaller.
Additivity of log-returns for portfolios: \(r_p \neq \sum \alpha_i r_i\) — additivity is temporal, not cross-sectional.
Ignoring FX risk: a USD asset that rises can yield a falling CHF NAV if the dollar depreciates.
FX hedging eliminates all risk: false — it has a cost (rate differential) and does not eliminate equity risk.
Continuous compounding is realistic: no — it’s a theoretical mathematical tool, the limit of infinite frequency.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: Why can’t we simply add simple returns over multiple periods?
Short answer: Because each return applies to a different capital — already revalued by previous periods. The correct operation is the product: \(1 + R_n = \prod(1 + R_i)\).

Q: What is the difference between simple return and log-return?
Short answer: The simple return \(R = P_t/P_{t-1} - 1\) is asymmetric and compounds by product. The log-return \(r = \ln(P_t/P_{t-1})\) is symmetric and adds over time. Relation: \(r = \ln(1+R) < R\).

Q: Why is \(r < R\)?
Short answer: Because the logarithm is a concave function: \(\ln(1+x) < x\) for all \(x > 0\). Example: \(R = 10\%\), \(r = \ln(1.1) \approx 9.53\%\).

Q: What is the time value of money?
Short answer: 1 CHF today is worth more than 1 CHF tomorrow, because it can be invested. The future value is \(FV = PV \cdot (1+R)^n\) in discrete, \(PV \cdot e^{rn}\) in continuous.

Q: How do you annualize a monthly return?
Short answer: By compounding: \(R_a = (1+R_m)^{12} - 1\). Multiplying by 12 is only an approximation valid for very small returns.

Q: A CHF investor buys AAPL shares (in USD). What risks is he exposed to?
Short answer: Two risks: equity risk (variation of AAPL price in USD) and FX risk (USD/CHF variation). The CHF NAV depends on both simultaneously.

Q: Can FX risk be eliminated? At what price?
Short answer: Yes, by hedging with an opposite USD position. The cost is the interest rate differential between the two currencies. Advantage: less volatile NAV because only one risk remains.

Q: Is the continuous return of a portfolio the weighted average of individual log-returns?
Short answer: No. \(r_p = \ln(1 + \sum \alpha_i R_i) \neq \sum \alpha_i r_i\). The additivity of log-returns applies to time (successive periods), not to assets in a portfolio.

title: Bonds — Oral Review
text: Imagine you are a pizzeria that needs an oven. You ask your neighbor to lend you 1,000 CHF. In exchange, you promise 50 CHF per semester for 2 years (the coupons), then you return the 1,000 CHF (the principal). You write a signed, immutable paper — that’s your bond. Your neighbor can then resell that paper on the market. If in the meantime pizzerias have become very risky, no one will want to pay 1,000 CHF for your promise: the price falls. If you have become very popular, everyone wants your paper: the price rises. The yield is what your neighbor expects to earn by buying that paper today.

text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

A bond = fixed contract between borrower (issuer) and lender (investor).
The price is the present value of all future cash flows (coupons + principal).
The price ↔︎ yield relationship is inverse and convex: this is THE fundamental property.
The implicit yield cannot be read directly → numerical trial and error.
Different coupon yields are not comparable → zero-coupon standard.
The yield curve (zero-coupon) is reconstructed by Bootstrap from observed prices.
The credit spread measures the risk premium of an issuer over the sovereign.

text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Coupon
Fixed periodic payment made to the investor.
The interest on a standard loan.


Principal (Face Value)
Amount repaid at maturity.
The initial capital returned at maturity.


Yield \(y\)
Rate of return required by the market.
The degree of freedom that balances the price.


Above par (Premium)
\(B > 100\): the coupon is more attractive than the market.
The market pays more for generous coupons.


Zero-coupon
Bond with no coupon, sold at a discount, redeemed at par.
Zero intermediary = 1 single cash flow at maturity.


Yield Curve
Graph of zero-coupon rates as a function of maturity.
The “price of time” for each horizon.


Bootstrap
Algorithm that extracts zero-coupon rates in cascade from the shortest to the longest.
We solve one unknown at a time using already calculated rates.


Credit Spread
Yield difference between a corporate bond and a sovereign bond of the same maturity.
The issuer’s credit risk premium.


Convexity
Curvature of the price-yield relationship, favorable to the investor.
Price gain > price loss for the same rate change.


Callable Bond
Bond that the issuer can redeem before maturity.
Forced reinvestment risk at unfavorable rates.

text:
📐 Essential Formulas








Formula
Meaning
To remember




\(B(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i \cdot e^{-y(t_i - t)} + P \cdot e^{-y(T-t)}\)
Price = sum of cash flows discounted at yield \(y\).
Central formula, everything follows from it.


\(y_{\text{corp}} = y_{\text{sov}} + \text{CS}\)
Corporate yield = risk-free rate + credit premium.
The spread is always positive.


\(r_{\text{real}} \approx r_{\text{nom}} - \pi\)
Real yield adjusted for inflation.
Inflation risk = silent erosion.


\(\text{residual}(y) = B_{\text{obs}} - B_{\text{calc}}(y)\)
Error to cancel out in trial and error.
We seek \(y\) such that residual \(= 0\).


Bootstrap: \(\sum c_i e^{-r_{t_i} t_i} + (P + c) e^{-r_T \cdot T} = B\)
Isolate \(r_T\) with short rates already known.
Cascade resolution, from short to long.

title: Bonds — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Confusing price and face value: a bond can be worth 109 even if par is 100.
Believing the price-yield relationship is linear: it is convex (curvature favorable to the investor).
Forgetting that capital preservation is conditional: valid only if held to maturity AND no default.
Thinking that bonds and stocks are always uncorrelated: 2022 showed the opposite (brutal rate hike → both fall together).
Confusing interest rate risk and reinvestment risk: they work in opposite directions (rate rise → price falls BUT coupon reinvestment improves).
On Bootstrap: forgetting to use the already calculated rates to discount intermediate coupons.
Callable bonds: the issuer exercises its call right when rates fall → always at the worst time for the investor.
Rating agencies do not incorporate ESG criteria into their rating.

title: Bonds — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is a bond and how is it structured?
Short answer: Debt contract between issuer and investor, with fixed periodic coupons and principal repayment at maturity. The contract is immutable.

Q: How is the price of a bond calculated?
Short answer: Present value of all future cash flows, discounted at yield \(y\): \(B = \sum c_i e^{-y(t_i-t)} + P e^{-y(T-t)}\).

Q: Why do price and yield move in opposite directions?
Short answer: If rates rise, future cash flows are more heavily discounted → present value decreases. If the coupon is fixed, only the price can adjust the effective yield.

Q: What is convexity and why is it favorable?
Short answer: The curvature of the price-yield relationship means that the price gain from a rate fall is greater than the loss from a rate rise of the same magnitude.

Q: How does the trial and error (Trial & Error) algorithm work?
Short answer: Start from a very high \(y\), compute the residual \(B_{\text{obs}} - B_{\text{calc}}\). If positive divide \(y\) by 2, if negative take the average with the previous \(y\). Iterate until convergence.

Q: Why do we use zero-coupon rates rather than raw yields?
Short answer: Yields depend on the coupon structure → not comparable across different bonds. Zero-coupon rates normalize to a common standard.

Q: Explain Bootstrap in one sentence.
Short answer: We extract zero-coupon rates from the shortest to the longest, using at each step the already calculated rates to isolate the remaining unknown.

Q: What is the credit spread and what does it reflect?
Short answer: Yield difference between a corporate bond and a sovereign bond of the same maturity; it reflects the issuer’s additional credit risk.

Q: List the 5 bond risks and their main protection.
Short answer: Rates (short duration), credit (high rating), inflation (TIPS), liquidity (liquid bonds), reinvestment (avoid callables).

Q: Why did 2022 challenge bond diversification?
Short answer: Central banks raised rates brutally → bond and stock prices fell simultaneously → correlation turned positive, canceling the diversification effect.

title: Bonds — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

Price = PV of future cash flows discounted at yield \(y\).
Price ↑ ⟺ yield ↓: inverse and convex relationship.
Above par if coupon > market rate; below if coupon < market rate.
Trial & Error: inverse problem, numerical bisection to find \(y\) from \(B\).
Zero-coupon = universal comparison standard.
Bootstrap: cascade from shortest to longest to reconstruct the yield curve.
Credit Spread = risk premium over the sovereign rate.
Reinvestment risk ≠ interest rate risk: they oppose each other.
2022: exception to the stock/bond decorrelation.
Callable = forced reinvestment risk for the investor.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
A portfolio is a set of financial assets of potentially different natures — stocks, bonds, real estate, commodities, etc. — held simultaneously by an investor.


The fundamental objective is to create an investment vehicle more robust than an isolated asset.
The notion of “robustness” varies according to the investor’s profile. It may designate:

The maximization of the return/risk ratio (Sharpe ratio or information ratio)
The minimization of the drawdown (maximum loss observed over a period)
The minimization of the recovery time after a loss (time-to-recovery), linked to liquidity
Other investor-specific objectives







TipIntuition



Holding several different assets allows smoothing fluctuations: when one loses value, another may gain or remain stable. This is the principle of diversification.





Building a good portfolio is not trivial. The main challenges are:

Characterizing assets: identifying relevant risk measures for each asset
Modeling future returns: forecasting expected returns is notoriously difficult
Managing changing correlations: in crisis periods, correlations between assets tend to increase sharply, reducing the diversification effect when it is most needed
Taking investor behaviors into account: psychological biases influence decisions

Building a good portfolio is not trivial. The main challenges are:
