title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Origins and Context
Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), known in French as Théorie Moderne du Portefeuille (TPM), was introduced by Harry Markowitz in 1952 in his seminal article.
This contribution earned him the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1990, jointly with Merton Miller and William Sharpe.






NoteKey takeaway



MPT remains today one of the reference theoretical frameworks for portfolio management, despite its simplifying assumptions (normality of returns, stability of correlations, etc.).

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
The Central Idea: Diversification
The key concept of MPT is diversification.
By selecting assets of different natures — that is, whose returns do not vary identically — an investor can:

Partially offset the risk of one asset with another
Preserve the returns of each







TipIntuition



If asset A falls during a recession but asset B remains stable or rises (for example, gold in a crisis), holding them together reduces the overall volatility of the portfolio without necessarily sacrificing the average return.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Expected Return of an Asset
The expected return of an asset \(i\), denoted \(E[R_i]\), is an estimate of the future return of that asset.
There are several methods to estimate it:

Historical Approach
The simplest method consists in calculating the arithmetic mean of past returns over a time window \(T\):
\[
E[R_i] = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} R_i(t)
\]
This approach relies on the assumption that history repeats itself, which is a strong and often debatable assumption.


Model-Based Approaches
More sophisticated models allow integrating more information:
Fundamental models: they use the nature of the asset (dividends, coupons, financial ratios) and macroeconomic variables to estimate long-term returns.
Opportunistic models: in addition to macro variables, they incorporate short-term subjective views on market evolution.






WarningAttention — Art or science?



Practitioners often say: “Expected returns are more an art than a science.”
This step is nonetheless crucial: a poor estimation of expected returns can lead to very suboptimal allocations. It is the most delicate part of the entire process.

title: Portfolio Construction
section: Variance and Volatility of an Asset
text:
Variance and Volatility of an Asset
The risk of an asset is measured by its variance, or its volatility which is its square root.
Variance is generally calculated from historical data:
\[
\text{Var}(R_i) = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( R_i(t) - E[R_i] \right)^2
\]






TipIntuition



Variance measures how much an asset’s returns deviate from their average. The larger the variance, the riskier the asset (its returns are unpredictable).


Models can also be used to estimate future volatility (e.g. GARCH), but the historical approach remains the most widespread in practice.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Asset Weights
A portfolio of \(N\) assets is defined by a weight vector \(\mathbf{w} = (w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_N)^T\) such that:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i = 1
\]
Each \(w_i\) represents the fraction of capital invested in asset \(i\).






NoteKey takeaway



Weights can be positive (long position) or negative (short selling). In the simplest case, one imposes \(0 \leq w_i \leq 1\).

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Portfolio Return
The portfolio return at date \(t\) is the weighted linear combination of the asset returns:
\[
R_p(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i R_i(t)
\]
Its expected return is then, thanks to the linearity of expectation:
\[
E[R_p] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i E[R_i]
\]
This relation follows directly from the property:
\[
E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]
\]






TipIntuition



The expected portfolio return is simply the weighted average of the expected returns of its components. This is intuitive — but the magic of diversification operates on risk, not on return.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Portfolio Variance
The portfolio variance is more complex. It involves the covariances between assets:
\[
\text{Var}(R_p) = \sigma_p^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_i w_j \, \text{Cov}(R_i, R_j)
\]
The covariance between two assets is defined as:
\[
\text{Cov}(X, Y) = E\left[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])\right]
\]
This formula generalizes the property:
\[
\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2 \text{Var}(X) + b^2 \text{Var}(Y) + 2ab\,\text{Cov}(X, Y)
\]






TipIntuition



The portfolio variance depends not only on the individual risks of each asset, but also on how their returns evolve together. If two assets rise and fall at the same time (positive covariance), they offer no diversification. If they move in opposite directions (negative covariance), they offset each other.



Required Data
The covariance matrix is generally estimated from historical data.






WarningAttention — Sample size



To statistically reliably estimate a covariance matrix of \(N\) assets, one needs at least \(N^2 / 2\) observations. For 20 assets, this represents a minimum of 200 data points per asset. A history that is too short makes the estimation unreliable.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Compact Matrix Form
In matrix notation, the portfolio variance is written very compactly:
\[
\sigma_p^2 = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{C} \, \mathbf{w}
\]
where \(\mathbf{C}\) is the covariance matrix.

Example for \(N = 2\) assets
For two assets, we develop explicitly:
\[
\sigma_p^2 =
\begin{pmatrix} w_1 & w_2 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{11} & \sigma_{12} \\ \sigma_{21} & \sigma_{22} \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \end{pmatrix}
= w_1^2 \sigma_1^2 + w_1 w_2(\sigma_{12} + \sigma_{21}) + w_2^2 \sigma_2^2
\]
where \(\sigma_{ii} = \sigma_i^2\) is the variance of asset \(i\).

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Definition
The correlation between two assets \(i\) and \(j\) is defined as the normalized covariance:
\[
\rho_{ij} = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_i, R_j)}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} = \frac{E\left[(R_i - E[R_i])(R_j - E[R_j])\right]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(R_i)} \sqrt{\text{Var}(R_j)}}
\]
By definition, the correlation of an asset with itself is:
\[
\rho_{ii} = 1
\]
And one can express the covariance from the correlation:
\[
\text{Cov}(R_i, R_j) = \rho_{ij} \sigma_i \sigma_j
\]

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Interpretation
The correlation is always between \(-1\) and \(+1\):

\(\rho = +1\) : the assets move perfectly together (no diversification)
\(\rho = 0\) : the assets are independent (partial diversification)
\(\rho = -1\) : the assets move in perfectly opposite directions (maximum diversification, possible risk cancellation)







TipIntuition



The covariance matrix encodes all the relationships between assets. Combined with expected returns and individual volatilities, it contains all the information necessary to search for optimal allocations.

title: Portfolio Construction
section: Reference Case: Same Risk, Same Return, Same Weights
text:
Reference Case: Same Risk, Same Return, Same Weights
Let us start with a simple case to illustrate the effect of correlation.
We fix:

\(E[R_1] = E[R_2] = 0.20\) (identical expected return)
\(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 0.10\) (identical volatility)
\(w_1 = w_2 = 0.50\) (equal weights)

Only the correlation \(\rho_{12}\) varies.
The portfolio volatility is given by:
\[
\sigma_P = \sqrt{w_1^2 \sigma_1^2 + w_2^2 \sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \rho_{12} \sigma_1 \sigma_2}
\]

Results by Correlation
a) \(\rho_{12} = 1\)
\[
\sigma_P = \sqrt{(w_1 \sigma_1 + w_2 \sigma_2)^2} = w_1 \sigma_1 + w_2 \sigma_2 = 0.10
\]
The portfolio volatility is equal to the weighted average of the volatilities. Combining the two assets brings no diversification benefit.
b) \(\rho_{12} = 0.5\)
\[
\sigma_P \approx 0.0866
\]
c) \(\rho_{12} = 0\)
\[
\sigma_P \approx 0.0707
\]
d) \(\rho_{12} = -0.5\)
\[
\sigma_P = 0.05
\]
e) \(\rho_{12} = -1\)
\[
\sigma_P = |w_1 \sigma_1 - w_2 \sigma_2| = 0.0
\]
With perfectly negatively correlated assets and the same weights/volatility, the portfolio risk is completely cancelled!






WarningAttention — Ideal case and real case



A correlation of \(-1\) is extremely rare in practice. It remains a theoretical limit case to illustrate the maximum potential of diversification.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
General Case: Asymmetric Assets
Let us now consider two assets with different characteristics:

\(E[R_1] = 0.10\), \(E[R_2] = 0.20\)
\(\sigma_1 = 0.07\), \(\sigma_2 = 0.10\)
\(w_1 = w_2 = 0.50\)

The portfolio expected return is fixed: \(E[R_P] = 0.15\).
The volatilities by correlation are:



Correlation
Volatility \(\sigma_P\)




\(\rho = 1\)
0.085


\(\rho = 0.5\)
0.074


\(\rho = 0\)
0.061


\(\rho = -0.5\)
0.044


\(\rho = -1\)
0.015









NoteKey takeaway



Even with a correlation of \(-1\), if the volatilities of the two assets are different, the portfolio risk is not entirely cancelled. A residual risk remains proportional to \(|w_1 \sigma_1 - w_2 \sigma_2|\).

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Effect of Variable Weights
When varying the weights \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) (while maintaining \(w_1 + w_2 = 1\)), the portfolio describes a curve in the (risk, return) space.
These curves form ellipses linking the two pure assets through the different correlation levels:

For \(\rho = 1\) : the curve is a straight line (no diversification)
For decreasing \(\rho\) : the curve bends to the left, revealing portfolios with less risk for the same return







TipIntuition



The lower the correlation (even negative), the more the curve bends to the left. It is this curvature that represents the diversification gain: one can obtain the same return with less risk, or more return for the same risk.

title: Portfolio Construction
section: From a 2-Asset Portfolio to an \(N\)-Asset Portfolio
text:
From a 2-Asset Portfolio to an \(N\)-Asset Portfolio
Generalizing to \(N\) assets, one can build all possible combinations of asset pairs, then triplets, etc.
The set of all feasible portfolios forms a cloud of points in the (risk, return) space. The upper-left envelope of this cloud is called the efficient frontier.






NoteKey takeaway



The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios that maximize expected return for a given level of risk — or equivalently, that minimize risk for a given level of return.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Graphical Interpretation
Consider three portfolios A, B, and C in the (risk, return) space:

A is on the efficient frontier (low risk)
B is on the efficient frontier (high return)
C is inside the cloud (suboptimal portfolio)

A is better than C : A offers the same return as C, but with less risk (\(\sigma_P\) lower).
B is better than C : B offers the same risk as C, but with more return (\(E[R_p]\) higher).






TipIntuition



No rational investor would choose C if he can obtain A or B. The choice between A and B depends on the investor’s risk tolerance: - A conservative investor will prefer A (less risk, less return) - An aggressive investor will prefer B (more return, more risk)

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Overview of Approaches
Three major families of methods allow calculating the efficient frontier:

Monte-Carlo : brute-force approach
Closed-Form : exact mathematical solution
Numerical Optimisation : the most widespread practical approach

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Monte-Carlo Method

Principle
The Monte-Carlo approach consists in:

Randomly drawing weight vectors \(\mathbf{w}\) whose components sum to 1
Calculating the return and risk of the corresponding portfolio
Placing the point \((\sigma_P, E[R_P])\) on a graph
Repeating a very large number of times



Results and Limits
Applying this to 4 fictitious assets with 5 million draws shows that:

The cloud of points reveals the general shape of the feasible region
Asset 4 (the riskiest) is at the rightmost end of the cloud
Less risky assets are inefficient at 100% allocation (visible by the ellipses around them)







WarningLimits of the Monte-Carlo approach



This method has several major drawbacks:

It is very computationally expensive: millions of draws are necessary, and this number grows with the number of assets
It is inefficient: extreme risk zones (very low or very high) are under-represented
It does not guarantee finding the true efficient frontier — it only approximates the feasible region

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Closed-Form Solution

Problem Formulation
By minimizing \(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{C} \mathbf{w}\) under the constraint \(\sum_i w_i = 1\), one can derive an exact analytical solution via Lagrange multipliers.
One defines the following scalars:
\[
a = \mathbf{1}^T \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{1}, \quad b = \mathbf{1}^T \mathbf{C}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\mu}
\]
\[
c = \boldsymbol{\mu}^T \mathbf{C}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\mu}, \quad d = a \cdot c - b^2
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (E[R_1], E[R_2], \ldots)^T\) and \(\mathbf{1} = (1, 1, \ldots)^T\).


Lagrange Multipliers
\[
\lambda_1 = \frac{c - b \cdot \mu_P}{d}, \quad \lambda_2 = \frac{a \cdot \mu_P - b}{d}
\]


Optimal Weight Solution
\[
\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{C}^{-1}(\lambda_1 \mathbf{1} + \lambda_2 \boldsymbol{\mu})
\]
The associated minimum variance is:
\[
\sigma^2 = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{C} \mathbf{w} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 \mu_P
\]
where \(\mu_P\) is the target expected return of the portfolio.


Practical Observations
The analytical solution produces:

An efficient frontier that passes above the Monte-Carlo cloud
Weights that can be negative or greater than 1 (short selling, leverage), leading to portfolios with even higher returns
If one caps allocations between 0 and 1, the frontier becomes more constrained and cannot reach high risk levels







WarningSign constraints



Allowing negative weights amounts to permitting short selling, which is not always feasible in practice (regulation, costs). Constraining weights between 0 and 1 represents a long only portfolio.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Numerical Optimisation

Why Numerical Optimisation?
It is the most used method in practice, because it is:

Simple to implement with standard libraries (e.g. scipy.optimize)
Flexible : it allows easily adding realistic constraints
Efficient : it requires only a small number of calls to the objective function



Problem Formulation
One solves the following minimization problem:
\[
\min_{\mathbf{w}} \left[ \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{C} \mathbf{w} - q \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\mu} \right]
\]
under the constraints:
\[
\mathbf{1}^T \mathbf{w} = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \leq w_i \leq 1
\]
where \(q \in [0, +\infty)\) is a risk parameter that allows navigating along the efficient frontier:

\(q = 0\) : one minimizes only risk → minimum variance portfolio
\(q \to \infty\) : one maximizes only return → maximum return portfolio







TipIntuition



By varying \(q\) from 0 to \(+\infty\), one progressively traces the efficient frontier from the least risky portfolio to the maximum return portfolio.




Implementation in Python
The code uses:

sci.Bounds to impose \(0 \leq w_i \leq 1\)
sci.LinearConstraint to impose \(\mathbf{1}^T \mathbf{w} = 1\)
sci.minimize with the 'trust-constr' method
A loop over \(q \in \{0, 0.5, 1, \ldots, 50\}\)

import scipy.optimize as sci
import numpy as np

# Definition of bounds and linear constraint
bounds = sci.Bounds([0, 0, 0, 0], [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
linear_constraint = sci.LinearConstraint([1, 1, 1, 1], [1], [1])

# Objective function
def to_minimise(x, q):
    return cov.dot(x).dot(x) - q * er.dot(x)

# Calculation of the efficient frontier
eff_risk = []
eff_ret = []
w_optim = []

for q in np.arange(0, 50, 0.5):
    x0 = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1]) / 3
    res = sci.minimize(to_minimise, x0, method='trust-constr',
                       bounds=bounds,
                       constraints=linear_constraint,
                       options={'verbose': 0},
                       args=(q))
    eff_risk += [np.sqrt(cov.dot(res.x).dot(res.x))]
    eff_ret += [er.dot(res.x)]
    w_optim += [res.x]


Results Without Constraints
Without additional constraints (only \(\sum w_i = 1\) and \(0 \leq w_i \leq 1\)):

The efficient frontier coincides with the upper boundary of the Monte-Carlo cloud
It goes from the minimum risk portfolio to the riskiest asset (here asset 4 at 100%)
Allocations to less risky assets progressively decrease as risk increases



Results With Constraints
One can impose more realistic constraints, for example:

\(10\% \leq w_1 \leq 100\%\)
\(5\% \leq w_2 \leq 100\%\)
\(0\% \leq w_3 \leq 25\%\)
\(0\% \leq w_4 \leq 90\%\)

Observed effects:

The constrained efficient frontier is lower than the unconstrained frontier
It cannot reach very high risk levels (those of pure asset 4 at 100%)
The constraints reflect realistic limits imposed by regulation or investment policy







NoteKey takeaway — Advantage of numerical optimisation



Numerical optimisation allows very easily integrating complex constraints: per-asset bound constraints, sector constraints, liquidity constraints, etc. This is why it is the reference method in the industry.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
The Risk-Free Asset
A risk-free asset is a financial instrument whose return is certain, without volatility.
In practice, these are short-term sovereign bonds issued by a central bank (e.g. US Treasury bills, German Bundesanleihen). The default risk of a State is considered negligible and approximated to zero.






NoteKey takeaway



The risk-free asset serves as a base reference. Its return \(r\) is low but guaranteed. It is not correlated with the other assets (\(\rho_{rf, P} = 0\)) and its variance is zero (\(\sigma_{rf}^2 = 0\)).

title: Portfolio Construction
section: Combining the Risk-Free Asset with a Portfolio
text:
Combining the Risk-Free Asset with a Portfolio
By combining the risk-free asset (weight \(w_{rf}\)) and a risky portfolio \(P_0\) (weight \(1 - w_{rf}\)), one obtains a new portfolio \(P_1\).

Expected Return of \(P_1\)
\[
E[R_{P_1}] = w_{rf} \, E[r] + (1 - w_{rf}) \, E[R_{P_0}]
\]


Risk of \(P_1\)
By developing the variance:
\[
\sigma_{P_1}^2 = w_{rf}^2 \underbrace{\sigma_{rf}^2}_{=0} + (1 - w_{rf})^2 \sigma_{P_0}^2 + 2 w_{rf}(1 - w_{rf}) \underbrace{\rho_{rf, P_0}}_{=0} \sigma_{rf} \sigma_{P_0}
\]
Only remains:
\[
\sigma_{P_1} = (1 - w_{rf}) \, \sigma_{P_0}
\]






TipIntuition



The risk and the return of \(P_1\) are both linear combinations of those of the risk-free asset and portfolio \(P_0\). In the (risk, return) space, the combined portfolios lie on a straight line linking the risk-free asset to portfolio \(P_0\).

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
The Capital Market Line (CML)
The CML (Capital Market Line) is the tangent line to the efficient frontier passing through the risk-free asset point.
The tangent portfolio (the tangency point) is called the market portfolio.






NoteKey takeaway



The CML represents the best possible combination between return and risk:

Below the CML : suboptimal portfolios (one can do better)
On the CML : optimal combinations risk-free asset + market portfolio
Beyond the tangent portfolio : use of leverage (borrowing to invest more)




Investment Decision
The choice of portfolio on the CML depends on:

The investor’s risk appetite
The level of \(r\) (the risk-free return)
The investor’s ability to hold cash (position below the tangent portfolio)
The ability to use leverage (position beyond the tangent portfolio)







TipIntuition



A conservative investor will place part of his capital in the risk-free asset and the rest in the tangent portfolio. An aggressive investor can borrow to invest more than 100% in the tangent portfolio — which amplifies both return and risk.

title: Portfolio Construction
text:
Institutional Context
A pension fund is an institutional investor that manages the retirement savings of its members.
Unlike an ordinary investment fund, a Swiss pension fund is subject to strict regulatory constraints (notably OPP2 — Ordinance on Occupational Pension) which dictate the maximum allocation limits by asset class.
Moreover, the relative size of the Swiss market obliges a significant geographic diversification.

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
text: Imagine you are a chef and you have to prepare a dish with several ingredients. If you use 100% chili peppers, you risk ruining everything. If you skillfully mix chili peppers, rice, and vegetables — some spicy, some mild — the result is stable even if one ingredient fails. That is exactly what a portfolio is: mixing assets that do not all react the same way to market shocks. Markowitz formalized this intuition in 1952, and received the Nobel Prize for it. The moral: never put all your eggs in one basket — it is the only free lunch in finance.

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Problem: a single asset is too volatile/risky; how to combine \(N\) assets to do better?
Solution: diversification — choosing low-correlation assets so that their risks offset each other.
Risk measure: the variance (or volatility) of the portfolio, governed by the covariances between assets.
Return: linear combination of individual returns (no diversification gain here).
Tool: the efficient frontier (set of optimal risk/return portfolios).
Extension: add a risk-free asset → the CML (Capital Market Line) dominates everything.

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Diversification
Combining low-correlation assets reduces overall risk without sacrificing return.
If one falls, the other compensates.


Portfolio variance
It depends not only on individual risks, but especially on the covariances between assets.
Correlation is the key, not just the volatility of each asset.


Efficient Frontier (Efficient Frontier)
Set of portfolios that maximize return for a given risk.
Any portfolio below is suboptimal — one can do better.


Covariance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\)
Encodes all co-movement relationships between assets.
Without it, impossible to calculate portfolio risk.


CML (Capital Market Line)
Straight line tangent to the efficient frontier from the risk-free rate.
It dominates the efficient frontier alone — best possible risk/return pair.


Tangency portfolio
Contact point between the CML and the efficient frontier — the optimal risky portfolio.
Every rational investor combines this portfolio with the risk-free asset.


Parameter \(q\)
Controls the risk/return trade-off in numerical optimization.
\(q=0\) → minimum risk ; \(q\to\infty\) → maximum return.

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

Individual assets (\(E[R_i]\), \(\sigma_i\)) → Covariance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\)
Weights \(\mathbf{w}\) + \(\mathbf{C}\) → Portfolio variance \(\sigma_p^2 = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{C}\, \mathbf{w}\)
Weights \(\mathbf{w}\) + \(E[R_i]\) → Expected return \(E[R_p] = \sum w_i E[R_i]\)
(\(\sigma_p\), \(E[R_p]\)) for all \(\mathbf{w}\) → Efficient frontier
Efficient frontier + risk-free asset → CML → Optimal portfolio
Correlation \(\rho \downarrow\) → frontier curvature \(\uparrow\) → diversification gain \(\uparrow\)

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
text:
📐 Essential Formulas








Formula
Meaning
To remember




\(E[R_p] = \sum_i w_i E[R_i]\)
Expected portfolio return
Linear — no magic here


\(\sigma_p^2 = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{C}\, \mathbf{w}\)
Portfolio variance (matrix form)
The magic is here


\(\sigma_p^2 = \sum_i\sum_j w_i w_j\,\text{Cov}(R_i,R_j)\)
Same, expanded
Involves all pairs


\(\rho_{ij} = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_i,R_j)}{\sigma_i\,\sigma_j}\)
Normalized correlation \(\in [-1,+1]\)
Links covariance and correlation


\(\sigma_P = \sqrt{w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2w_1 w_2\rho_{12}\sigma_1\sigma_2}\)
Volatility for 2 assets
Reference pedagogical case


\(\sigma_{P_1} = (1-w_{rf})\,\sigma_{P_0}\)
Risk: risk-free asset + portfolio combo
Linear → straight line in \((\sigma, E[R])\) space


\(\min_{\mathbf{w}}\;\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w} - q\,\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\mu}\)
Numerical optimization problem
Varying \(q\) traces the frontier

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Expected returns: difficult to estimate (“art rather than science”) — small error → very bad allocation.
Correlations in crisis: all tend toward \(+1\) during shock periods → diversification disappears exactly when it is most needed.
\(\rho = -1\): theoretical only; almost nonexistent in practice.
If \(\sigma_1 \neq \sigma_2\), even with \(\rho = -1\), risk is not zero: \(\sigma_P = |w_1\sigma_1 - w_2\sigma_2|\).
Sample size: estimating \(\mathbf{C}\) reliably requires at least \(N^2/2\) observations.
Negative weights (closed-form solution): imply short selling, often unrealistic.
Weight constraints: any constraint lowers the efficient frontier — less freedom = less efficiency.
Monte-Carlo: never finds exactly the true frontier — only an approximation.

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is diversification and why does it work?
Short answer: Combining low-correlation assets makes their fluctuations offset each other. Expected return remains the weighted average, but risk decreases — it is the only free lunch in finance.

Q: Why is portfolio variance more complex than its return?
Short answer: Return is a linear sum of individual returns. Variance involves all pairs of covariances \(\text{Cov}(R_i, R_j)\) — hence the double-sum formula \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w}\).

Q: What happens when \(\rho = 1\) vs \(\rho = -1\) for a 2-asset portfolio?
Short answer: \(\rho = 1\): volatility is the weighted average of individual volatilities, no gain. \(\rho = -1\) with equal weights and volatilities: zero risk. This is the extreme theoretical case.

Q: What is the efficient frontier?
Short answer: The set of portfolios that maximize return for a given risk level. Any portfolio off the frontier is dominated: there exists something better for the same risk or the same return.

Q: Compare the three methods for computing the efficient frontier.
Short answer: Monte-Carlo: intuitive but slow and approximate. Closed form (Lagrange): exact and fast but negative weights possible, few constraints. Numerical optimization (scipy): standard method — flexible, realistic constraints, slight risk of local optimum.

Q: What is the role of the risk-free asset and the CML?
Short answer: The risk-free asset (\(\sigma=0\), \(\rho=0\) with any other asset) allows drawing the CML, a straight line tangent to the efficient frontier. The CML dominates the frontier alone: for any risk level, one can do better by combining the risk-free asset and the tangency portfolio.

Q: How does the parameter \(q\) allow tracing the efficient frontier?
Short answer: \(q\) weights the risk/return trade-off in the problem \(\min \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w} - q\,\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\mu}\). By varying \(q\) from 0 to \(+\infty\), one traverses the frontier from the minimum-variance portfolio to the maximum-return portfolio.

Q: Why are correlations a pitfall during crisis periods?
Short answer: During crises, correlations between assets tend toward \(+1\) (all assets fall together). Diversification disappears exactly when the investor needs it most.

title: Portfolio Construction — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

Diversification reduces risk without reducing expected return — the only free lunch in finance.
Portfolio return is linear in weights; variance involves covariances.
Key formula: \(\sigma_p^2 = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{w}\).
The lower \(\rho\), the greater the diversification gain.
The efficient frontier: set of dominant allocations (minimum risk for fixed return).
Practical method: numerical optimization with parameter \(q\) swept from 0 to \(+\infty\).
The CML dominates the efficient frontier as soon as a risk-free asset is added.
Major pitfall: correlations rise toward \(+1\) in crisis — diversification vanishes.
Estimating \(\mathbf{C}\) reliably requires \(\geq N^2/2\) observations.
Expected returns are more art than science — they are the weak link of the model.

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
text:
Imagine you are piloting a plane (your options portfolio) in a turbulent sky.

Delta is your altimeter: it tells how much the plane climbs if you pull the stick.
Gamma tells how fast this altimeter itself gets out of calibration when the weather changes.
Theta is the fuel gauge: it drops inexorably, no matter what you do.
Vega measures atmospheric turbulence (volatility).
Rho captures the slope of the landing runway (interest rate).

Managing options is keeping all these dials stable at the same time — without losing track.

Delta is your altimeter: it tells how much the plane climbs if you pull the stick.
Gamma tells how fast this altimeter itself gets out of calibration when the weather changes.

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

An option is exposed to several risks simultaneously: underlying price, time, volatility, rates.
The Greeks decompose these risks into independent and actionable metrics.
Naive strategies (naked, covered, stop-loss) are insufficient: too risky, too costly, or too expensive in transaction fees.
The rigorous answer is Delta hedging (continuous dynamic hedging).
Gamma measures the imperfection of the Delta hedge; neutralizing it requires other options.
Θ–Γ triangle: long Gamma costs Theta. There is no free lunch.
Black-Scholes has its limits; alternative models and advanced numerical methods exist.

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Delta (Δ)
Change in option price for +1 USD in the underlying.
Transmission coefficient between underlying and option; also ≈ risk-neutral prob. of exercise.


Gamma (Γ)
Speed at which Delta itself evolves.
Curvature; indicates whether the Delta hedge will quickly become obsolete.


Theta (Θ)
Loss of option value each passing day.
Buyer’s enemy, seller’s ally; not hedgeable.


Vega (ν)
Sensitivity of price to +1% implied volatility.
Captures uncertainty about uncertainty.


Rho (ρ)
Impact of a change in risk-free rates.
Less critical short-term; important for long-dated options.


Delta hedge
Hold Δ shares per option to neutralize directional risk.
Makes the portfolio insensitive to small underlying moves.


Gamma hedge
Add options to neutralize residual curvature.
Corrects the linear approximation error of Delta.


Naked option
Sell an option without any hedge.
Simple but theoretically unlimited loss if S rises sharply.


Stop-loss
Buy if \(S > K\), sell if \(S < K\).
Dynamic but high transaction costs and ambiguity at \(K\).


AD (automatic differentiation)
Exact derivative calculation in a single code pass.
O(1) vs O(n) for finite differences.

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

Option price → partial derivative in \(S\) → Delta (Δ)
Delta → partial derivative in \(S\) → Gamma (Γ)
Option price → partial derivative in \(t\) → Theta (Θ)
High Γ → Delta changes fast → frequent rebalancing needed
Long Γ ↔︎ Very negative Θ (fundamental trade-off, imposed by the Black-Scholes PDE)
Delta hedge neutralizes \(Δ\,δS\) but leaves \(\frac{1}{2}Γ\,δS^2\)
Gamma hedge → trade options (underlying has \(Γ = 0\))
Delta adjust after Gamma hedge → trade the underlying
Δ call = \(N(d_1)\) ≈ risk-neutral probability of exercise
Δ put = \(N(d_1) - 1\) = Δ call − 1 (call-put parity)

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
text:
📐 Essential Formulas








Formula
Meaning
To remember




\(\Delta_c = N(d_1)\)
Call delta
Always in \([0, 1]\)


\(\Delta_p = N(d_1) - 1\)
Put delta
Always in \([-1, 0]\)


\(\Delta_c - \Delta_p = 1\)
Delta parity
Consistent with put-call parity


\(\Gamma = \dfrac{N'(d_1)}{S_0\,\sigma\,\sqrt{T}}\)
Gamma (call = put)
Always \(> 0\), max ATM


\(\Theta_c = -\dfrac{S_0 N'(d_1)\sigma}{2\sqrt{T}} - rKe^{-rT}N(d_2)\)
Call theta
Generally negative


\(\delta c \approx \Theta\,\delta t + \Delta\,\delta S + \tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma\,\delta S^2\)
2nd-order Taylor
The 3 Greeks in action


\(w_T = -\Gamma_\Pi / \Gamma_T\)
Quantity of options for Gamma hedge
Then adjust Δ via underlying


\(d_1 = \dfrac{\ln(S_0/K) + (r + \sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}\)
Black-Scholes parameter
\(d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}\)

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Theta ATM diverges: when \(T \to 0\) and option ATM, Theta tends to \(-\infty\). Do not ignore it near expiration.
Negative Gamma = option seller: a large move (up or down) is always unfavorable; the Delta hedge quickly becomes obsolete.
Stop-loss ≠ Black-Scholes: the theoretical cost \(\max(S_0 - K, 0)\) differs from \(c_{BS}\) because one must discount cash flows and manage the ambiguity at \(K\).
One does not hedge Theta: time is certain, no strategy avoids it.
Gamma hedge order: neutralize Γ first (via options), then restore Δ (via underlying) — not the reverse.
American put < European call in the course example: early exercise with dividends gives a counter-intuitive result.
AD ≠ finite differences: AD gives exact derivatives in \(O(1)\), not approximations.
Confusing Vega and Gamma: Vega = sensitivity to \(\sigma\) (volatility), Gamma = curvature in \(S\).

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is the Delta of an option and how is it used to hedge?
Short answer: \(\Delta = \partial c / \partial S\) ; to hedge a call sale, one buys \(\Delta \times N_{\text{options}}\) shares. The portfolio is then insensitive to small underlying moves.

Q: Why is Delta hedging alone insufficient?
Short answer: Delta approximates the option-underlying relationship linearly, but the true relationship is convex. The quadratic term \(\frac{1}{2}\Gamma\,\delta S^2\) is ignored, creating a gap for large moves.

Q: How does one make a portfolio Gamma-neutral?
Short answer: Add \(w_T = -\Gamma_\Pi / \Gamma_T\) hedge options to cancel Gamma, then restore Delta neutrality by trading the underlying.

Q: Why can Theta not be hedged?
Short answer: The passage of time is certain and non-random; no financial asset protects against it. It is simply the daily cost of holding an option.

Q: What is the link between Theta and Gamma for a Delta-neutral portfolio?
Short answer: The Black-Scholes PDE imposes a strict trade-off: long Gamma implies very negative Theta. Benefiting from curvature has a daily cost.

Q: Why is the stop-loss strategy suboptimal?
Short answer: It generates high transaction costs (especially if the underlying oscillates around \(K\)) and its theoretical cost does not coincide with the Black-Scholes price because of discounting and ambiguity at \(K\).

Q: What is the difference between finite differences and automatic differentiation for computing the Greeks?
Short answer: Finite differences require \(O(n)\) model evaluations (one per parameter) and give approximate results. AD calculates all exact derivatives in \(O(1)\) by automatic backpropagation.

Q: What are the limits of Black-Scholes and how are they addressed?
Short answer: Constant volatility (→ Heston), no jumps (→ Merton), American options (→ binomial trees). For complex relationships or optimal hedging, neural networks or Reinforcement Learning are used.

title: Option Greeks — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

5 Greeks: Δ (direction), Γ (curvature), Θ (time), ν (vol), ρ (rates).
Δ call = \(N(d_1) \in [0,1]\) ; Δ put = \(N(d_1)-1 \in [-1,0]\).
Γ > 0 always (long position); max ATM; explodes ATM when \(T \to 0\).
Θ < 0 generally; ATM diverges to \(-\infty\) near expiration.
Delta hedge = hold Δ shares per option; daily rebalancing.
Gamma hedge = options first (Γ), then underlying (Δ).
Θ–Γ triangle: long Γ = very negative Θ; no free lunch.
Θ cannot be hedged; Γ can only be neutralized with options.
Taylor: \(\delta c \approx \Theta\,\delta t + \Delta\,\delta S + \frac{1}{2}\Gamma\,\delta S^2\).
AD: exact derivatives in \(O(1)\) — best method for large portfolios.

Key formulas
SMA — window \(n\) :
\[\text{SMA}(t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} X_{t-i}\]
Update : \(\text{SMA}(t+1) = \text{SMA}(t) - \dfrac{X_{t-n+1}}{n} + \dfrac{X_{t+1}}{n}\)
WMA — denominator \(= \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\) :
\[\text{WMA}(t) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot X_{t-n+i}}{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}\]
EMA — recursive form (central formula) :
\[\boxed{\text{EMA}(t) = \alpha \cdot X_t + (1-\alpha) \cdot \text{EMA}(t-1)}\]

title: Options — Fundamental Notions — Oral Review
text: Imagine you buy an inverse lottery ticket: you pay €5 for the right to sell your apartment for €300,000 in 6 months, even if the market collapses to €200,000. If the market rises to €400,000, you throw the ticket away and sell at market price. If it falls, you exercise your right and prevent the disaster. This is a put: insurance against a decline. Chapter 9 lays the foundations of these contracts, their price, and the models to value them.

If the market rises to €400,000, you throw the ticket away and sell at market price. If it falls, you exercise your right and prevent the disaster. This is a put: insurance against a decline. Chapter 9 lays the foundations of these contracts, their price, and the models to value them.

title: Options — Fundamental Notions — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

An option is an asymmetric right: the buyer chooses whether to exercise or not, the seller bears the obligation.
The price of this right (the premium) depends on \(S_0\), \(K\), \(T\), \(\sigma\), \(r\) and dividends.
No-arbitrage bounds always frame this price.
Put-call parity links the two option types through a fundamental equilibrium equation.
Pricing rests on the idea of perfectly hedging risk (delta-hedging) and using risk-neutral probabilities.
The binomial tree discretizes prices; Black-Scholes is its continuous analytical limit.
In practice, implied volatility is not constant: the smile reveals the limits of BS.

title: Options — Fundamental Notions — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Call
Right to buy at price \(K\) at maturity \(T\)
Bet on a rise, loss limited to the premium


Put
Right to sell at price \(K\) at maturity \(T\)
Insurance against a decline


Premium
Price paid to acquire the right
Cost of the insurance


European vs American
European = exercise only at \(T\) ; American = at any time
American more flexible, therefore more expensive or equal


Moneyness
Relationship between \(S_0\) and \(K\) indicating whether the option has intrinsic value
ITM = already in the right direction, OTM = not yet


No-arbitrage
Any price outside bounds allows a guaranteed risk-free profit
The market corrects immediately


Put-call parity
Call + discounted cash = Put + underlying asset
One can synthesize any instrument from the other three


Delta (\(\Delta\))
Number of assets to hold to neutralize the option position risk
The closer \(\Delta\) is to 1, the more the call behaves like the asset


Risk-neutral probability
Artificial probability that makes the asset just earn the risk-free rate
Allows discounting payoffs without risk premium


Implied volatility
Value of \(\sigma\) that BS should have to reproduce the observed price
Barometer of market expectations


Volatility smile
U-shaped curve of implied vol. according to strike
The market fears fat tails that BS ignores

title: Options — Fundamental Notions — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

Option → right to buy (call) or sell (put) → payoff at maturity
Payoff + premium → Profit (can be negative)
\(S_0\), \(K\), \(T\), \(\sigma\), \(r\) → determine the price of the option
Price → framed by no-arbitrage bounds
Call and put (same \(K\), same \(T\)) → linked by put-call parity
Put-call parity → allows building synthetic strategies (bull spread, butterfly, protective put)
Binomial tree → price via \(\Delta\) and risk-neutral probability \(p\) → converges to Black-Scholes
BS price observed on the market → inversion → implied volatility
Implied vol. ≠ constant according to \(K\) → smile → limits of the BS model

title: Options — Fundamental Notions — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Short call ≠ short put: the short call is the only position with theoretically unlimited loss (the price can rise indefinitely).
Volatility increases the value of calls and puts: counter-intuitive but logical (more dispersion = more chances of being ITM).
Risk-neutral probability \(p\) ≠ real probability: it is used only for pricing, not for predicting.
Bounds: if the lower bound gives a negative number, the true lower bound remains 0 (an option cannot be worth less than zero).
Put-call parity applies only to European options on a non-dividend-paying asset.
1-step binomial tree: the obtained price differs from BS because discretization is coarse; with \(n \to \infty\), it converges to BS.
Implied volatility ≠ historical volatility: one is forward-looking (market), the other backward-looking (data).
Smile does not mean BS is useless: it remains the traders’ lingua franca — but its assumptions are violated in practice.

title: Options — Fundamental Notions — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is the difference between a call and a put?
Short answer: The call gives the right to buy (bet on a rise), the put gives the right to sell (protection against a decline). Both have loss limited to the premium for the buyer.

Q: Why does volatility increase the value of both types of options?
Short answer: High volatility widens the distribution of future prices, increasing the probability that the option will be ITM at maturity, for both a call and a put.

Q: Prove the lower bound of the call: \(c \geq S_0 - Ke^{-rT}\).
Short answer: Compare two portfolios: A = call + cash \(Ke^{-rT}\), B = asset \(S\). A is always worth at least as much as B at maturity → \(c + Ke^{-rT} \geq S_0\).

Q: What is put-call parity and how is it proven?
Short answer: \(c + Ke^{-rT} = p + S_0\). We show that two portfolios (A = call + cash, C = put + asset) have exactly the same payoff \(\max(S_T, K)\) at maturity → same value today by no-arbitrage.

Q: What is the risk-neutral probability and why do we use it?
Short answer: It is an artificial probability \(p = (e^{rT}-d)/(u-d)\) under which the asset grows at the risk-free rate. It allows discounting payoffs without risk premium, simplifying pricing.

Q: What is the intuition behind the hedge delta?
Short answer: \(\Delta\) is the number of units of the asset that the option issuer must hold so that his portfolio is risk-neutral: whatever the scenario, its value is identical.

Q: How does Black-Scholes relate to the binomial tree?
Short answer: BS is the limit of the binomial tree when the number of steps \(n \to \infty\) and the duration of each step \(\to 0\). The binomial price converges to the BS price.

Q: What is the volatility smile and what does it reveal?
Short answer: The implied vol. calculated via BS varies according to the strike (U-shape). This reveals that real assets have fatter distribution tails than the log-normal law assumed by BS.

Q: When should one prefer the binomial tree to Black-Scholes?
Short answer: For exotic options (barrier, binary, American) where no analytical formula exists. BS applies only to European vanillas.

Q: What is the VIX and what is its link to this chapter?
Short answer: The VIX is the implied volatility index of the S&P 500, built from option prices. It is a direct barometer of market fear, based on the notion of implied vol.

title: Options — Fundamental Notions — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

Call = right to buy at \(K\) ; Put = right to sell at \(K\) ; the buyer pays the premium, his risk is limited.
Short call = only position with unlimited loss.
Volatility ↑ → call value ↑ and put value ↑ (both!).
Bounds: \(S_0 - Ke^{-rT} \leq c \leq S_0\) and \(Ke^{-rT} - S_0 \leq p \leq K\).
Put-call parity: \(c + Ke^{-rT} = p + S_0\) (no-arbitrage, European options).
Binomial tree: price = \(e^{-rT}[p\,f_u + (1-p)\,f_d]\) with \(p\) risk-neutral.
\(p\) risk-neutral ≠ real probability ; \(u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{T}}\), \(d = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{T}}\).
Black-Scholes = continuous limit of the tree; closed formula for vanillas only.
Implied volatility = \(\sigma\) that BS must have to reproduce the market price.
Smile = implied vol. not constant according to \(K\) → proof of BS limits (fat tails).

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Introduction to Time Series

Formal Definition
A univariate time series (Univariate Time Series) is a sequence of observations of a single real variable, indexed by time:
\[
X(t_i) \in \mathbb{R}, \quad t_i \text{ occurrences}
\]
Typical example — the EUR/USD exchange rate observed every day:
\[
X(t_i) = \ldots,\ 1.3012,\ 1.3014,\ 1.3022,\ \ldots
\]
\[
t_i = \{\ldots,\ \text{Jan 7, 2013 00:00:00},\ \text{Jan 8, 2013 00:00:00},\ \ldots\}
\]
In this example, the frequency is daily. This already raises a practical question: when exactly does a day begin? Time zones, holidays, and market opening hours are all subtleties that complicate the definition of instants \(t_i\) in practice.






NoteKey Takeaway



The order of observations is fundamental in a time series. Unlike information theory where occurrences can be freely rearranged, temporal order carries information — this is precisely what the models in this chapter seek to exploit.




Time Lag (Lag)






TipDefinition — Lag



The lag \(\tau\) is the duration separating two observations. We also speak of lagged variables (Lagged Variables): \(X_{t-\tau}\) denotes the value of variable \(X\) observed \(\tau\) periods before time \(t\).


The lag is the central notion of autoregressive models.
Examples:

Lag \(\tau = 1\) : we compare \(X_t\) to \(X_{t-1}\) (immediately preceding observation)
Lag \(\tau = 5\) : we compare \(X_t\) to \(X_{t-5}\) (e.g. same day of the previous week for daily data)



Statistical Characteristics of a Series
Basic statistics provide a first description of the series:

Expected Value (Expected Value) : \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) — long-term average value
Variance (Variance) : \(\text{Var}[X]\) — dispersion of values around the mean
Volatility (Volatility / Standard Deviation) : \(\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}\) — the standard deviation, very widely used in finance

These global statistics are necessary but insufficient: they completely ignore the temporal structure of the series. This chapter presents tools to go well beyond.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Objectives of Time Series Analysis
A time series analysis can pursue several objectives, which are not necessarily compatible with each other:

Identification : spot the structural elements of the series (trends, seasonalities, breaks)
Explanation : understand how the past influences the present and quantify these effects
Modeling : have a formal and parsimonious representation of the underlying process
Prediction : anticipate future observations with a quantification of uncertainty







WarningImportant — Objective and Model Choice



A model can be excellent for explaining and poor for predicting, and vice versa. These two objectives can lead to very different model architectures. It is therefore essential to clarify the objective before choosing a model.


Classic references in this field:

Box, Jenkins, Reinsel, Ljung — Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control, 5th ed., 2015
Brockwell, Davis — Introduction to Time Series and Forecasting, 3rd ed., 2016

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Overview of Time Series Models
There are many econometric models (Econometric Models) for time series. We distinguish two major families.
Regression Models (Regression Models):

Linear Regression (Linear Regression)
Ridge, Lasso (regularized regressions)
Polynomial Regression (Polynomial Regression)

Autoregressive Models (Autoregressive Models):

AR(p) : AutoRegressive of order \(p\)
MA(q) : Moving Average of order \(q\) (Moving Average)
ARMA(p,q) : combination of AR and MA







TipIntuition — Why Autoregressive?



In an autoregressive model, the current value of the series is expressed as a function of its own past values. The series “explains itself” — hence the prefix auto. This approach is natural for modeling phenomena where the past influences the present: asset prices, GDP, temperature, etc.


This chapter focuses on simple autoregressive models, as they constitute a classic and analytically tractable foundation.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Stationarity (Stationarity)
Stationarity is the prerequisite for any serious autoregressive analysis. This section explains the reasons, the forms, and the methods to obtain it.

Why Require Stationarity?
Using autoregressive models on non-stationary data leads to incorrect results. Four fundamental reasons motivate this requirement:

Consistency (Consistency) : relationships between variables must remain stable over time for estimated parameters to be valid over the entire period
Reliable Estimation (Reliable Estimation) : parameters estimated on non-stationary data produce misleading conclusions
Simplified Analysis (Simplified Analysis) : stationarity considerably simplifies the mathematical and statistical properties of estimators
Avoiding Spurious Results (Avoiding Spurious Results) : two non-stationary series may appear strongly correlated without any real causal relationship



Sources of Non-Stationarity

Trend (Trend)
A series exhibits a trend when its mean evolves systematically over time, upward or downward.
Example: the price of an asset in a bull market rises progressively. The mean calculated over the entire period is representative of no particular instant.






TipIntuition — Trend



Imagine weighing a person every day during a weight-loss diet. The weight series has a downward trend. The “global average” corresponds to no real state of the system, neither at the beginning nor at the end of the diet.




Seasonality (Seasonality)
Seasonality refers to periodic and predictable variations that repeat at regular intervals.
Common examples:

Temperatures: annual cycle (cold winter, hot summer)
Retail trade: sales peaks in December (holidays)
Financial markets: weekly effects (lower volumes on Friday)



Heteroskedasticity (Heteroskedasticity)
Heteroskedasticity refers to non-constant volatility over time: the dispersion of observations varies from one period to another.
Financial example: markets experience calm periods (low volatility) and crises (high volatility). The variance of returns is not constant over time.






WarningImportant — Heteroskedasticity in Finance



Heteroskedasticity is particularly frequent in finance. We speak of volatility clusters (Volatility Clustering): turbulent periods tend to group together. Specialized models such as GARCH (Generalized AutoRegressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) have been developed to treat this phenomenon.





Formal Definitions of Stationarity

Strict Stationarity (Strict Stationarity)
A process \(\{X_t\}\) is strictly stationary if its joint distribution is invariant under time translation:
\[
F(X_{t_1+\tau}, \ldots, X_{t_n+\tau}) = F(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n}) \quad \forall\, \tau,\, n
\]
where \(F\) is the joint cumulative distribution function (Cumulative Distribution Function).
This means that all the probabilistic structure of the process is identical regardless of the period considered — not only the mean and variance, but also skewness, tail behavior, etc.






WarningLimitation of Strict Stationarity



Strict stationarity is very restrictive and difficult to verify empirically because it concerns the complete joint distribution. In practice, we settle for weak stationarity.




Weak Stationarity (Weak Stationarity)
Weak stationarity (also called second-order stationarity, or Wide-Sense Stationarity) imposes two conditions concerning only the first two moments:
Condition a — Constant mean:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mu = \text{constant} \quad \forall\, t
\]
Condition b — Autocovariance depending only on lag:
\[
\text{Cov}(X_t,\, X_{t+\tau}) = \gamma(\tau) \quad \forall\, \tau
\]
where \(\gamma\) is called the autocovariance function (Autocovariance Function). Crucial: it does not depend on the absolute instants \(t\) and \(t+\tau\), only on their difference \(\tau\).






NoteKey Takeaway — Weak Stationarity



A process is weakly stationary if:

Its mean is constant over time
Its autocovariance depends only on lag \(\tau\), not on absolute instants

Weak stationarity is much less restrictive than strict stationarity and sufficient for the vast majority of practical analyses.





Stationarity Tests

Visual Inspection
A first evaluation consists in plotting the series and checking:

Does the mean appear constant over the entire period?
Does the dispersion around the mean appear stable?
Are there visible trends or cycles?



Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test (ADF — Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test)
The ADF test is the reference statistical test for weak stationarity.

Null hypothesis \(H_0\) : the series has a unit root → non-stationary
Alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) : the series is stationary

Decision rule:

p-value > 0.05 : we do not reject \(H_0\) → the series is probably non-stationary
p-value ≤ 0.05 : we reject \(H_0\) → the series is probably stationary




How to Make a Series Stationary?
Several transformations can be combined depending on the type of non-stationarity:

Differencing (Differencing) : calculate \(\Delta X_t = X_t - X_{t-1}\)
Returns (Returns) : \(r_t = (X_t - X_{t-1})\,/\,X_{t-1}\) (simple) or \(r_t = \ln(X_t\,/\,X_{t-1})\) (log-returns)
Decomposition : identify and subtract trend and seasonality components
Logarithmic transformation (Log Transform) : \(\ln(X_t)\) attenuates the effects of increasing volatility







NoteKey Takeaway — Financial Practice



In finance, we almost systematically work with returns rather than raw prices.

Prices tend to grow → generally non-stationary
Returns oscillate around zero → stationary in most cases





Illustrative Examples

Simulation — Prices vs. Returns
We consider three simulated price series over 252 days (1 year of trading):

Plain : no drift nor volatility seasonality
Seasonality : volatility low → high → low (low-high-low)
Drift : annual drift of 30%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

# Parameters
mu     = 0.30   # annual drift
sigma  = 0.15   # base volatility
dsigma = 0.80   # amplitude of volatility variation

S0 = 100  # initial price
T  = 1    # horizon in years
N  = 252  # number of trading days

dt = T / N
np.random.seed(6)

# Generation of random shocks
random_numbers_1   = np.random.normal(0 * dt, sigma * np.sqrt(dt), N)
random_numbers_2_1 = np.random.normal(0 * dt, sigma * (1 - dsigma) * np.sqrt(dt), N)
random_numbers_2_2 = np.random.normal(0 * dt, sigma * (1 + dsigma) * np.sqrt(dt), N)
random_numbers_3   = np.random.normal(mu * dt, sigma * np.sqrt(dt), N)

# Price evolution
price_series_1    = np.zeros(N)
price_series_1[0] = S0
price_series_2    = price_series_1.copy()
price_series_3    = price_series_1.copy()

for t in range(1, N):
    price_series_1[t] = price_series_1[t-1] * (1 + random_numbers_1[t-1])
    if t > N * 0.2 and t < N * 0.6:
        price_series_2[t] = price_series_2[t-1] * (1 + random_numbers_2_2[t-1])
    else:
        price_series_2[t] = price_series_2[t-1] * (1 + random_numbers_2_1[t-1])
    price_series_3[t] = price_series_3[t-1] * (1 + random_numbers_3[t-1])

# Display
plt.plot(price_series_1, label='no seasonality, no drift')
plt.plot(price_series_2, label='seasonality (low-high-low) vol')
plt.plot(price_series_3, label='drift (30%)')
plt.ylabel('prices')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# ADF test on prices
print('Augmented Dickey Fuller test')
print(f'prices plain,       p-value = {adfuller(price_series_1)[1]:.2f}')
print(f'prices seasonality, p-value = {adfuller(price_series_2)[1]:.2f}')
print(f'prices drift,       p-value = {adfuller(price_series_3)[1]:.2f}')
print()
# ADF test on returns

print(f'returns seasonality, p-value = {adfuller(random_numbers_2_1)[1]:.2f}, '
      f'{adfuller(random_numbers_2_2)[1]:.2f}')

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Autocorrelation (Autocorrelation)
Autocorrelation is the central concept that links a series’ observations to its own past. Its measure, the autocorrelation function (ACF), is the main diagnostic tool before any modeling.

Reminder — Correlation between Two Variables
Correlation (Correlation) between two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) measures the intensity of their linear relationship:
\[
\text{Cor}(X, Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X) \cdot \text{Var}(Y)}} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] \cdot \mathbb{E}[(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])^2]}}
\]
It belongs to \([-1,\, 1]\) :

\(+1\) : perfect positive linear relationship
\(-1\) : perfect negative linear relationship
\(0\) : absence of linear relationship



Definition of Autocorrelation
Autocorrelation is the correlation of a time series with itself, lagged by \(\tau\):
\[
\text{Cor}(X_t,\, X_{t+\tau}) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X_t - \mu_0)(X_{t+\tau} - \mu_\tau)]}{\sigma_0\, \sigma_\tau}
\]
where \(\mu_0,\, \mu_\tau\) are the means and \(\sigma_0,\, \sigma_\tau\) the standard deviations at times \(t\) and \(t+\tau\).

Simplification under Stationarity
When the series is weakly stationary, we have \(\mu_0 = \mu_\tau = \mu\) and \(\sigma_0 = \sigma_\tau = \sigma\). Autocorrelation then simplifies to:
\[
\rho_\tau = \text{Cor}(X_t,\, X_{t+\tau}) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X_t - \mu)(X_{t+\tau} - \mu)]}{\sigma^2}
\]
It then depends only on the lag \(\tau\), and not on absolute instants. This is why stationarity is a prerequisite: without it, autocorrelation is not a well-defined concept.



The Autocorrelation Function (ACF — Autocorrelation Function)
The autocorrelation function associates to each lag \(\tau\) its autocorrelation:
\[
\text{ACF}(\tau) = \rho_\tau
\]
It is represented graphically by a correlogram: a vertical bar chart where each bar corresponds to a lag.






NoteKey Takeaway — Role of the ACF



The ACF describes the temporal structure of a series and makes it possible to identify patterns:

Trend (Trend) : ACF decreasing slowly from high positive values
Seasonality (Seasonality) : ACF with regularly spaced peaks (e.g. every 5 bars for a weekly cycle on daily data)
Short memory : ACF null beyond a low lag
White noise (White Noise) : ACF null at all lags (within statistical limits)





Confidence Intervals on the Correlogram
On a correlogram, confidence intervals (Confidence Intervals) are drawn as dotted lines on either side of zero.

Any bar exceeding these intervals indicates a statistically significant autocorrelation
For a series of length \(n\), the intervals are approximately \(\pm\, 1.96\,/\, \sqrt{n}\) (at 95 % confidence)
In the absence of structure, approximately 5 % of bars may exceed the intervals by chance



Detection of Hidden Patterns
Consider the following process, whose structure is invisible to the naked eye:
\[
X_t = \varepsilon_t + \sin\!\left(2\pi\, \frac{t}{10}\right)
\]
The sinusoidal component of period 10 is masked by the noise \(\varepsilon_t\). The plotted series appears random.
However, the correlogram reveals the hidden structure: significant bars appear at multiples of 10, unambiguously signaling the periodicity.






TipIntuition — The ACF as a Temporal Microscope



The ACF acts as a microscope for the temporal structure of a series. Where the raw plot shows only disorder, the ACF can reveal:

Hidden cycles (regularly spaced peaks)
Persistent dependencies (slow decay)
Regular alternations (positive/negative oscillation)





ACF and Typical Behaviors

Trending Series (Positive Autocorrelation — Trend)
A series with trend exhibits high positive autocorrelations that decrease slowly with lag:

A high value today predicts a high value tomorrow (and the day after, etc.)
The “memory” of the series is long

Financial implication: this type of structure lends itself to momentum strategies (buy assets that have recently performed well).


Counter-Trend Series (Negative Autocorrelation — Counter-trend)
A counter-trend series exhibits a significantly negative autocorrelation at lag 1:

A high value today predicts a low value tomorrow
The series alternates regularly around its mean (mean-reversion)

Financial implication: this type of structure lends itself to mean-reversion strategies (buy after a fall, sell after a rise).

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Autoregressive Models (Autoregressive Models)
The ACF indicates how past events influence the present. We formalize this relationship in three major families of models.

AR(p) Model — AutoRegressive of order p
\[
X_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \varphi_i\, X_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t
\]
Parameters:

\(c\) : constant (intercept)
\(\varphi_i\) : autoregressive coefficients (AR Coefficients)
\(p\) : model order (number of lags used)
\(\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)\) : white noise (White Noise), independent of the past

The AR(p) model expresses the current value as a linear combination of its \(p\) past values, plus a random shock.






TipIntuition — AR(p)



The AR(p) model is analogous to an individual who predicts their mood of the day based on their \(p\) most recent moods, plus an unpredictable part. If \(p = 1\), only yesterday counts; if \(p = 5\), the whole week counts.




MA(q) Model — Moving Average of order q (Moving Average)
\[
X_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\,\varepsilon_{t-1} + \cdots + \theta_q\,\varepsilon_{t-q}
\]
Parameters:

\(\mu\) : series mean
\(\theta_i\) : moving average coefficients (MA Coefficients)
\(q\) : model order
\(\varepsilon_{t-i}\) : past shocks (errors)

The MA(q) model expresses the current value as a linear combination of the \(q\) past errors.






TipIntuition — AR vs MA




AR(p) : “My current state depends on my \(p\) past states.” The series remembers its values.
MA(q) : “My current state depends on the \(q\) unexpected shocks I received.” The series remembers its errors, not its levels. A shock received more than \(q\) periods ago no longer has any influence.





ARMA(p,q) Model — AutoRegressive Moving Average
\[
X_t = c + \varepsilon_t + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \varphi_i\, X_{t-i} + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \theta_i\, \varepsilon_{t-i}
\]
The ARMA(p,q) model combines the two approaches: the current value depends both on past values (AR component) and past errors (MA component). It offers more flexibility with a potentially lower number of parameters than an AR or MA alone of the same order.






NoteKey Takeaway — Orders and Estimation




The integers \(p\) and \(q\) are the orders of the model
For AR(1), the parameter \(\varphi_1\) admits an analytical formula — see next section
For AR(p) with \(p > 1\), the parameters must be estimated numerically by maximum likelihood (Maximum Likelihood Estimation, MLE)
The choice of optimal orders relies on information criteria (AIC, BIC)

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
The AR(1) Model in Detail
This course focuses on the AR(1) model because it is the simplest in the family and admits analytical results (closed-form formulas), making it a first-rate pedagogical tool.

Definition of the AR(1) Model
For \(p = 1\), the AR(1) model is:
\[
X_t = c + \varphi_1\, X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t
\]
with \(\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)\) independent of \(X_{t-1}\).


Calculation of the Mean
Assuming stationarity, the mean is constant over time: \(\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mathbb{E}[X_{t-1}] = \mu\).
Taking the expectation of both sides of the model:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mathbb{E}[c] + \varphi_1\,\mathbb{E}[X_{t-1}] + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_t]
\]
\[
\mu = c + \varphi_1\,\mu + 0
\]
Solving for \(\mu\):
\[
\mu = \frac{c}{1 - \varphi_1}
\]
Practical normalization: by centering the series (\(X_t \leftarrow X_t - \mu\)), we can set \(c = 0\) and thus \(\mu = 0\) without loss of generality. This simplifies the following calculations.


Calculation of the Variance
Stationarity implies that the variance is constant: \(\text{Var}[X_t] = \text{Var}[X_{t-1}]\).
Calculating the variance of the model (with \(c = 0\)):
\[
\text{Var}[X_t] = \text{Var}[\varphi_1\, X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t]
\]
Since \(X_{t-1}\) and \(\varepsilon_t\) are independent, the variances add:
\[
\text{Var}[X_t] = \varphi_1^2\,\text{Var}[X_{t-1}] + \sigma_\varepsilon^2
\]
Using \(\text{Var}[X_t] = \text{Var}[X_{t-1}]\):
\[
\text{Var}[X_t] = \varphi_1^2\,\text{Var}[X_t] + \sigma_\varepsilon^2
\implies \text{Var}[X_t]\,(1 - \varphi_1^2) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2
\]
\[
\text{Var}[X_t] = \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{1 - \varphi_1^2}
\]






WarningStationarity Condition



For the variance to be strictly positive (\(\text{Var}[X_t] > 0\)), we need \(1 - \varphi_1^2 > 0\), i.e.:
\[
|\varphi_1| < 1
\]
This is the stationarity condition of the AR(1) model. If \(\varphi_1 = 1\), we obtain a random walk (Random Walk), a non-stationary process with infinite variance. If \(|\varphi_1| > 1\), the process explodes.




Calculation of Autocorrelation at Lag 1
With \(\mu = 0\), the autocovariance at lag 1 is:
\[
\gamma_1 = \text{Cov}(X_t,\, X_{t+1}) = \mathbb{E}[X_t\, X_{t+1}]
\]
Substituting \(X_{t+1} = \varphi_1\, X_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}\):
\[
\gamma_1 = \mathbb{E}\bigl[X_t\,(\varphi_1\, X_t + \varepsilon_{t+1})\bigr] = \varphi_1\,\mathbb{E}[X_t^2] + \mathbb{E}[X_t\,\varepsilon_{t+1}]
\]
Since \(\varepsilon_{t+1}\) is independent of \(X_t\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t+1}] = 0\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t\,\varepsilon_{t+1}] = \mathbb{E}[X_t] \cdot \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{t+1}] = 0 \cdot 0 = 0
\]
And since \(\mu = 0\), we have \(\mathbb{E}[X_t^2] = \text{Var}[X_t]\). Therefore:
\[
\gamma_1 = \varphi_1\,\text{Var}[X_t]
\]
The autocorrelation at lag 1 is:
\[
\rho_1 = \frac{\text{Cov}(X_t,\, X_{t+1})}{\text{Var}(X_t)} = \varphi_1
\]






NoteKey Takeaway — Fundamental Result of AR(1)



In an AR(1) model, the parameter \(\varphi_1\) is exactly the autocorrelation at lag 1:
\[
\varphi_1 = \rho_1
\]
This considerably simplifies estimation: it suffices to compute the empirical autocorrelation at lag 1 on the data to directly obtain the estimator of \(\varphi_1\). No numerical optimization needed.




Summary of Analytical Properties of AR(1)



Property
Formula




Mean
\(\mu = c\, /\, (1 - \varphi_1)\)


Variance
\(\sigma^2 = \sigma_\varepsilon^2\, /\, (1 - \varphi_1^2)\)


Autocorrelation lag 1
\(\rho_1 = \varphi_1\)


Stationarity condition
\(|\varphi_1| < 1\)





Interpretation of Parameter \(\varphi_1\)
The sign and magnitude of \(\varphi_1\) determine the qualitative behavior of the series:

\(\varphi_1 > 0\) — trending behavior (Trending) : a high value today predicts a high value tomorrow. The closer \(\varphi_1\) is to 1, the longer the memory and the more persistent the series.
\(\varphi_1 < 0\) — mean-reverting behavior (Mean-reverting) : a high value today predicts a low value tomorrow. The series alternates regularly around its mean.
\(\varphi_1 = 0\) — the series is white noise (White Noise) : no memory, the past does not inform about the future.
\(\varphi_1 \to 1\) — the series tends towards a random walk : infinite memory, non-stationary process.







TipIntuition — Memory of the AR(1) Process



The smaller \(|\varphi_1|\) is (close to 0), the faster the series “forgets” its past. For example:

\(\varphi_1 = 0.9\) : a shock takes approximately \(\ln(0.05)\,/\,\ln(0.9) \approx 28\) periods to dissipate (reduction to 5 %)
\(\varphi_1 = 0.1\) : the same shock dissipates in just 1 to 2 periods

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
section: Applications and Examples of the AR(1) Model
text:
Applications and Examples of the AR(1) Model

Example 1 — The Random Walk (Random Walk)
Consider the process:
\[
X_t = X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1)
\]
This is an AR(1) with \(\varphi_1 = 1\) — a limit case that is non-stationary.
Observed characteristics:

The ACF shows very high positive autocorrelations at all lags (quasi-null decay)
The estimated coefficient is close to 1 (≈ 0.999)
The in-sample fitting is quasi-perfect (error ≈ 0.999)







WarningPitfall of the Random Walk — In-sample vs Out-of-sample



Despite an excellent in-sample fit, out-of-sample prediction is disastrous. The model predicts a straight line (last known level + possible drift), while the series continues to evolve randomly in a totally unpredictable manner.
A good in-sample fit does not guarantee good predictive power.




Example 2 — EUR/USD Returns (January–March 2012)
For daily EUR/USD returns over this period:

The ACF shows very low autocorrelations at all lags, most within confidence intervals
The estimated coefficient is \(\varphi_1 = -0.125\), fitting error = 0.017
The fit is poor : no significant autoregressive structure is detected







TipIntuition — Efficient Market Hypothesis (Efficient Market Hypothesis)



The quasi-total absence of autocorrelation on EUR/USD returns is consistent with the efficient market hypothesis: prices instantly incorporate all available information, making future returns quasi-unpredictable. An AR(1) model cannot capture what markets have already integrated.




Example 3 — VIX Returns (Negative Autocorrelation)
The VIX is the implied volatility index of the S&P 500, nicknamed the “fear index”.
Observations over the period January 2010 – September 2013:

The raw VIX series is non-stationary (visible trend and volatility clusters)
The daily returns of the VIX exhibit significant negative autocorrelations at lag 1







TipIntuition — Mean-Reversion of the VIX



The VIX is intrinsically mean-reverting: after a strong rise (market panic), it tends naturally to fall back towards its historical average. A day of strong VIX rise is often followed by a fall, producing a negative autocorrelation. An AR(1) model with \(\varphi_1 < 0\) captures this behavior.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Beyond the AR(1) Model

Estimation of Higher-Order Models
For \(p > 1\), the coefficients \(\varphi_1,\, \ldots,\, \varphi_p\) have no closed-form analytical formula. They must be estimated numerically, typically by the maximum likelihood method (Maximum Likelihood Estimation, MLE).


Selection of the Optimal Order
Order selection is a key issue: an order that is too low underfits the data, an order that is too high overfits (overfitting). We use information criteria (Information Criteria) that penalize complexity.

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC — Akaike Information Criterion)
\[
\text{AIC} = 2p - 2\ln(L)
\]


Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC — Bayesian Information Criterion)
\[
\text{BIC} = \ln(n) \cdot p - 2\ln(L)
\]
Notation:

\(p\) : number of estimated parameters
\(L\) : maximized value of the likelihood (Maximized Likelihood)
\(n\) : number of observations







NoteKey Takeaway — AIC / BIC Principle



Both criteria seek a balance between two antagonistic objectives:

Goodness of fit is rewarded via the term \(+2\ln(L)\) : the better the model fits the data, the larger \(L\) is and the lower the criterion (better)
Complexity is penalized via the number of parameters \(p\) : adding an unnecessary parameter increases the criterion

We seek the model that minimizes AIC or BIC.








TipIntuition — AIC vs BIC




AIC : penalizes complexity by factor \(2\) — more tolerant, it favors slightly richer models
BIC : penalizes by \(\ln(n)\) — more severe, it favors more parsimonious models. For \(n > 8\), we have \(\ln(n) > 2\), so BIC penalizes each additional parameter more heavily

In practice, BIC often identifies the “true” order of the generating process more precisely, while AIC may select a slightly too high order.





Application Examples

S&P 500 (November 2023 – September 2024)

S&P 500 returns exhibit low autocorrelation, difficult to distinguish from statistical noise
An AR(3) model is fitted: it captures the general trend but not daily fluctuations
AIC continues to decrease with order (favors higher orders)
BIC stabilizes quickly and recommends a low order
Conclusion: little exploitable autoregressive structure in S&P 500 daily returns



Swiss Quarterly GDP (CH GDP)

Quarterly data are less numerous but exhibit more marked autocorrelation
The quarterly frequency introduces natural persistence: one quarter’s growth is linked to the next’s
The AR model captures the structure better, with a visible quality of fit on the fitted values plot



Artificial Process — \(X_t = -0.5\,X_{t-1} + 0.5\,X_{t-3} + \varepsilon\)
This example is particularly instructive because the true generating process is known. It is an AR(3) with:
\[
\varphi_1 = -0.5, \quad \varphi_2 = 0, \quad \varphi_3 = 0.5
\]
Observations:

The ACF shows significant autocorrelations at lags 1 and 3 (as expected from the true structure)
BIC correctly identifies order 3 as optimal (minimum BIC at \(p = 3\))
AIC continues to decrease slightly beyond, illustrating its tendency to overestimate the order
The fitted AR(3) model faithfully reproduces the main fluctuations of the series







TipIntuition — Validation by Known Process



When the true generating process is known, we can verify that the information criteria recover the correct order. This is an ideal consistency test. On real data, there is no “true” order, but AIC and BIC guide towards the best bias-variance compromise available in the data.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models
text:
Key Takeaways






NoteChapter Summary



Time Series (Time Series):

A time series describes the evolution of a variable over time
The lag \(\tau\) is the offset between two observations — temporal order carries information

Stationarity (Stationarity):

Prerequisite for any autoregressive modeling
In practice, we work on returns rather than raw prices
Formal test: ADF (p-value < 0.05 → stationary)

Autocorrelation — ACF (Autocorrelation Function):

Measures the correlation of the series with itself at different lags
Positive ACF → trend ; Negative ACF → counter-trend (mean-reversion)
The ACF reveals hidden patterns and guides model choice

Autoregressive Models:

\(\text{AR}(p)\) : \(X_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^p \varphi_i X_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t\)
\(\text{MA}(q)\) : \(X_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \sum_{i=1}^q \theta_i \varepsilon_{t-i}\)
\(\text{ARMA}(p,q)\) : combination of the two

AR(1) Model — analytical results:

Single parameter: \(\varphi_1 = \rho_1\) (autocorrelation at lag 1)
Variance: \(\text{Var}[X_t] = \sigma_\varepsilon^2\, /\, (1 - \varphi_1^2)\)
Stationarity condition: \(|\varphi_1| < 1\)
\(\varphi_1 > 0\) → trend ; \(\varphi_1 < 0\) → mean-reversion

Order Selection:

AR(p) with \(p > 1\) : numerical estimation by MLE
AIC and BIC (minimize) — BIC more parsimonious than AIC for large samples
A good in-sample fit does not imply good out-of-sample predictive power

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Oral Review
text: Imagine a doctor tracking a patient’s blood pressure every day. To establish a valid diagnosis, the patient must be in a stable state — this is stationarity. He can then ask: “Does high blood pressure yesterday predict high blood pressure tomorrow?” → trending (\(\varphi_1 > 0\)). Or: “Does it predict a return to normal?” → mean-reversion (\(\varphi_1 < 0\)). The ACF measures this memory. The AR(1) model formalizes it in a single equation. If the patient takes a drug (external shock) whose effect dissipates in \(q\) days — this is the MA component.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Oral Review
text: Imagine a doctor tracking a patient’s blood pressure every day. To establish a valid diagnosis, the patient must be in a stable state — this is stationarity. He can then ask: “Does high blood pressure yesterday predict high blood pressure tomorrow?” → trending (\(\varphi_1 > 0\)). Or: “Does it predict a return to normal?” → mean-reversion (\(\varphi_1 < 0\)). The ACF measures this memory. The AR(1) model formalizes it in a single equation. If the patient takes a drug (external shock) whose effect dissipates in \(q\) days — this is the MA component.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

A time series exploits the order of observations: the past informs the present
Absolute prerequisite: stationarity — otherwise estimated parameters are meaningless
The ACF reveals hidden structure (trend, seasonality, mean-reversion)
AR(p): \(X_t\) is explained by its \(p\) past values + noise
Key AR(1) result: \(\varphi_1 = \rho_1\) — the parameter is the lag-1 autocorrelation
For \(p > 1\): numerical estimation, order selection by AIC / BIC

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Prices ≠ stationary — systematically transform to returns before modeling
ADF test inverted: p-value > 0.05 = not stationary (reading trap)
\(\lvert\varphi_1\rvert \geq 1\) → non-stationary (\(= 1\): random walk) or explosive (\(> 1\))
Good in-sample fit ≠ good prediction — random walk: perfect fit, null prediction
AIC vs BIC: BIC penalizes more (\(\ln n > 2\) if \(n > 8\)) → lower orders selected
Strict stationarity ≠ weak: weak suffices in practice, strict is rarely verifiable

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: Why do we need stationarity?
Short answer: So that estimated parameters remain valid over time and to avoid spurious correlations between series with no real relationship.

Q: What is the difference between strict and weak stationarity?
Short answer: Strict requires invariance of the entire joint distribution; weak only requires a constant mean and autocovariance function of lag only.

Q: Why are prices not stationary but returns are?
Short answer: Prices drift upward — their mean and variance change over time. Returns oscillate around zero without systematic drift.

Q: How do you interpret \(\varphi_1\) in an AR(1)?
Short answer: It is the lag-1 autocorrelation. Positive → trend, negative → mean-reversion, zero → white noise. Its absolute value must be strictly less than 1.

Q: What is the ACF for and how do you use it?
Short answer: It measures the series’ memory at each lag. Significant bars (outside confidence intervals) indicate relevant lags and guide model choice.

Q: What is the difference between AR and MA?
Short answer: AR depends on past values (infinite memory if \(\lvert\varphi\rvert < 1\)); MA depends on past errors (finite memory, exactly \(q\) periods).

Q: How do you choose the order \(p\) of an AR?
Short answer: Minimize AIC or BIC which penalize adding useless parameters. BIC is more parsimonious and often recovers the true order.

text:
This chapter addresses three fundamental themes in computational finance:

Intrinsic Time: an alternative framework to physical time, with its scaling laws
