title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time
text:
Data in Real Life

What We Imagine
When we think of a financial time series, we often picture an ideal mathematical object, characterized by three properties:

Equidistant : observations arrive at regular and predictable time intervals.
Smooth : prices evolve continuously, without noise or parasitic fluctuations.
Continuous : there are no abrupt jumps between two consecutive instants.

This vision corresponds to that of a clean signal, as one might produce in a theoretical framework or in simulation.






TipIntuition



Imagine a price chart drawn with a ruler, with a perfectly regular curve rising or falling gently. This is the ideal image — and rarely the reality of markets.





What We Actually Observe
In practice, high-frequency financial data present very different characteristics from this ideal model.

Bid/Ask/Mid Structure
Market data are not simply a single price: they consist of three distinct components:

Ask Price : the price at which a seller is willing to part with an asset.
Bid Price : the price at which a buyer is willing to acquire that asset.
Mid Price : the average between bid and ask, often used as an approximation of the “true” price.







NoteKey Takeaway



The difference between the ask price and the bid price is called the bid-ask spread. This spread is a direct measure of market liquidity: the tighter it is, the more liquid the market.




Three Key Characteristics of Real Data
Observations on real high-frequency data reveal the following properties:
1. Non time-equidistant activity (Non time-equidistant activity)
Transactions do not arrive at regular intervals. Activity is intense during market opening hours (for example at the opening of New York or London), and very low at night or on weekends.
2. Noisy behaviour (Noisy behaviour)
Prices oscillate continuously around a trend, generating a very noisy signal. This noise reflects market microstructures (buy and sell orders, market making, etc.).
3. Possibly non-continuous prices (Possibly non-continuous prices)
Price jumps can occur during major events (macroeconomic announcements, earnings releases, crises). The price may therefore not be continuous over certain time ranges.






TipIntuition



Unlike an evening course presented in a textbook, real data more closely resemble an electrocardiogram: irregular, sometimes silent, sometimes very agitated, and subject to discontinuities.






How to Handle Imperfect Data?
Faced with these characteristics, two major approaches exist for working with raw market data.

Approach 1 : Discretisation (Discretisation)
This is the approach used in 99.9 % of cases in practice.
We choose a fixed time grid (for example, every minute, hour, or day) and associate to each instant the last price observed before that instant.
Advantage: Simple, efficient, universally adopted.
Disadvantages:

Information between two consecutive ticks is lost (tick = arrival of a data point).
Intra-period trends go unnoticed.
The observed price is instantaneous : it represents only a frozen instant, not a behavior.







WarningImportant Point



Discretisation is convenient but induces a loss of information. In a high-frequency context, this loss can be significant if the time grid is too coarse.




Approach 2 : Interpolation (Interpolation)
Less frequent, this approach consists in reconstructing values between observed ticks using an interpolation method (linear, spline, etc.).
Advantage: Makes it possible to use past information to infer new values.
Disadvantages:

Strong assumptions are necessary about the shape of the signal between two observations.
Physical time remains the reference framework, which may seem arbitrary (why start at midnight? at 5 PM?).
Alternative approaches can be envisaged (see the section on intrinsic time).

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time
text:
Moving Averages
Whether discretized or not, financial time series are often noisy. To extract the underlying trend, we use smoothing operators, of which moving averages are the most widespread.






NoteKey Takeaway



A moving average transforms a noisy series into a more regular series, by aggregating past observations. It always introduces a time lag : the smoothed value reflects the past, not the present instant.




Simple Moving Average — SMA (Simple Moving Average)

Definition
Let \(X_t\) be a time series. The Simple Moving Average over a window of size \(n\) is defined by:
\[
SMA(t) = \frac{X_{t-n+1} + X_{t-n+2} + \cdots + X_t}{n}
\]
Each observation in the window receives an identical weight of \(\frac{1}{n}\).


Incremental Update
A crucial property for computational efficiency is the update formula:
\[
SMA(t+1) = SMA(t) - \frac{X_{t-n+1}}{n} + \frac{X_{t+1}}{n}
\]
This means that at each time step, we remove the oldest observation and add the most recent observation.






WarningImportant Point



To calculate and update the SMA, it is necessary to keep in memory the \(n\) most recent observations. If \(n\) is large, this can represent a non-negligible memory cost.




Main Limitations of the SMA
The SMA presents two major flaws:
1. Uniform weight regardless of age
An observation \(n\) periods old has exactly the same weight (\(\frac{1}{n}\)) as an observation from the previous period. Yet, intuitively, recent information is often more relevant than old information.
2. Time lag (Time Lag)
The SMA “lags” behind the original series. The larger the window \(n\), the more important this lag is. This lag is irreducible : the more we smooth, the more we delay.






TipIntuition



Imagine that you calculate the average temperature over the last 100 days. This average will react only slowly to a brutal temperature change today — you have to wait for the previous 99 days to “exit” the window.




Illustration of Time Lag
The lag is all the more visible graphically as it creates a systematic “delay”: the SMA curve follows the original trend with a certain delay, and this delay increases with \(n\).





%%{init: {"theme": "default"}}%%
graph LR
    A[Original series X_t] --> B[SMA with small window\nLittle smoothing\nShort lag]
    A --> C[SMA with large window\nStrong smoothing\nLong lag]










Weighted Moving Average — WMA (Weighted Moving Average)

Motivation
To remedy the uniformity flaw of the SMA, we can assign decreasing weights to past observations: the older an observation, the lower its weight.


Definition
The Weighted Moving Average over a window of size \(n\) is defined by:
\[
WMA(t) = \frac{1 \cdot X_{t-n+1} + 2 \cdot X_{t-n+2} + \cdots + (n-1) \cdot X_{t-1} + n \cdot X_t}{n + (n-1) + \cdots + 2 + 1}
\]
The denominator is \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\) (sum of integers from 1 to \(n\)).
The most recent observation \(X_t\) receives a weight of \(n\), while the oldest \(X_{t-n+1}\) receives a weight of 1.


Incremental Update
The update of the WMA is more complex. We first define an auxiliary quantity:
\[
Total(t) = X_{t-n+1} + X_{t-n+2} + \cdots + X_{t-1} + X_t
\]
Its update is:
\[
Total(t+1) = Total(t) - X_{t-n+1} + X_{t+1}
\]
Then the WMA updates as:
\[
WMA(t+1) = \frac{(1 \cdot X_{t-n+1} + \cdots + n \cdot X_t) + n \cdot X_{t+1} - Total(t)}{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}
\]






WarningImportant Point



The update of the WMA is more costly than that of the SMA, both in terms of computation and memory (the \(n\) most recent observations must still be stored). This overhead is the price to pay for a more relevant weighting scheme.




Weighting Scheme: SMA vs WMA









Indicator
Weight of the oldest
Weight of the most recent
Shape




SMA
\(\frac{1}{n}\)
\(\frac{1}{n}\)
Uniform


WMA
\(\frac{2}{n(n+1)}\)
\(\frac{2}{n+1}\)
Linearly decreasing towards the past









TipIntuition



In the WMA, weights decrease linearly: the last observation weighs \(n\) times more than the oldest. It’s as if we give more credit to what happened recently.






Exponential Moving Average — EMA (Exponential Moving Average)

Motivation
The WMA improves the SMA but remains heavy to compute. The Exponential Moving Average offers a decreasing weighting scheme — even more “natural” than that of the WMA — with an extremely simple update using a single parameter.


Formal Derivation
We first define the general form of the EMA:
\[
EMA(t) = \frac{X_t + (1-\alpha) X_{t-1} + (1-\alpha)^2 X_{t-2} + \cdots}{1 + (1-\alpha) + (1-\alpha)^2 + \cdots}
\]
The geometric series in the denominator converges (for \(0 < \alpha < 1\)):
\[
1 + (1-\alpha) + (1-\alpha)^2 + \cdots = \frac{1}{\alpha}
\]
We can then rewrite:
\[
EMA(t) = \frac{X_t}{1/\alpha} + (1-\alpha) \cdot \frac{X_{t-1} + (1-\alpha) X_{t-2} + \cdots}{1 + (1-\alpha) + \cdots}
\]
The second term is exactly \(\alpha \cdot (1-\alpha) \cdot \frac{1}{\alpha} \cdot EMA(t-1) = (1-\alpha) \cdot EMA(t-1)\).
We obtain the fundamental recursive formula:
\[
\boxed{EMA(t) = \alpha \cdot X_t + (1-\alpha) \cdot EMA(t-1)}
\]


Interpretation of the Recursive Formula
This formula is remarkably simple:

\(\alpha\) : weight given to the current observation
\(1-\alpha\) : weight given to the previous EMA (which already contains all past history)







TipIntuition



The EMA is a weighted average between the present and the summarized past. At each instant, we “forget” a bit of the past (factor \(1-\alpha\)) and integrate the novelty (factor \(\alpha\)). It is analogous to how our memory works: recent events have more impact than old ones.








NoteKey Takeaway



Unlike the SMA and WMA, the EMA does not need to store the \(n\) most recent observations. It suffices to know the previous value of the EMA. This is its major computational advantage.




Weighting Scheme of the EMA
The weights of past observations in the EMA decrease exponentially:

Observation at \(t\) : weight \(\alpha\)
Observation at \(t-1\) : weight \(\alpha(1-\alpha)\)
Observation at \(t-k\) : weight \(\alpha(1-\alpha)^k\)

The smaller \(\alpha\) is, the slower the decay, and the more past observations retain influence.




Comparison of Weighting Schemes



Indicator
Scheme shape
Memory required
Update




SMA
Uniform
\(n\) observations
Simple


WMA
Linearly decreasing
\(n\) observations
Moderately complex


EMA
Exponentially decreasing
1 scalar value
Very simple









TipIntuition



The EMA is the ideal compromise: it weights observations in a decreasing manner (like the WMA), but is as simple to calculate as a scalar update. This is why it is by far the most used in practice.





Initial Conditions of Moving Averages
Any moving average must be initialized before it can produce values.

For SMA and WMA
We need \(n\) observations to calculate the first value. During the first \(n\) instants, the moving average is not defined.


For EMA
Several initialization strategies exist:
Option 1 — Initialization to the first observation:
\[
EMA(1) = X_1 \quad \text{(equivalent to } EMA(0) = 0 \text{)}
\]
Option 2 — Initialization by an SMA:
\[
EMA(n) = SMA(n)
\]
We first calculate an SMA over the first \(n\) points, then launch the EMA recursion from there.






WarningImportant Point



Whatever the initialization method, the EMA needs a warm-up period to stabilize. The first calculated values may be poorly representative. It is common to wait a few multiples of \(1/\alpha\) observations before using the values.








NoteKey Takeaway



The general rule is as follows: the larger \(n\) is, and the smaller \(\alpha\) is, the longer the time lag. This trade-off between smoothing and reactivity is at the heart of parameter choice.






Choice of EMA Parameter \(\alpha\)

Method 1 : Equivalence with an SMA of size \(n\)
We seek \(\alpha\) such that the average age of observations in the EMA is equal to that in an SMA of window \(n\).
The average age in an SMA of size \(n\) is \(\frac{n+1}{2}\).
The average age in an EMA is \(\frac{1}{\alpha}\).
By equating the two:
\[
\frac{1}{\alpha} = \frac{n(n+1)/2}{n} = \frac{n+1}{2}
\]
Which gives the classic formula:
\[
\boxed{\alpha = \frac{2}{n+1}}
\]






WarningImportant Point



Attention: with \(\alpha = \frac{2}{n+1}\), the EMA and the SMA have the same average age, but their values are not identical. They behave similarly but do not coincide.




Method 2 : Definition via the residual impact of an observation
We can define \(\alpha\) by imposing that an observation \(k\) instants old has a residual impact of \(\epsilon_k\):
\[
(1-\alpha)^k = \epsilon_k
\]
Taking the logarithm:
\[
\log(1-\alpha) = \frac{\log(\epsilon_k)}{k}
\implies
\alpha = 1 - e^{\frac{\log(\epsilon_k)}{k}}
\]
Numerical examples:

For \(k = 100\) and \(\epsilon_k = 1\%\) : \(\alpha \approx 0.045\)
For \(n = 100\) (method 1) : \(\alpha = \frac{2}{101} \approx 0.0198\)







TipIntuition



Method 2 is more intuitive: we ask “how much influence should an observation 100 periods old have?” If we want it to have only 1% impact, we calculate \(\alpha\) accordingly. This allows fine-tuning according to the economic context.






Graphical Example: Comparison of EMAs
The comparison graph illustrates the behavior of several EMAs on the same series:

\(\alpha = 0.1\) (large) : reactive, closely follows the series, little smoothing, short lag.
\(\alpha = 0.01\) (small) : very smooth, long lag — the curve reacts slowly to trend changes.
\(\alpha = \frac{2}{101}\) and \(SMA(100)\) : similar but non-identical behaviors, illustrating the approximate equivalence of the two methods.







NoteKey Takeaway



There is no universal “good” \(\alpha\). The choice depends on the desired trade-off between reactivity (high \(\alpha\)) and smoothing (low \(\alpha\)), according to the trading horizon and market characteristics.





Extension to Asynchronous Data

Problem
Until now, moving averages implicitly assume that data arrive at regular intervals. But on high-frequency markets, ticks arrive irregularly: activity varies strongly according to the hours.


Solution: EMA Adapted to Continuous Time
According to the book Introduction to High Frequency Finance [1], a basic operator is defined as follows.
Given two consecutive observations arriving at times \(t_{n-1}\) and \(t_n\), we define:
\[
\alpha = \frac{t_n - t_{n-1}}{\tau}, \quad \mu = e^{-\alpha}, \quad \nu = \frac{1-\mu}{\alpha}
\]
with \(\tau\) a characteristic time parameter.
The EMA adapted to continuous time is then:
\[
EMA(\tau; x)(t_n) = \mu \cdot EMA(\tau; x)(t_{n-1}) + (\nu - \mu) \cdot x_{n-1} + (1 - \nu) \cdot x_n
\]


Interpretation of Parameters







Symbol
Role




\(\mu = e^{-\alpha}\)
Forgetting factor depending on elapsed time


\(\nu\)
Interpolation parameter between the previous and current observation


\(x_{n-1}\)
Last observation


\(x_n\)
Current observation









TipIntuition



The introduction of \(\mu = e^{-\alpha}\) is key: if a lot of time has elapsed since the last observation (\(\alpha\) large), \(\mu\) is close to 0, and the EMA “forgets” the past quickly. If little time has elapsed (\(\alpha\) small), \(\mu \approx 1\) and memory is long. Time is thus naturally integrated into the operator.




Iterative EMA and Generalized SMA
From this basic operator, more sophisticated operators can be constructed.
Iterative EMA:
\[
EMA(\tau, n; x) = EMA(\tau; EMA[\tau, n-1; x])
\]
with \(EMA(\tau, 1; x) = EMA(\tau; x)\).
Generalized SMA on asynchronous data:
\[
SMA(\tau, n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} EMA\left[\tau'; k\right], \quad \text{with } \tau' = \frac{2\tau}{n+1}
\]
These operators make it possible to treat irregular market data with the same rigor as classical operators.

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time
text:
Intrinsic Time

Limits of Physical Time
Physical time — the watch that runs at constant speed — is the usual reference framework for time series analysis.
Yet, several observations invite us to question it:

Subjective time accelerates and slows down : in our daily experience, time seems to slow down during sleep and accelerate during important events.
Important events can go unnoticed between two observations, if the interval is too long.
The starting point is arbitrary : why start at midnight? At 5 PM?
Physical time is rigid : it flows at constant speed, independently of market activity.







TipIntuition



During a weekend, foreign exchange markets (Forex) are closed. Physical time flows, but no market event takes place. Counting these hours as “market time” makes no economic sense.




Alternatives to Physical Time
Several ideas have been explored to define an “adaptive” time:
Volume Time : time advances by one unit each time a certain trading volume is reached.

Advantage : captures real economic activity.
Disadvantage : volumes are only known after the transaction.

Transaction Time : similar to volume time, but counting transactions.

Disadvantage : also known a posteriori.

Price-Based Time : prices are always observable in real time. Why not let the market itself dictate its own rhythm, through price movements?



Definition of Intrinsic Time
Intrinsic time is a measure of time dictated by the occurrence of Directional Change Events.
A directional change (DC) is defined by:

A trend reversal of the price of a minimum amplitude of \(\delta\) (threshold).
After a rise, if the price falls by \(\delta\) in relative value → DC down.
After a fall, if the price rises by \(\delta\) in relative value → DC up.







NoteKey Takeaway



The parameter \(\delta\) controls the temporal resolution : a small \(\delta\) generates many events (“fast” intrinsic time) ; a large \(\delta\) generates few events (“slow” intrinsic time). Time thus becomes adaptive and multiscale.



Fundamental Properties
The intrinsic time framework presents several remarkable properties:

The number of directional changes relative to physical time is linked to market volatility.
Between two directional changes, we observe what is called the overshoot (OS) : the price movement that exceeds the threshold triggering the next DC. The length of the overshoot is linked to market liquidity.
The total price movement between two extrema is:

\[
TM = DC + OS
\]
where TM is the Total Move, DC is the Directional Change and OS is the Overshoot.




Intrinsic Time Algorithm
The directional change detection algorithm is defined with the following elements:

Initial mode : arbitrarily “up” (bullish).
Parameter : \(\delta > 0\), the directional change threshold.
Variable : \(x_{ext}\), the extreme price (maximum or minimum) reached in the current mode.

For each price x in AllTicks :

    If mode = "up" :
        If x < x_ext :
            x_ext = x          // Update local minimum
        Else if (x_ext - x) / x_ext >= δ :
            print("New DC up")    // A DC down is detected
            x_ext = x
            mode = "down"

    Else (mode = "down") :
        If x > x_ext :
            x_ext = x          // Update local maximum
        Else if (x - x_ext) / x_ext >= δ :
            print("New DC down")  // A DC up is detected
            x_ext = x
            mode = "up"






TipIntuition



The algorithm is a local trend detector. In “up” mode, we look for a downward reversal of at least \(\delta\%\). When this reversal is detected, we switch to “down” mode and look for the next upward reversal. Intrinsic time advances by one notch at each detection.








NoteKey Takeaway



Unlike physical time, intrinsic time does not take into account the duration between ticks. Two DCs separated by 1 millisecond and two DCs separated by 1 hour count exactly the same way in intrinsic time.





Scaling Laws

Motivation
Intrinsic time is an alternative framework to physical time. But how to relate the two? How to know, for example, how many seconds a directional change lasts on average for a given threshold \(\delta\)?
Scaling laws answer this question. They establish empirical relationships between quantities measured in intrinsic time and quantities in physical time.


Examples of Scaling Laws
Law 1 — Relationship between price and time:
\[
\langle \Delta x \rangle \sim \Delta t^{\alpha}
\]
The average price variation over an interval \(\Delta t\) follows a power law in \(\Delta t\).
Law 2 — Average duration of a DC as a function of threshold:
\[
\langle \Delta t_{dc} \rangle \sim \left(\frac{\delta}{c}\right)^{\alpha}
\]
The average duration (in physical time) of a directional change of threshold \(\delta\) also follows a power law.






TipIntuition



Scaling laws are the financial analogue of physical universality laws: they show that markets obey robust statistical regularities, independently of the level of detail (\(\delta\)) at which they are observed. These are fractal properties of markets.




Tick-Count Scaling Law
One of the most striking scaling laws is that of the number of ticks : the average number of ticks observed between two consecutive DCs is a power function of the threshold \(\delta\).
This law has been empirically verified on 13 different currency pairs (EUR-USD, GBP-JPY, AUD-USD, etc.) and on data covering several years.
The robustness of these laws on such different markets suggests that they capture a fundamental property of market microstructure.


Overview of Scaling Laws
A systematic study [2] identified 20 distinct scaling laws, covering notably:

Average price move (\(\langle \Delta x \rangle\))
Average quadratic price move (\(\langle \Delta x^2 \rangle\))
Number of directional DCs
Number of total price moves
Average duration of a DC
Duration of an overshoot
Number of ticks in a DC or an OS
Cumulative price move (coastline)

All these indicators follow power laws in \(\delta\), and this, consistently across different currency pairs — including relative to a reference model (Gaussian random walk).






WarningImportant Point



The consistency of these scaling laws across many assets and periods suggests that they are not anecdotal: they reflect a universal structure of high-frequency market data, independent of the currency pair or period observed.

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time
text:
Chapter Key Takeaways

Real Financial Data
Real financial data are composed of bid and ask prices, are generally non-equidistant in time, and exhibit noisy or even discontinuous behavior.


Smoothing Operators
Several operators exist to smooth time series:

SMA : simple but equally weights all observations and induces a lag.
WMA : improves weighting at the cost of heavier computation.
EMA : optimal in practice — exponentially decreasing weighting, scalar update, adjustable parameter \(\alpha\).



Physical Time vs Intrinsic Time
Physical time is the universal standard, but it presents a fundamental limitation: it favors information loss during periods of low activity and treats uniformly instants that are nonetheless very different in terms of market activity.


Intrinsic Time
Intrinsic time is an alternative based on directional price changes:

It is adaptive and guided by the market itself.
It allows analyzing markets at different resolutions via the parameter \(\delta\).
It reveals hidden properties linked to volatility and liquidity.



Scaling Laws
A large number of scaling laws relate intrinsic time to physical time. These laws, empirically robust across many markets, constitute a valuable tool for modeling and understanding high-frequency markets.

Objective : find \(y\) knowing \(B\) (inverse problem, no analytical solution).

\[\text{residual}(y) = B_{\text{observed}} - B_{\text{calculated}}(y)\]

title: Returns and Time Value of Money
text:
Switzerland has implemented a retirement provision system structured around three complementary pillars. This system aims to guarantee the financial security of the elderly while combining collective solidarity, occupational pension provision, and individual savings.






NoteKey Takeaway — Social Impact



The three-pillar system helped reduce the proportion of people over 65 threatened by poverty from 51 % in 1979 to approximately 15 to 20 % today. By way of comparison, this proportion in the working-age population is only 4.3 %.







The first pillar is state pension provision, mandatory for all residents in Switzerland. It is based on solidarity between generations: the working population directly funds retirees.
It comprises three components:

AVS — Old-age and survivors’ insurance: covers risks related to old age and death
IAI — Disability insurance: covers risks of permanent incapacity for work
PC — Complementary benefits: supplement pensions that are insufficient to cover the minimum subsistence level

Primary objective: ensure coverage of the minimum subsistence level.






TipIntuition



The first pillar is a pay-as-you-go system (pay-as-you-go): it is not individual savings, but a collective redistribution mechanism. It guarantees a minimal basic income but does not claim to maintain the pre-retirement standard of living.





The second pillar is occupational pension provision, mandatory for employees exceeding a certain income threshold. It operates on a funded system: contributions are saved and invested.
It is based on two federal laws:

LPP — Federal Law on Occupational Old Age, Survivors’ and Invalidity Pension Provision: governs employment-linked old-age insurance
LAA — Federal Law on Accident Insurance: covers occupational and non-occupational accidents

Primary objective: maintain the customary standard of living in retirement, as a complement to the first pillar.






TipIntuition



Combined, the first and second pillars aim to secure approximately 60 to 70 % of the final salary. The second pillar plays a central role in the financial stability of retirement in Switzerland.





The third pillar is private pension provision, optional, allowing each individual to adapt their retirement savings to their personal needs and objectives.
It is divided into two sub-categories:

3a — Tied pension provision: savings with significant tax advantages, subject to conditions and annual contribution limits
3b — Flexible pension provision: savings without particular constraints, but without specific tax advantages

Primary objective: meet additional needs and personalize retirement planning.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money
text:
Introduction to Returns

What Is a Return?
A return (or yield in English) measures the profit or loss generated by an investment over a given period. Returns are usually expressed as a percentage (%), which makes it possible to compare investments of different amounts or time horizons.






NoteKey Takeaway



Two fundamental questions guide this chapter:

How to calculate a return between two observations?
How to calculate and combine a series of returns over a period?

And a more advanced question: what do continuous returns (logarithmic) mean?




Notation and Conventions
We work with a price time series (price timeseries):

\(P(t)\) denotes the price of an asset at time \(t\)
\(t\) represents equally spaced time steps: daily, weekly, monthly, etc.

Example:
\[P(t) = \{100,\ 100.4,\ 102,\ 101.3,\ 102.8,\ \ldots\}\]
This convention applies uniformly to all types of returns presented in this chapter.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money
text:
Simple Returns

Return over a Single Period
The simple return over one period between \(t-1\) and \(t\) is defined by:
\[R_1(t) = \frac{P(t) - P(t-1)}{P(t-1)}\]
Which can be rewritten equivalently as:
\[R_1(t) = \frac{P(t)}{P(t-1)} - 1\]
Or, in the so-called gross return form:
\[1 + R_1(t) = \frac{P(t)}{P(t-1)}\]






TipIntuition



The simple return measures the relative change in price. By normalizing with the initial price, comparisons become possible between assets of very different values. A gain of 10 CHF on an asset at 100 CHF (+10 %) is more significant than the same gain on an asset at 1 000 CHF (+1 %).



Asymmetry of Simple Returns
Simple returns exhibit a fundamental asymmetry illustrated by the following example:

If \(P(t-1) = 50\) and \(P(t) = 60\): \[R_1(t) = \frac{60}{50} - 1 = +20\%\]
If \(P(t-1) = 60\) and \(P(t) = 50\): \[R_1(t) = \frac{50}{60} - 1 \approx -16.7\%\]







WarningAsymmetry — Important Point



A rise of +20 % is not offset by a fall of −20 %. To return to the initial price after a rise of 20 %, a fall of \(1 - 1/1.2 \approx 16.7\%\) would be needed. This asymmetry is a structural property of simple returns, corrected by logarithmic returns.





Return over Multiple Periods
To calculate the simple return over two periods (from \(t-2\) to \(t\)):
\[R_2(t) = \frac{P(t) - P(t-2)}{P(t-2)} = \frac{P(t)}{P(t-2)} - 1\]
By decomposing the price ratio:
\[R_2(t) = \frac{P(t)}{P(t-1)} \cdot \frac{P(t-1)}{P(t-2)} - 1\]
We obtain the fundamental compounding relation:
\[1 + R_2(t) = \bigl(1 + R_1(t)\bigr) \cdot \bigl(1 + R_1(t-1)\bigr)\]

Generalization to \(n\) Periods
For \(n\) consecutive periods, the return is calculated by a product:
\[1 + R_n(t) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl(1 + R_1(t-i)\bigr)\]






ImportantGolden Rule — Do Not Sum Simple Returns



We do not sum simple returns over multiple periods. We compound them by multiplication. The sum of individual returns constitutes an acceptable approximation only for very small returns. For rigorous calculations, the multiplicative formula is mandatory.





Complete Numerical Example
Suppose the following price evolution for a given asset:

The total return from \(t=1\) to \(t=4\) is:
\[R_4(4) = \frac{16 - 10}{10} = 60\%\]
Verification by summation (incorrect method):
\[20\% + 16.7\% + 14.3\% = 50.9\% \neq 60\%\]
Verification by product (correct method):
\[(1 + 20\%) \times (1 + 16.7\%) \times (1 + 14.3\%) - 1 = 60\% \checkmark\]






TipIntuition — Compound Interest



The difference between 50.9 % and 60 % illustrates the effect of compound interest (compounding): at each period, the return is applied to capital already appreciated by previous periods. The higher the returns and the longer the period, the more significant this gap becomes.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money
text:
Portfolio Returns

Definition of a Portfolio
A portfolio (portfolio) is a collection of \(n\) assets. Each asset \(i\) is characterized by:

an individual return \(R_i\)
an allocation (or weight) \(\alpha_i\) representing the fraction of capital invested in that asset

The normalization constraint requires that the allocations sum to 1:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i = 1\]
This constraint means that the entire capital is allocated (no leverage, no unaccounted residual liquidity).


Portfolio Return
The portfolio return is defined as the weighted average of individual returns:
\[R_p = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i R_i\]

Consistency Check
We verify that this definition is consistent by developing the final value of the portfolio:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i (1 + R_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i R_i = 1 + R_p\]
This result confirms that the portfolio return, defined as a linear combination of individual returns, is indeed consistent with the economic definition of portfolio value.






TipIntuition — Concrete Example



A portfolio composed of 60 % equities (return 10 %) and 40 % bonds (return 3 %) generates:
\[R_p = 0.60 \times 10\% + 0.40 \times 3\% = 7.2\%\]
The weighting directly reflects the share of capital allocated to each asset.








NoteKey Takeaway — Limitation over Multiple Periods



The portfolio return formula \(R_p = \sum \alpha_i R_i\) is valid for a single period. For multi-period returns (simple), compounding is no longer linear. This additivity property is, however, preserved for continuous returns, as we shall see.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money
text:
Annualization of Returns

Why Annualize?
Annualization makes it possible to compare returns measured over different horizons by bringing them back to a common annual basis. Without this standardization, it is impossible to compare a monthly fund to a daily fund.


Annualization Formulas
Let the following notation be:

\(R_a\) : annual return (annual return)
\(R_m\) : monthly return (monthly return)
\(R_d\) : daily return (daily return)

Applying the compounding formula over 12 months:
\[1 + R_a = \bigl(1 + R_m\bigr)^{12}\]
\[R_a = \bigl(1 + R_m\bigr)^{12} - 1\]
For daily returns, assuming 256 business days per year:
\[R_a = \bigl(1 + R_d\bigr)^{256} - 1\]






NoteKey Takeaway — Convention on Business Days



The number of business days used for annualization varies according to market conventions: 250, 256 or 300 days depending on institutions and markets. It is important to specify which convention is adopted to guarantee the comparability of results.








WarningCommon Mistake — Do Not Simply Multiply



Annualization is not done by multiplying the monthly return by 12. Multiplication is an approximation valid only for very small returns:
\[R_a \approx 12 \times R_m \quad \text{(approximation, small returns)}\] \[R_a = (1 + R_m)^{12} - 1 \quad \text{(exact formula)}\]








TipIntuition — Compounding Effect



A monthly return of 1 % does not give 12 % annually. In reality: \((1.01)^{12} - 1 \approx 12.68\%\). The gap comes from interest applied on interest accumulated each month. The higher the monthly return, the larger the gap with simple multiplication.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money
text:
Time Value of Money

Fundamental Principle
The time value of money is one of the foundational principles of finance: 1 CHF available today is worth more than 1 CHF available in the future, because present money can be invested to generate a return.
This principle justifies the use of discount rates to compare financial flows at different dates.


Discrete Compounding
If \(R\) is the return per period and \(PV\) the present value (Present Value), the future value (Future Value) at horizon \(n\) is:
\[FV_n^1 = PV \cdot (1 + R)^n\]
The progression over time is as follows:



Time
Future Value




\(t = 1\)
\(PV \cdot (1+R)\)


\(t = 2\)
\(PV \cdot (1+R)^2\)


\(\vdots\)
\(\vdots\)


\(t = n\)
\(PV \cdot (1+R)^n\)




Higher Compounding Frequency
If interest is paid \(m\) times per year over \(n\) years:
\[FV_n^m = PV \cdot \left(1 + \frac{R}{m}\right)^{m \cdot n}\]






TipIntuition — Frequency and Final Value



The more frequent the compounding (monthly, weekly, daily), the higher the future value grows, because interest is reinvested and itself generates interest sooner. This is the effect of compound interest.





Continuous Compounding
By letting the number of payments per year tend to infinity (\(m \to \infty\)), we obtain continuous compounding (continuous compounding):
\[FV_n^\infty = \lim_{m \to \infty} PV \cdot \left(1 + \frac{R}{m}\right)^{m \cdot n} = PV \cdot e^{Rn}\]
This result follows directly from the definition of Euler’s number \(e\):
\[\lim_{m \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{R}{m}\right)^m = e^R\]


Numerical Example — Impact of Frequency
With \(PV = 1\,000\) CHF, \(R = 10\%\) and \(n = 1\) year:

NoteKey Takeaway — Theoretical Role of Continuous Compounding



Continuous compounding gives the maximum theoretical future value for a given rate \(R\). In practice, it is not realistic but serves as a preferred mathematical framework in theoretical models, because the exponential is simpler to differentiate and integrate than powers of fractions.




Link between Continuous Return and Simple Return
By setting the equivalence between discrete and continuous compounding:
\[PV \cdot (1+R)^n = FV_n = PV \cdot e^{rn}\]
We deduce the fundamental relation between the continuous rate \(r\) and the simple rate \(R\):
\[\ln(1 + R) = r \quad \Longrightarrow \quad r < R\]






TipIntuition — Why \(r < R\) ?



The logarithm is a concave function: \(\ln(1+x) < x\) for all \(x > 0\). The continuous rate \(r\) is therefore always lower than the corresponding simple rate \(R\). The difference is small for small returns but can become significant for high rates.


Numerical example: If \(R = 10\%\), then \(r = \ln(1.10) \approx 9.53\%\).
Verification : \(1000 \cdot e^{0.0953} \approx 1100\) CHF \(\checkmark\)






ImportantConversion Between the Two Conventions



The conversion relation is simple and must be mastered:
\[r = \ln(1 + R) \quad \text{et} \quad R = e^r - 1\]
It allows converting a simple rate to a continuous rate and vice versa.

title: Returns and Time Value of Money
text:
Continuous Returns (Continuous Returns / Log Returns)

Definition of the Logarithmic Return
The continuous return over one period, also called logarithmic return (log return), is defined by:
\[r(t) = \ln\!\left(1 + R(t)\right) = \ln\!\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right) = \ln P_t - \ln P_{t-1}\]
It is a difference of consecutive log prices.






TipIntuition — Why Log-Returns?



The logarithmic return is the continuous version of the simple return. It measures the relative price change in a continuous framework. Its mathematical properties (symmetry, additivity) make it the tool of choice in theoretical financial modeling and in financial asset statistics.




Key Properties of Logarithmic Returns

Symmetry
Unlike simple returns, logarithmic returns are perfectly symmetric:
If an asset goes from 100 to 110 then back to 100:

Simple return: \(+10\%\) then \(-9.09\%\) (asymmetric)
Log-return: \(+\ln(1.1) \approx +9.53\%\) then \(-\ln(1.1) \approx -9.53\%\) (symmetric)



Ease of Analytical Manipulation
The presence of logarithms considerably simplifies:

Stochastic calculus computations (geometric Brownian motion)
Analytical demonstrations involving products of returns
Statistical estimation (normal distributions, etc.)




Multi-Period Continuous Returns
For two periods:
\[r_2(t) = \ln\!\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-2}}\right) = \ln\!\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} \cdot \frac{P_{t-1}}{P_{t-2}}\right)\]
Using the property \(\ln(a \cdot b) = \ln a + \ln b\):
\[r_2(t) = \ln\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} + \ln\frac{P_{t-1}}{P_{t-2}} = r_1(t) + r_1(t-1)\]

Generalization to \(n\) Periods
\[r_n(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} r_1(t-i)\]






ImportantAdditivity of Multi-Period Continuous Returns



Logarithmic returns over \(n\) periods are additive: we simply sum them. This is a major advantage over simple returns which require multiplication. This property greatly facilitates the statistical analysis of financial time series.





Continuous Returns of a Portfolio
On the other hand, additivity does not apply to the cross-sectional dimension (portfolio). With the same notation (\(n\) assets, allocations \(\alpha_i\), \(\sum \alpha_i = 1\)):
\[r_p = \ln(1 + R_p) = \ln\!\left(1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i R_i\right) \neq \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i r_i\]






WarningWarning — Portfolio and Continuous Returns



The continuous return of a portfolio is not the weighted average of individual continuous returns. The additivity of log-returns only holds for temporal aggregation (series of successive periods), not for cross-sectional aggregation (combination of simultaneously held assets).
In practice, the approximation \(r_p \approx \sum \alpha_i r_i\) is often used for small returns.

Key Takeaways






NoteSimple Returns — Multiplicative Compounding




Return over one period: \(R_1(t) = P(t)/P(t-1) - 1\)
Over multiple periods: compounding by multiplication — \(1 + R_n = \prod (1 + R_i)\)
Portfolio return: linear combination \(R_p = \sum \alpha_i R_i\)
Exhibit an intrinsic asymmetry









NoteContinuous (Logarithmic) Returns — Additive Compounding




Definition: \(r(t) = \ln(P_t / P_{t-1})\)
Over multiple periods: summation — \(r_n = \sum r_i\)
Are symmetric and simpler to manipulate analytically
The continuous return of a portfolio does not simplify: \(r_p \neq \sum \alpha_i r_i\)









NoteTime Value of Money




Discrete compounding: \(FV = PV \cdot (1+R)^n\)
Continuous compounding (limit): \(FV = PV \cdot e^{rn}\)
Relation between continuous and simple rate: \(r = \ln(1+R) < R\)
Continuous compounding is a convenient theoretical framework but not realistic in practice









NoteBookkeeping and Portfolio Management




A portfolio’s NAV must always be expressed in the investor’s reference currency
A foreign asset exposes to foreign exchange risk (FX risk) in addition to the asset’s own risk
This risk can be hedged by an inverse currency position, but hedging has a cost
Hedging reduces NAV volatility but does not eliminate it completely

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG — Oral Review
text: Imagine you manage a huge communal water reservoir. Some neighbors draw from it massively, throw waste into it, and leave the pump running at night. You can decide to whom you lend money to buy pumps. Does lending more cheaply to thrifty neighbors and more expensively to polluters change anything? Yes — that is exactly what sustainable finance is: using capital allocation as a lever to steer behaviors. It does not solve everything, but it no longer finances problems with eyes closed.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Current human activities are not sustainable (climate, biodiversity, inequalities).
Finance allocates trillions every year → powerful lever but not sufficient alone.
ESG = framework for integrating non-financial criteria into investment decisions.
Measuring impact requires data, indicators, and specific tools.
There is a spectrum of strategies, from the most passive (exclusion) to the most active (impact).
ESG scoring is relative (sector-based), not absolute — major pitfall.

section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




ESG
3-pillar framework (Environmental, Social, Governance) for measuring a company’s sustainability.
The non-financial report card of a company.


ESG rating
Relative score within a sector, aggregated by a weighted E, S, G average.
Like a graded-on-a-curve score: being AA in oil does not mean being virtuous in absolute terms.


Scope 1/2/3
Three carbon emission scopes, from the most direct (Scope 1) to the most indirect (Scope 3).
Scope 3 = everything your customers and suppliers emit because of you.


ITR (Implied Temperature Rise)
Temperature rise implied if all companies behaved like the one analyzed.
Translates a carbon trajectory into degrees Celsius to compare with the Paris Agreement.


SDG
17 UN global goals (2015, horizon 2030) now quantified in portfolios.
The planetary sustainable development shopping list.


Best-in-class
Overweight the best ESG students by sector, without excluding polluting sectors.
We keep the least bad oil companies to push them to do better.


Shareholder engagement
Dialogue with management + voting at AGMs to influence ESG practices.
The shareholder speaks up instead of slamming the door.


Impact Investing
Investing while seeking a measurable, intentional, and additional social/environmental impact.
Not just avoiding harm: proving we do good, with figures to back it up.


Greenwashing
Sustainability communication that exceeds actual actions.
Shell claiming to contribute to environmental SDGs — to be verified with third-party data.


Rater divergence
Two ESG providers can give very different scores for the same company.
R² ≈ 0.32 between MSCI and Sustainalytics: agreement on trend, divergence in details.

🔗 Concept Mind Map

Measurement → relies on data (MSCI, Sustainalytics…) + tools (dashboards, ESG benchmarks)
Data → feed the 7 ESG strategies (Eurosif 2019)
Strategies → from least to most engaged: Exclusion → Norms-based → Best-in-class → Thematic → Integration → Engagement → Impact
Engagement + Voting → pressure on companies → improvement of practices
Integration → ESG risks = long-term financial risks
Impact → triple condition: intentionality + measurability + additionality

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Relative ≠ Absolute: a AA score in a very polluting sector does not mean the company is virtuous in absolute terms.
Rater divergence: never treat a single provider’s ESG score as an objective truth.
Scope 3 ignored: it is often the most important scope (e.g.: automobiles, oil) — omitting it skews the entire analysis.
Rising scores over time: may mean real improvement or simply better reporting — distinguish the two.
Exclusion ≠ impact: excluding a company does not push it to change; only engagement dialogue does.
Best-in-class ≠ absolute virtue: a coal producer can be best in its category while remaining very polluting.
Additionality (Impact Investing): if the impact would have happened without the investment, it is not impact investing.
Greenwashing: company claims on SDGs must be validated by independent third-party data.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is ESG and why did it emerge?
Short answer: 3-pillar framework (Environmental, Social, Governance) for integrating non-financial risks into investment. It responds to climate, social, and governance crises — finance must reflect these risks.

Q: What is the difference between Scope 1, 2 and 3?
Short answer: Scope 1 = direct emissions. Scope 2 = indirect purchased energy. Scope 3 = all other indirect upstream (suppliers) and downstream (customers) emissions. Scope 3 is often the largest but the hardest to measure.

Q: Why do ESG ratings from different providers diverge?
Short answer: Each provider uses its own methodologies, sources, weightings. R² ≈ 0.32 between MSCI and Sustainalytics — non-financial data are far less standardized than accounting data.

Q: What is the difference between exclusion and best-in-class?
Short answer: Exclusion bans entire sectors. Best-in-class keeps all sectors but overweights the best ESG students in each sector, incentivizing a race to the top.

Q: What are the three conditions of impact investing?
Short answer: Intentionality (the impact is intended), measurability (it is quantified), additionality (it would not have happened without this investment).

Q: What does compenswiss concretely do in terms of ESG?
Short answer: Four combined axes: ESG integration in benchmarks and dashboards, AGM voting (~100 meetings/year in Switzerland), engagement via ASIR (150+ issuers), and exclusions (~100 companies — normative + coal with threshold lowered to 30%).

Q: What is the ITR score and what is the target?
Short answer: The Implied Temperature Rise is the temperature rise implied if all companies behaved like the one analyzed. Target: ≤ 1.5 °C to be aligned with the Paris Agreement.

Q: Why do ESG scores tend to rise over time?
Short answer: Double possible cause: real improvement of practices AND improvement of reporting. One must distinguish the two, otherwise real progress is overestimated.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

ESG = 3 pillars, 10 themes, 37 issues (MSCI 2023) → relative sector-based rating, scale CCC to AAA.
Scopes 1/2/3: direct emissions → indirect energy → everything else (often the largest).
ITR translates carbon trajectory into °C → target ≤ 1.5 °C.
7 strategies (Eurosif): Exclusion · Norms-based · Best-in-class · Thematic · Integration · Engagement · Impact.
Impact investing = intentionality + measurability + additionality.
Rater divergence: R² ≈ 0.32 → a single ESG score is not an absolute truth.
Compenswiss: 4 axes = Integration + Voting (~100 AGMs/year) + ASIR Engagement (150+ issuers) + Exclusions (~100 companies).
Greenwashing: always validate company claims with third-party data.
Sustainable finance steers capital but does not replace public policy.
Young and moving field: growing regulation (SFDR, green taxonomy, FINMA).

title: Bonds: Sensitivity to Time and Rates — Oral Review
text: Imagine you are skiing on the snowy slope of the yield curve. The forward rates tell you the steepness you will encounter further down the slope — even if you are not there yet. Duration measures how much your speed (the bond price) will drop if the slope changes abruptly. And convexity? It is the curvature of the slope itself: thanks to it, the fall in case of a shock is less catastrophic than predicted, and the rebound is more generous. A true structural advantage for the Geneva investor-skier.

title: Bonds: Sensitivity to Time and Rates — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

The zero-coupon curve implicitly contains all future rates → forward rates.
In the absence of arbitrage (no-arbitrage), two equivalent strategies must produce the same result: they determine the forward rate.
Duration (double role): time-weighted average of cash flows AND price sensitivity to rates.
For small shocks: the linear approximation by duration is sufficient.
For large shocks: we must add convexity (2nd-order term).
Convexity is always favorable to the holder of a standard bond.
Portfolio duration is additive (weighted) → active risk management tool.

title: Bonds: Sensitivity to Time and Rates — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Forward rate
Rate implicitly contained in the zero-coupon curve for a future period
Two investment paths = same result → no arbitrage


No-arbitrage
If the forward deviates from its equilibrium value, a risk-free profit becomes possible
“Free lunch” eliminated by the market


Parallel shift
All rates move by the same amount, regardless of maturity
Central bank changes rates uniformly


Flattening
The short–long rate spread narrows
Early signal of economic slowdown


Steepening
The short–long rate spread widens
Anticipation of recovery or inflation


Macaulay duration
Weighted average of an bond’s payment dates
Time center of gravity of cash flows


Convexity
Measures the curvature (non-linearity) of the price–rate relationship
Favorable asymmetry: smaller losses / larger gains


Modified duration
Duration adjusted for discrete compounding convention
Direct price elasticity to rates


DV01 / Dollar duration
Absolute price change in dollars for 1 basis point
Universal currency of risk management


Key rate duration
Price sensitivity to a shock on a specific segment of the curve
Essential for non-parallel shocks

title: Bonds: Sensitivity to Time and Rates — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Forward ≠ actual future spot rate: the forward rate is implicit in today’s curve, not a certain prediction.
\(D <\) maturity for a coupon bond (intermediate coupons pull the center of gravity forward); \(D =\) maturity only for a zero-coupon.
Duration alone insufficient for \(|\delta y| \geq 0{,}5\,\%\): overestimates losses and underestimates gains — always add convexity.
Macaulay vs. modified: under continuous compounding they are equal; in discrete, \(D_{\text{mod}} = D\,/\,(1 + y/n_c)\) — do not confuse.
Convexity always positive for a standard bond (no option) — it is structurally an advantage, never a risk.
Multi-currency portfolio: compute one duration per currency, never a single global duration.
Do not neglect non-parallel shocks: classical duration is not enough — use key rate duration.

title: Bonds: Sensitivity to Time and Rates — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is a forward rate and how is it derived?
Short answer: Rate implicit in the zero-coupon curve for a future period. Formula: \(r = (R_2 T_2 - R_1 T_1)/(T_2 - T_1)\). Derived from the no-arbitrage condition between two equivalent investment strategies.

Q: Why is the duration of a coupon bond less than its maturity?
Short answer: Intermediate coupons produce cash flows before the final maturity, pulling the time center of gravity toward the present.

Q: What is the difference between Macaulay duration and modified duration?
Short answer: Under continuous compounding, they are identical. Under discrete compounding (\(n_c\) periods/year): \(D_{\text{mod}} = D\,/\,(1 + y/n_c)\). Modified duration is directly a price–rate elasticity.

Q: Why is convexity said to be “favorable” to the holder?
Short answer: The price–rate relationship is convex (bulging upward): in case of a rate rise, the actual loss is smaller than linearly predicted; in case of a rate fall, the gain is larger.

Q: An examiner gives you \(\delta y = 1\,\%\), duration = 2,653, \(C = 7{,}570\), \(B = 94{,}21\). Estimate \(\delta B\).
Short answer: \(\delta B \approx -94{,}21 \times 2{,}653 \times 0{,}01 + \frac{1}{2}\times 94{,}21 \times 7{,}570 \times (0{,}01)^2 \approx -2{,}464\) USD.

Q: How does one steer portfolio duration in the face of an anticipated rate rise?
Short answer: We reduce duration by selling long-maturity bonds and buying short-maturity bonds.

Q: What is the purpose of DV01 compared to Macaulay duration?
Short answer: DV01 expresses sensitivity in absolute value ($) for 1 basis point — directly comparable across bonds of different sizes, used in risk management.

Q: What are the three typical yield curve movements?
Short answer: Parallel shift (all rates move by the same amount), flattening (short–long spread narrows), steepening (short–long spread widens).

title: Bonds: Sensitivity to Time and Rates — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

Forward rate = implicit future rate extracted from the zero-coupon curve by no-arbitrage.
Formula: \(r = (R_2 T_2 - R_1 T_1)/(T_2 - T_1)\) — continuous compounding mandatory.
Duration = time center of gravity of cash flows = rate sensitivity (\(\delta B / B \approx -D\,\delta y\)).
Zero-coupon: \(D =\) maturity. Coupon bond: \(D <\) maturity.
Large shock → add convexity: \(+\frac{1}{2}C\,(\delta y)^2\).
Positive convexity → always favorable to the holder (gain/loss asymmetry).
\(D_{\text{mod}} = D/(1+y/n_c)\) ; \(\text{DV01} = D_{\text{mod}} \cdot B / 100\).
Portfolio duration = \(\sum w_k D_k\) → steer according to rate expectations.
3 curve movements: parallel / flattening / steepening.
Key rate duration for non-parallel shocks (flattening, steepening).

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG
text:
Sustainable investing — also called sustainable finance or responsible investing — emerges as a response to the major systemic crises facing our contemporary world. Before understanding its financial mechanisms, it is important to grasp why this approach has become indispensable.
Several converging phenomena alarm the scientific community and economic decision-makers:

Climate change: global temperatures have risen by more than 1°C above the 1951–1980 baseline, with records reached in 2016 and 2020. The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) documents this trajectory rigorously.
Biodiversity collapse: the Global Living Planet Index has fallen by 69% between 1970 and 2020. This index, calculated from the monitoring of thousands of vertebrate species, illustrates the alarming speed at which animal populations are disappearing.
Social imbalances: gender inequalities, forced migrations, unequal access to essential resources (water, health, education) constitute deep fractures in the global social fabric.
Governance problems: corruption, systemic financial instability, lack of transparency in corporate practices.







TipIntuition



Imagine a planetary thermometer rising, a biodiversity counter falling, and social inequalities deepening. The question becomes: can finance, which allocates trillions of euros every year, steer these resources differently to contribute to solutions?





The question posed in the course is direct: in the face of climate change, biodiversity collapse, social imbalances, and governance problems, can finance be of any help?
The answer is nuanced but affirmative. Finance cannot, by itself, resolve these crises — that would be illusory. However, it wields a powerful lever: capital allocation. By directing investments toward more responsible companies and projects, financial actors can:

Raise the cost of capital for polluting companies (incentivizing them to change),
Finance the energy and ecological transition,
Exert pressure through their voting rights at general meetings,
Engage in direct dialogue with company management.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG
text:
Definitions and Terminology

One concept, many names
The field of sustainable finance is characterized by a proliferation of terms that, in reality, designate a common central concept. One speaks interchangeably of:

Sustainable Finance
ESG Investing — ESG for Environmental, Social, Governance
Socially Responsible Investing — SRI
Green Finance
Responsible Investment
Sustainable Development
Climate Risk







NoteKey takeaway



All these terms belong to the same conceptual universe: integrating non-financial criteria (environmental, social, governance) into investment decisions. The major academic reference on this subject is the course by Thierry Roncalli (2022–2023), available at https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4339823, comprising 1,114 slides and still evolving.




Why is sustainable investing difficult?
Despite its obvious interest, sustainable investing is described as daunting for several reasons:

The complexity of the issues is immense: climate change alone mobilizes disciplines as varied as physics, economics, law, and sociology.
Data are imperfect, partial, and non-standardized.
Indicators are multiple and sometimes contradictory.
Trade-offs (arbitrages between financial performance and impact) are real and difficult to quantify.
Regulation evolves rapidly and varies by country.

This is why entering this field resembles — as the course’s graphic metaphor shows — pulling a ball of yarn that reveals an increasingly heavy block: greenhouse gases and global warming.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG

text:
The ESG Pillars: Definition and Structure

The three pillars
The acronym ESG structures the entire non-financial analysis framework around three pillars:

E — Environmental: impact on the natural environment
S — Social: impact on human stakeholders
G — Governance: quality of management and control structures



The 10 themes and 37 key issues (MSCI, 2023)
Data provider MSCI has structured ESG criteria into 10 themes grouped within the 3 pillars, themselves broken down into 37 key issues.

Environmental Pillar
The Environmental pillar covers four main themes:
1. Climate Change
This theme analyzes a company’s exposure to risks and opportunities linked to climate change. Key issues include:

Carbon Emissions ★
Product Carbon Footprint
Financing Environmental Impact

2. Natural Resources

Water Stress ★
Biodiversity & Land Use
Raw Material Sourcing

3. Pollution & Waste
