Corruption & Instability
Financial System Instability







NoteKey takeaway



★ indicates “universal” issues, evaluated for all companies in the MSCI World Index.
★★ indicates that Board, Pay, Ownership, and Accounting directly contribute to the Corporate Governance score for all companies — but the 0-to-10 sub-scores are not yet available.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG
text:
ESG Scoring

Basic principles

Multiplicity of scoring systems
There are many ESG scoring systems offered by different data providers, among which:

MSCI — one of the most widely used in the world
Sustainalytics (Morningstar subsidiary)
S&P Global ESG
Refinitiv (LSEG subsidiary)
Bloomberg ESG
ISS ESG

Each provider builds its own methodology, with different weights, data sources, and scales.


Correlation between systems
Although ratings present sometimes significant differences from one provider to another, the overall correlation remains positive. A comparative study between Sustainalytics and MSCI on the 1,200 stocks of the S&P 1200 (January 2016) shows an R² of approximately 0.32: the two systems agree on the general direction, but display notable dispersion.






TipIntuition



Think of credit rating agencies (Moody’s, S&P, Fitch): they often agree on the broad balances but may diverge on the details. ESG presents a similar situation, perhaps with even more dispersion because non-financial data are less standardized than accounting data.








WarningImportant point



A positive correlation does not mean that the two systems give the same score to every company. ESG rater divergence (rating disagreement) is a well-documented problem in the academic literature. It complicates the interpretation and comparison of ESG portfolios.





Structure of ESG scoring (MSCI, since 2023)
Since 2023, MSCI calculates the overall ESG rating as a weighted average of the scores obtained on the three E, S, and G pillars. The weighting reflects the materiality of each issue for the company’s sector of activity.
The rating corresponds to a relative ranking within a sectoral universe. It is expressed on a scale ranging from CCC (very poor) to AAA (leader), passing through B, BB, BBB, A, AA.

Example: AstraZeneca (AZN)
AstraZeneca, a British pharmaceutical group, illustrates well how the scoring works:

MSCI rating: AA (stable since September 2016)
Positioning: leader among 93 pharmaceutical companies in the MSCI ACWI index
Distribution in the industry: approximately 29% of companies have a CCC or B rating, while a minority reaches AA or AAA

AstraZeneca’s strengths lie in human capital development and access to health care. Its relative weaknesses concern product safety and quality.


General trend of scores






NoteKey takeaway



Academic research (Lundström, 2021) shows that ESG scores tend to increase over time. This may reflect a real improvement in corporate practices, but also a growing reporting effect (companies learn to better document their actions) and methodological biases of raters.





Carbon emissions (Scope 1, 2, and 3)
A central component of ESG scoring concerns greenhouse gas emissions, measured or estimated according to three scopes:

Scope 1: direct emissions produced by the company (e.g., boilers, fleet vehicles)
Scope 2: indirect emissions linked to consumed energy (e.g., purchased electricity)
Scope 3: all other indirect emissions, upstream (suppliers) and downstream (product use by customers)







TipIntuition



For an automobile manufacturer, Scope 3 is by far the most important: emissions from cars on the road with customers are far greater than emissions from its factories. Ignoring Scope 3 would lead to a very incomplete picture of the company’s real climate impact.




Modeling the future: the ITR score
The ITR score (Implied Temperature Rise), developed notably by MSCI, attempts to model the future climate trajectory of a company or portfolio.

It expresses, in degrees Celsius, the global warming that would result from a world where all companies adopt the same behavior as the one analyzed.
An ITR of 1.5°C is aligned with the Paris Agreement; an ITR of 3°C or 4°C is very concerning.

This type of indicator allows comparison of companies’ climate commitments against scientifically defined trajectories.


Gender equality
Gender parity is an increasingly monitored social indicator. Companies are required to report it and, in many jurisdictions, a legal minimum will soon be mandatory (notably in Europe with the directive on gender balance in boards of directors).


The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted by the UN in 2015, constitute a universal framework of 17 goals to be achieved by 2030:

No Poverty
Zero Hunger
Good Health and Well-being
Quality Education
Gender Equality
Clean Water and Sanitation
Affordable and Clean Energy
Decent Work and Economic Growth
Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure
Reduced Inequalities
Sustainable Cities and Communities
Responsible Consumption and Production
Climate Action
Life Below Water
Life on Land
Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions
Partnerships for the Goals

These goals are now quantified by data providers and integrated into portfolio analyses.

Example of SDG use: Shell (2022)
Shell’s 2022 sustainability report illustrates how a large oil company appropriates the SDG framework. Shell indicates that it directly contributes to 13 of the 17 SDGs through its Powering Progress strategy — including notably:

SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy
SDG 13: Climate Action
SDG 14: Life Below Water
SDG 15: Life on Land







WarningImportant point



These corporate declarations should be appreciated with a critical eye. The fact that an oil company claims a contribution to environmental SDGs raises the question of greenwashing: communication on sustainable development can sometimes surpass concrete actions. ESG scoring tools attempt to go beyond statements of intent to measure real impacts.




Example of SDG use: Switzerland (national level)
The SDGs also apply to States. The SDG dashboard for Switzerland (source: sdgindex.org) presents, for example:

SDG rank: 8th out of 163 countries
SDG score: 80.8
Spillover Score: 52.1 — this indicator measures the negative effects that a country imposes on others through its trade, supply chains, and investments

Switzerland is progressing in many areas but still faces significant challenges, notably for life below water (SDG 14) and responsible consumption (SDG 12).

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG
text:
Possible ESG Strategies

A taxonomy in seven categories
The Eurosif classification (2019), adopted by Thierry Roncalli, identifies seven major ESG investment strategies, ranging from the most passive to the most active:





flowchart TD
    A[ESG Strategies] --> B[1. Exclusion]
    A --> C[2. Values / Norms]
    A --> D[3. Positive Selection]
    A --> E[4. Thematic]
    A --> F[5. Integration]
    A --> G[6. Engagement]
    A --> H[7. Impact]








Strategy 1: Exclusion (Exclusion Policy & Negative / Worst-in-class Screening)
Definition: This strategy consists of excluding from the investment universe certain companies, sectors, or countries that do not meet minimum criteria.
Two main variants:

Normative exclusion: companies that violate international conventions are excluded (e.g., manufacturers of anti-personnel mines, cluster bombs — banned by the Ottawa and Oslo conventions).
Sectoral exclusion: entire industries deemed incompatible with the investor’s values are excluded (e.g., tobacco, gambling, weapons, coal beyond a certain threshold).
Worst-in-class: the lowest-rated ESG companies in each sector are excluded.







TipIntuition



This is the simplest strategy to understand and implement. An “ethical” fund that refuses to invest in tobacco producers applies a sectoral exclusion. The drawback is that it does not push these companies to change — it simply ignores them.


Advantages: Easy to communicate; strong consistency with certain ethical values.
Limitations: Does not create dialogue with the company; can generate significant sectoral bias in the portfolio; does not guarantee a better impact on the world.


Strategy 2: Values / Norms-based Screening (Norms-based Screening)
Definition: The investment universe is filtered by verifying companies’ compliance with international standards and norms, such as:

The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
ILO (International Labour Organization) conventions
The UN Global Compact
OECD conventions for multinational enterprises







NoteKey takeaway



The difference with sectoral exclusion is subtle but important: norms-based screening excludes companies on the basis of behaviors contrary to universal norms (e.g., use of child labor), regardless of the sector of activity.




Strategy 3: Positive Selection / Best-in-class (Positive or Best-in-class Screening)
Definition: The best-rated ESG companies within each sector of activity are actively selected.
Operation:

The same sectoral exposure as the benchmark index is maintained,
But within each sector, “ESG leaders” are overweighted and “ESG laggards” are underweighted.







TipIntuition



Rather than excluding polluting sectors, one invests in oil companies that pollute the least and make the most efforts toward the transition. The idea is to incentivize a race to the top rather than abandoning difficult sectors.


Advantage: Allows greater sectoral diversification to be maintained.
Limitation: A company can be “best in its class” while remaining objectively not very virtuous in absolute terms.


Strategy 4: Thematic Investing (Sustainability Themed Investing)
Definition: Investments are concentrated on specific sustainability themes, such as:

Green Bonds: bonds whose proceeds are earmarked for environmental projects
Renewable energy funds
Clean water funds
Sustainable agriculture funds
Circular economy funds







NoteKey takeaway



Thematic investing is often associated with strong growth potential, because these sectors benefit from increasing regulatory support (European taxonomy, Green Deal). However, it can generate concentration risks and valuation problems if themes become overvalued.




Strategy 5: ESG Integration (ESG Integration)
Definition: ESG criteria are fully integrated into the portfolio management process, on the same footing as traditional financial criteria (valuation, profitability, risk).
Concrete operation:

ESG scores enter asset-selection models,
Financial analysts integrate ESG risks into their valuation models,
Benchmarks are constructed with ESG filters,
ESG dashboards allow the extra-financial profile of the portfolio to be tracked in real time.







TipIntuition



Integration starts from the assumption that ESG risks are real long-term financial risks: a highly polluting company exposes itself to stricter regulations, carbon taxes, lawsuits — all risks that ultimately translate into risks for the stock’s value.




Strategy 6: Engagement and Voting (Voting Policy & Shareholder Activism)
Definition: As a shareholder, influence is exerted on companies via:

Voting at the General Meeting on resolutions submitted to shareholders
Direct dialogue (engagement) with management and boards of directors
Publication of critical reports or shareholder proposals

Examples of resolutions on which an investor may vote:

Approval of annual accounts
Executive remuneration (Say on Pay)
Composition of the board of directors
Company climate strategy







WarningImportant point



Engagement is an active and resource-intensive strategy: it requires specialized teams, legal knowledge, and the ability to dialogue in several languages with hundreds of companies. This is why it is often carried out through coalitions or specialized service providers.




Strategy 7: Impact Investing (Impact Investing)
Definition: The aim is to generate, beyond financial return, a measurable and intentional social or environmental impact.
Distinctive characteristics:

Intentionality: the impact is intended, not a by-product,
Measurability: the impact is quantified (e.g., tonnes of CO₂ avoided, number of people lifted out of poverty),
Additionality: the investment creates an impact that would not have occurred without it.

Examples:

Microfinance funds that lend to entrepreneurs in emerging countries without access to bank credit,
Social Impact Bonds,
Green infrastructure funds in areas vulnerable to climate change.







NoteKey takeaway



Impact investing represents the most accomplished expression of sustainable finance: the goal is not simply to avoid harm, but to contribute positively in a verifiable manner. It is also the most difficult strategy to standardize and evaluate objectively.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG
section: Practical Example: Compenswiss, from Theory to Practice
text:
Practical Example: Compenswiss, from Theory to Practice

Presentation of Compenswiss
Compenswiss is the manager of the AVS/AI/APG Compensation Fund (old-age and survivors insurance, disability insurance, and income loss allowances), the Swiss national pension fund. It is one of the large institutional investors in Switzerland, managing several tens of billions of francs.
Its ESG approach, presented in the course (end-2022 situation), illustrates how theoretical strategies are concretely implemented in the management of a pension fund.


The four pillars of Compenswiss’s ESG approach
Compenswiss’s approach is structured around four practical axes:





quadrantChart
    title Compenswiss ESG Approach
    x-axis Low engagement --> High engagement
    y-axis Indirect --> Direct
    quadrant-1 Active engagement
    quadrant-2 Direct dialogue
    quadrant-3 Measurement & Monitoring
    quadrant-4 Formal rights
    Integration: [0.2, 0.2]
    Voting rights exercise: [0.7, 0.3]
    Engagement via ASIR: [0.8, 0.8]
    Exclusions: [0.3, 0.7]







Axis 1: Integration
ESG integration at Compenswiss involves:

Using ESG benchmarks as a reference for management mandates,
A proprietary ESG dashboard allowing the E, S, and G indicators of the portfolio to be tracked in real time,
Monitoring the Swiss Climate Scores — a framework developed in Switzerland to measure the climate compatibility of portfolios.

The dashboard tool notably allows visualization of:

The overall ESG score of the portfolio vs. the benchmark (e.g., AA for both at end-2022)
The decomposition by pillar (E, S, G) with scores and weights
The distribution of ESG ratings in the portfolio
The coverage rate — the proportion of assets under management for which ESG data is available



Axis 2: Exercise of voting rights in Switzerland
Compenswiss votes at the General Meetings of Swiss companies in which it is invested — approximately 100 AGMs per year in Switzerland.
This activity is entrusted to a specialized external consultant, because the analysis of each resolution is time-consuming and requires specific expertise. Voting rules defined in advance guide the decisions.
Historical data (2015–2022) show:

An increase in the share of “all motions accepted”, linked to the gradual deployment of the Swiss law on abusive remuneration,
A stable proportion of votes with “one motion rejected”, mainly on questions of executive remuneration.







TipIntuition



The right to vote is a form of soft but real pressure. When a large institutional investor votes against a manager’s remuneration, it makes headlines and can influence management. Multiplied by dozens of large funds that coordinate their votes, this effect becomes significant.




Axis 3: Engagement via ASIR
Engagement is carried out through ASIR (Swiss Association for Responsible Investments), of which Compenswiss is a co-founder. This structure allows resources to be pooled and the voice of investors to be amplified.
ASIR engagement covers:

Dialogue with more than 150 issuers (companies in which members are invested)
Various themes: business ethics, environment, human rights, workers’ rights
A specific emblematic subject: child labor in the cocoa supply chain

The evolution of engagements between 2019 and 2022 shows:

An increase in the total number of cases, notably driven by engagements on human rights,
A relatively stable thematic distribution on the other dimensions (business ethics, environment, labor rights).







WarningImportant point



Engagement is a long-term process. An open dialogue with a company on its social practices can last several years before producing tangible effects. Patience and persistence are necessary conditions for the effectiveness of this approach.




Axis 4: Exclusions
Compenswiss applies exclusions to approximately 100 companies, on two bases:

Normative exclusions: companies that violate fundamental international conventions (e.g., manufacturers of prohibited weapons)
Coal exclusions: companies whose revenue exceeds a threshold linked to coal extraction or use (the threshold was lowered from 50% to 30%, illustrating a progressive tightening of the policy)




Analysis of Compenswiss’s portfolio carbon footprint
A concrete example of analysis concerns the tracking of the carbon footprint of the portfolio over the period June 2020 – December 2022, measured in tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per million dollars invested (tCO₂e / M$ invested).
Key observations:

The ideal benchmark (target trajectory) shows a regular decline over the period — consistent with a decarbonization trajectory,
The market benchmark also follows a downward trend, albeit less pronounced,
The Compenswiss portfolio has a carbon footprint higher than the ideal benchmark, but with a decreasing trend,
The coal exclusion thresholds (50% then 30%) had a visible impact on the portfolio’s trajectory.







NoteKey takeaway



This example illustrates the usefulness of ESG data and tools: they allow progress to be visualized, gaps from the target trajectory to be detected, and unexpected consequences of certain investment decisions to be highlighted. Without measurement, there is no steering possible.








TipIntuition



ESG management is analogous to managing a diet: without precise measurement of caloric intake (here, carbon emissions), one moves blindly. ESG data tools play the role of this indispensable tracking dashboard.




Data and tools: a central issue
Compenswiss’s experience highlights a crucial point: the concrete implementation of ESG rests on the quality and richness of available data.
The data sources used include:

MSCI: ESG scores and ratings
ASIR: engagement data
Delegated fund managers: ESG reports from outsourced mandates

The challenge is twofold:

Coverage: not all companies are rated (notably SMEs, sovereign issuers, unlisted assets),
Time traversal: ESG data evolve, methodologies change — one must be able to analyze the portfolio at different dates to track progress.







WarningImportant point



The quality of IT tools for ESG data management is a competitive advantage for institutional investors. Traversing data over time (historical comparisons) and through structures (look-through of delegated funds down to the underlying assets) is a key skill that conditions the reliability of the analysis.

title: Sustainable Investing and ESG
text:
Main Lessons

What sustainable investing can and cannot do
Sustainable finance is a rapidly growing field, but it is important to have a lucid and balanced view of it.
What it can do:

Steer capital toward less polluting and more responsible activities,
Exert pressure on companies through share ownership,
Contribute to reducing the cost of capital for virtuous companies and increasing it for others,
Improve awareness of long-term non-financial risks,
Directly finance projects with measurable positive impact.

What it cannot do:

Resolve environmental and social crises alone,
Replace public policy and regulation,
Guarantee superior short-term returns,
Eliminate problems of imperfect data and greenwashing.



Summary of key concepts






NoteKey takeaway — Essential points of the chapter



On the context: current human activities are not sustainable. Climate change, biodiversity collapse, and inequalities call for a systemic response. Finance is one lever among others.
On indicators: many acronyms structure the field — ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance), SDGs (Sustainable Development Goals), ITR (Implied Temperature Rise), carbon emissions Scope 1/2/3. Each responds to a different measurement need.
On data: measuring, analyzing, forecasting, and anticipating — all of this requires reliable data. Managing data over time and across portfolio structures is a major operational issue.
On strategies: a whole palette of ESG strategies exists — Integration, Engagement, Voting, Impact, Exclusion — and they are often combined in practice.
On practice: Compenswiss’s experience shows that a rigorous institutional ESG approach simultaneously combines integration into processes, exercise of voting rights, shareholder engagement, and an exclusion policy.




Sustainable finance: a young and moving field
Sustainable finance is a relatively recent field in the history of finance, but it is growing very rapidly:

Volumes of assets under management with ESG criteria increase every year,
Regulation is becoming denser (SFDR in Europe, European green taxonomy, PACTE law in France, FINMA recommendations in Switzerland),
Data are gradually improving (increasing mandatory reporting),
Academic research on the effectiveness of ESG strategies is intensifying.







TipIntuition



Investing in sustainable finance today is like investing in risk management in the early 1990s: the tools are imperfect, regulation still incomplete, but the direction is irreversible. The actors who develop ESG skills and data today will have a lasting advantage.

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
text:
You are the on-call nurse in the financial emergency room. The patient’s vital signs (prices) arrive irregularly — sometimes every millisecond, sometimes nothing for hours. The measurements are noisy, with three thermometers in disagreement (bid, ask, mid), and occasionally the patient faints (discontinuity).
To avoid panicking: we smooth (moving averages) and, rather than looking at the clock, we count the fever episodes (intrinsic time). Clever.

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Real data are irregular, noisy, discontinuous — nothing like theoretical series.
They are almost always processed by discretisation (fixed grid + last known price).
Moving averages smooth noise but introduce an inevitable lag.
The EMA is the optimal compromise: decreasing weighting + update with a single scalar.
Intrinsic time replaces the clock with price events (directional changes).
Universal scaling laws link intrinsic time and physical time across 13 FX pairs.

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
One-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Bid-ask spread
Gap between purchase price (bid) and sale price (ask), measure of liquidity
The lower it is, the more liquid the market


Discretisation
Fixed time grid, we keep the last price before each node
We read the clock every hour, we ignore the in-between


SMA
Moving average with equal weights over a window of \(n\) observations
The observation from \(n\) days ago weighs as much as yesterday’s


WMA
Linearly decreasing weights towards the past
We give more credit to the recent


EMA
Exponentially decreasing weighting, recursive update on 1 value
We gradually forget the past via \((1-\alpha)\)


Time lag
Systematic delay of the smoothed series relative to the original signal
Inevitable: more smoothing = more delay


Intrinsic time
Time measured by price reversals, not by the clock
The market clock only ticks when something happens


DC (Directional Change)
Price reversal of amplitude \(\geq \delta\) since the last extreme
A true trend reversal according to a threshold \(\delta\)


Overshoot (OS)
Price movement after the DC until the next reversal
The market overshoots the threshold before turning back


Scaling laws
Power-law relations between intrinsic time and physical time magnitudes
Universal fractal structure of markets
crumbs: 4. Data, Moving Average and Intrinsic Time

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

Real data → non-equidistant + noisy + bid/ask/mid
Non-equidistant → Discretisation (99.9%) or Interpolation (rare)
Noisy data → SMA → WMA → EMA (optimal compromise)
Smoothing → Time lag inevitable (↑ \(n\) or ↓ \(\alpha\) ⟹ ↑ lag)
EMA → \(\alpha\) calibrated by SMA(\(n\)) equivalence or by residual impact
Asynchronous data → Generalised EMA with \(\mu = e^{-\alpha}\) and \(\nu\)
Physical time → limits (arbitrary, insensitive to activity)
Intrinsic time → DC (threshold \(\delta\)) → Overshoot → TM = DC + OS
Number of DC ∝ Volatility; Length of OS ∝ Liquidity
Intrinsic time → 20 universal scaling laws
crumbs: 4. Data, Moving Average and Intrinsic Time

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
text:
📐 Essential Formulas








Formula
Meaning
To remember




\(\text{SMA}(t+1) = \text{SMA}(t) - \frac{X_{t-n+1}}{n} + \frac{X_{t+1}}{n}\)
Incremental SMA update
Remove the oldest, add the most recent


\(\text{WMA}(t) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n i \cdot X_{t-n+i}}{n(n+1)/2}\)
Linearly increasing weights towards the recent
Denominator = \(n(n+1)/2\)


\(\text{EMA}(t) = \alpha X_t + (1-\alpha)\,\text{EMA}(t-1)\)
EMA recursion
Absolute central formula


\(\alpha = \frac{2}{n+1}\)
Average age equivalence EMA ↔︎ SMA(\(n\))
Same average age ≠ same values


\(\alpha = 1 - e^{\log(\epsilon_k)/k}\)
Residual impact \(\epsilon_k\) after \(k\) steps
Ex: \(k=100\), \(\epsilon=1\% \Rightarrow \alpha \approx 0{,}045\)


\(\text{TM} = \text{DC} + \text{OS}\)
Total movement = DC + overshoot
Fundamental decomposition


\(\langle \Delta t_{\text{dc}} \rangle \sim (\delta/c)^{\alpha}\)
Average duration of a DC
Power law in \(\delta\)
crumbs: 4. Data, Moving Average and Intrinsic Time

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

EMA ≠ SMA with \(\alpha = 2/(n+1)\) — only the average age is equivalent, not the numerical values.
Lag is inevitable: you cannot smooth strongly and be perfectly reactive — it is a choice, not a bug.
EMA: theoretically infinite memory — it is not a window of \(n\) points, but a weight \((1-\alpha)^k\) that tends to 0.
Warm-up period: the first EMA values are biased by the initialisation, wait before using them.
Arbitrary initial mode in the DC algorithm — converges quickly but should be mentioned if asked.
Discretisation = loss of information between ticks — too coarse a grid ⟹ intra-period events invisible.
Confusing DC and OS: DC triggers the mode change, OS is the movement in the new mode.
Trick question: “How many observations does the EMA store?” → Only 1 value (the previous EMA).
crumbs: 4. Data, Moving Average and Intrinsic Time

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What are the 3 ideal properties of a time series and why does reality differ?
Short answer: Equidistant, smooth, continuous — in practice: irregular activity, noise, jumps, and price decomposed into bid/ask/mid.

Q: What is the essential difference between SMA, WMA and EMA?
Short answer: SMA = equal weights; WMA = linearly decreasing weights; EMA = exponentially decreasing weights with only 1 value in memory.

Q: Why is the EMA preferred in practice?
Short answer: Scalar update (1 value), naturally decreasing weighting, parameter \(\alpha\) simple to interpret and calibrate.

Q: How do we calibrate \(\alpha\) for an EMA?
Short answer: Either equivalence with SMA(\(n\)): \(\alpha = 2/(n+1)\). Or by residual impact: we impose that an observation \(k\) steps old has a weight \(\leq \epsilon_k\).

Q: What is intrinsic time and why introduce it?
Short answer: Time defined by directional changes (DC \(\geq \delta\)), not by the clock. Advantage: adaptive to activity, avoids the bias of quiet periods.

Q: What do the number of DCs and the length of OSs measure?
Short answer: Number of DCs / physical time ∝ volatility; length of OSs ∝ liquidity.

Q: What is a scaling law and why is it remarkable?
Short answer: Empirical power-law relation between intrinsic time and physical time. 20 laws identified, universal across 13 FX pairs — fractal structure of markets.

Q: How is the EMA adapted to asynchronous data?
Short answer: We replace fixed \(\alpha\) by \(\alpha = \Delta t / \tau\) and \(\mu = e^{-\alpha}\): the longer the interval, the larger the forgetting factor. Time is naturally integrated.
crumbs: 4. Data, Moving Average and Intrinsic Time

title: Data, Moving Averages and Intrinsic Time — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

Real data: bid/ask/mid, irregular, noisy, discontinuous.
Processing: discretisation (99.9%), interpolation (rare).
SMA = equal weights, lag; WMA = linear weights; EMA = exponential weights, only 1 value.
EMA: \(\text{EMA}(t) = \alpha X_t + (1-\alpha)\,\text{EMA}(t-1)\) — formula to know by heart.
Lag inevitable: ↑ smoothing ⟹ ↑ delay.
\(\alpha = 2/(n+1)\) → same average age as SMA(\(n\)), not the same values.
Intrinsic time = time dictated by DC (reversals \(\geq \delta\)).
DC ∝ volatility; OS ∝ liquidity; TM = DC + OS.
20 scaling laws robust across 13 FX pairs → universal fractal.
Small \(\delta\) → fast time (volatile market); large \(\delta\) → slow time (calm market).

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
text: A farmer sows wheat in March and trembles at the thought that the price may collapse in September. Solution: he calls his banker and says “I sell at 200 €/tonne in 6 months, whatever happens”. Contract signed. Irrevocable agreement. No one can back out. This is a forward: firm commitment on both sides, no premium, no emergency exit. The futures is the same thing but in industrial version: standardized, exchange-traded, with a controller (the clearing house) who watches everyone every evening.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Fix today the price of a future transaction → eliminates price uncertainty.
Unlike options: obligation of both parties (no premium, no choice at maturity).
The fair price of a futures = replication cost = spot price carried through time at the risk-free rate.
The value of an already open contract = latent gain/loss discounted.
The margin mechanism eliminates counterparty risk in futures (daily, marking to market).
The term structure can be in contango or backwardation, but always converges to spot at maturity.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Forward
OTC tailor-made contract: buy/sell at \(T\) at price \(K\), irrevocable.
Farmer who sells his harvest before reaping it.


Futures
Same principle but standardized, exchange-traded, settled every evening.
Industrial version of the forward, more liquid.


Roll-over
Close the contract before maturity and open a new, more distant one.
Stay exposed to gold without ever receiving bars.


Initial margin
Collateral deposited at opening, fraction of the total contract value.
Proof of solvency, not the price of the contract.


Maintenance margin
Floor threshold below which a margin call is triggered.
Account alarm level.


Margin call
Replenish the account up to the initial margin (not just maintenance).
We reset the counters to zero, not to halfway.


Futures price \(F_t\)
Current market delivery price, determined by no-arbitrage.
Spot + financing cost until \(T\).


Futures value \(f_t\)
Latent gain/loss of an already open contract relative to the initial \(K\).
Worth 0 at opening, then evolves.


Contango
\(F_t >\) expected spot: upward-sloping curve with maturity.
Market anticipates rise or high carrying cost.


Backwardation
\(F_t <\) expected spot: downward-sloping curve with maturity.
Strong immediate demand, high convenience yield.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

Forward contract → obligation (≠ option = right)
Forward (OTC) → high counterparty risk
Futures (exchange) → clearing house → near-zero risk
Futures → daily settlement (marking to market) → requires margin system
Initial margin → threshold = maintenance margin → exceeded → margin call → replenishment to initial margin
Spot price \(S_t\) + rate \(r\) + maturity \(T\) → futures price \(F_t\) by no-arbitrage
Discrete income \(I\) or continuous yield \(q\) → adjustment of \(F_t\)
Current \(F_t\) vs initial \(K\) → value \(f_t\) (discounted)
\(F_t\) vs \(E[S_T]\) → contango or backwardation
Approach of \(T\) → \(F_t \to S_T\) (universal convergence)

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
text:
📐 Essential Formulas








Formula
Meaning
To remember




\(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\)
Futures price with no income or cost
Base: spot + financing


\(F_t = (S_t - I) \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\)
With discrete income \(I\) (discounted dividend)
\(I\) reduces \(F_t\)


\(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{(r-q)(T-t)}\)
With continuous yield/cost \(q\)
\(q>0\) income → \(F_t\) ↓ ; \(q<0\) storage cost → \(F_t\) ↑


\(f_t = (F_t - K) \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\)
Value of an existing contract
Discount the expected gain/loss


\(f_t = S_t - K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\)
Simplified value (no dividend)
\(f_0 = 0\) always at opening


Daily gain \(= \Delta F_t \times\) size
Daily marking to market
Basis of the margin mechanism

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

Futures ≠ Options: no premium, no choice — firm obligation on both sides.
Margin call → replenishment up to the initial margin, not just up to maintenance.
\(q\) represents income → \(F_t\) decreases; \(q\) represents storage cost → \(F_t\) increases. Do not confuse the sign.
\(f_0 = 0\) at opening: no premium exchanged, \(K = F_0\) by construction.
\(F_t \ne\) value \(f_t\): \(F_t\) is the market price today; \(f_t\) is the economic value of a contract already open with strike \(K\) fixed in the past.
Convergence at maturity: \(F_T = S_T\) always, whether in contango or backwardation.
Forward OTC ≠ Futures: the forward settles only at maturity; the futures settles every day.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is the fundamental difference between a futures and an option?
Short answer: The futures is a bilateral obligation; the option is a right (buyer only). No premium in a futures.

Q: Why is the price of a futures \(S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\) and not simply \(S_t\)?
Short answer: Because holding the underlying until \(T\) costs the financing of the position. If that were not the case, there would be an arbitrage opportunity.

Q: Explain the arbitrage argument if \(F_t > S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\).
Short answer: Borrow \(S_t\), buy spot, short the futures → at maturity, deliver and repay → risk-free profit. Selling pressure brings \(F_t\) back to its equilibrium value.

Q: What is the purpose of the margin mechanism?
Short answer: Eliminate counterparty risk by materializing gains and losses every day. If an investor can no longer pay, they are liquidated before the loss becomes irrecoverable.

Q: What is the value of a futures at opening? Why?
Short answer: \(f_0 = 0\). At opening, \(K = F_0\), so the latent gain is zero: neither party has an advantage over the other.

Q: What is contango? And backwardation?
Short answer: Contango: \(F_t >\) expected spot (upward-sloping curve). Backwardation: \(F_t <\) expected spot (downward-sloping curve). In both cases, \(F_T \to S_T\) at maturity.

Q: How can an investor stay exposed to a commodity indefinitely without ever receiving it physically?
Short answer: Via roll-over: close the contract before maturity and reopen a more distant contract on the same delivery.

Q: What is the impact of a dividend on the price of a futures?
Short answer: The discounted dividend \(I\) reduces \(F_t\): holding the asset directly provides an advantage (dividend) that the futures does not provide → \(F_t = (S_t - I) \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\).

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

Obligation firm on both sides (≠ option).
Futures = Forward but standardized, listed, settled daily.
Daily settlement → margins (initial, maintenance, call).
Margin call → replenishment to initial margin.
Price: \(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\) — adjust with \(I\) (discrete) or \(q\) (continuous).
Value: \(f_t = S_t - K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\) — worth 0 at opening.
Contango: \(F_t >\) expected spot. Backwardation: \(F_t <\) expected spot.
Universal convergence: \(F_T = S_T\) always.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards
text:
A forward contract (Forward / Futures) is an agreement between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a specific future date (the maturity, denoted \(T\)) at a price agreed upon today (the strike price or strike, denoted \(K\)).
Unlike options, forward contracts confer an obligation rather than a right: both parties must honor the transaction at expiration.






NoteKey takeaway



In a forward contract, the buyer and the seller commit irrevocably. There is no premium to pay as with options.




Forward contracts were originally created by and for farmers. The goal was to let them lock in the sale price of their crop in advance, thereby eliminating the uncertainty associated with fluctuations in agricultural commodity prices.






TipIntuition



Imagine a farmer who sows wheat in March. He does not know what the price of wheat will be in September at harvest time. By entering into a forward contract in March at a fixed price, he secures a predictable income, regardless of market conditions at harvest.





Forward contracts cover a wide variety of underlyings:

Commodities: precious metals (gold, silver), grains (wheat, corn), energy (oil, natural gas)
Equity: contracts on an index such as the S&P 500
Currencies: for example EUR/USD
Treasury bonds: contracts on U.S. Treasury bonds




Forward contracts serve two main purposes:

Exposure to an asset without physical delivery: an investor can gain exposure to gold or oil without ever taking delivery of the metal or the barrel. He simply needs to roll (renew) his position before expiration.
Hedging: a company exposed to foreign-exchange or commodity-price risk can use futures to neutralize that risk.







TipIntuition



The roll of a contract consists of closing the contract approaching expiration and simultaneously opening a new one on the same delivery but with a more distant maturity. This allows continuous exposure to be maintained without ever taking delivery of the underlying.

text:
Forwards versus Futures
Although based on the same fundamental principle, forwards and futures differ on several important aspects.

Comparison table








Characteristic

Futures

Standardization

Delivery dates

Settlement

Explanation of key differences
Standardization and exchange
Futures are traded on organized markets such as the CME (Chicago Mercantile Exchange). Contracts are fully standardized: lot size, expiration date, precise underlying asset. This facilitates liquidity and price transparency.
Forwards, on the other hand, are bespoke contracts negotiated over the counter (OTC, Over The Counter) between two parties. They offer more flexibility but are less liquid and carry counterparty risk (the risk that the other party does not honor its commitments).
Daily settlement of futures
Daily settlement (daily settlement or marking to market) is a fundamental characteristic of futures: every day, gains and losses are calculated and credited or debited directly to the investor’s account. This mechanism is closely linked to the margin system, detailed in the next section.






NoteKey takeaway



Counterparty risk is virtually nil for futures thanks to the clearing house, which guarantees transactions. By contrast, this risk is fully present for OTC forwards.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards
text:
Operation of Margins

The counterparty-risk problem
When an investor enters into a futures contract, there is a risk that the counterparty may not be able to honor its financial obligations at expiration. To guard against this risk, organized exchanges have established a margin system managed by the clearing house.
This system rests on three mechanisms:

Depositing an initial margin when the contract is opened
Maintaining a minimum maintenance margin
Margin calls when the balance falls below the maintenance threshold



The three components of the margin system

Initial Margin
When a futures contract is opened, the investor must deposit a guarantee with his broker. This sum, the initial margin, represents a fraction of the total contract value.






TipIntuition



The initial margin works like a deposit: it shows that the investor has the resources needed to cope with short-term losses. It does not represent the price of the contract, but a good-faith guarantee.




Maintenance Margin
The maintenance margin is the minimum balance below which the investor’s account must not fall. It is generally lower than the initial margin.


Margin Call
When accumulated losses drive the account balance below the maintenance margin, a margin call is triggered. The investor must then restore his balance up to the level of the initial margin (and not merely up to the maintenance margin).
Conversely, if the balance exceeds the initial margin because of cumulative gains, the excess may be freely withdrawn by the investor.



Detailed numerical example
Consider the following example (taken from the course):

An investor opens 2 futures contracts on June 5 to buy 200 ounces of gold in June of the following year.
Initial futures price: 400 USD/ounce
Contract size: 100 ounces
Initial margin: 2,000 USD per contract → 4,000 USD in total
Maintenance margin: 1,500 USD per contract → 3,000 USD in total

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards
text:
Futures Pricing

Notation and theoretical framework
To value the price of a futures contract, we define the following variables:

\(t\) : current date
\(T\) : maturity of the contract (in years)
\(S_t\) : price of the underlying at date \(t\)
\(F_t\) : price of the futures contract today
\(r\) : annual risk-free interest rate (continuously compounded)

We assume for the moment that the underlying pays no income, dividend, or yield.


Economic intuition of the futures price
The central valuation logic rests on the cost of replication: what is the cost of ending up in possession of the underlying at date \(T\)?
The simple replication strategy is as follows:

Borrow \(S_t\) dollars today at the risk-free rate \(r\)
Immediately buy one unit of the underlying at price \(S_t\)
At maturity \(T\), repay the loan, whose value has become \(S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\)

Since this strategy exactly replicates what a futures contract would provide, the fair futures price is:
\[F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\]






TipIntuition



The price of a futures contract is the spot price carried forward in time at the risk-free rate. In other words, it incorporates the cost of financing (cost of capital tied up) to hold the asset until maturity. If you could buy gold today at 400 USD and finance it at the risk-free rate for 4 months, the total forward cost is \(400 \cdot e^{r \cdot 4/12}\).




Proof by arbitrage argument
The arbitrage argument is a rigorous way to prove that \(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\) is the only coherent price.

Case 1: the futures price is too high
Suppose \(F_t' > S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\).
An arbitrageur can then:

Borrow \(S_t\) at rate \(r\)
Buy one unit of the underlying at \(S_t\)
Sell (short) a futures contract at price \(F_t'\)
At maturity, deliver the underlying and collect \(F_t'\), then repay the loan \(S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\)

Risk-free profit: \(F_t' - S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)} > 0\)


Case 2: the futures price is too low
Suppose \(F_t'' < S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\).
An arbitrageur can then:

Short sell the underlying and collect \(S_t\)
Invest \(S_t\) at the risk-free rate \(r\)
Buy a futures contract at price \(F_t''\)
At maturity, use the accumulated \(S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\), pay \(F_t''\) to receive the underlying and return it to the lender

Risk-free profit: \(S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)} - F_t'' > 0\)






NoteKey takeaway



The conclusion is that any deviation from \(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\) creates an arbitrage opportunity. Assuming markets are efficient and no arbitrage opportunity persists, this price is the only possible one.





Adjustments: income, dividends, and yields
In practice, many underlyings generate intermediate income that modifies the base formula.

Case with discrete income or dividend \(I\)
If the underlying pays an income or dividend \(I\) (discounted to date \(t\)), the investor who holds the underlying benefits from this income. The replication cost is reduced accordingly:
\[F_t = (S_t - I) \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\]






TipIntuition



Holding the asset directly provides an advantage (the dividend \(I\)) compared with simply holding the futures contract. The futures price must therefore be lowered to compensate for this advantage.




Case with continuous yield or storage cost \(q\)
If the underlying offers a continuous yield \(q\) (for example, a dividend yield on a stock, or a coupon on a Treasury bond) or incurs a carrying cost \(q\) (for example, storage costs for oil or grains):
\[F_t = S_t \cdot e^{(r-q)(T-t)}\]

If \(q > 0\) corresponds to income (dividend, coupon), the futures price is reduced
If \(q < 0\) corresponds to a cost (storage), the futures price is increased







NoteKey takeaway



Without loss of generality, the course focuses on futures with no income, dividend, or yield, which corresponds to the base formula \(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\).





Numerical example (Hull, Example 3.5)
Statement: Consider a 4-month forward contract to buy a zero-coupon bond maturing in one year from today.

Current bond price: \(S_0 = 930\) USD
At contract maturity (in 4 months), the bond will still have 8 months remaining
4-month risk-free rate: \(r = 6\%\) per annum

Calculation: Because the zero-coupon bond pays no coupon, we use the base formula directly:
\[F_0 = 930 \cdot e^{0{,}06 \times \frac{4}{12}} = 930 \cdot e^{0{,}02} \approx 948{,}79 \text{ USD}\]
Interpretation: The delivery price negotiated today to buy the bond in 4 months would be 948.79 USD. This price simply compensates for the cost of financing the position over 4 months.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards
section: Valuation of a Futures Contract During Its Life
text:
Valuation of a Futures Contract During Its Life

Distinction between price and value
It is essential to distinguish two quantities:

\(F_t\) : the futures price at date \(t\) — this is the current market delivery price, determined by supply and demand
\(f_t\) : the value of the futures at date \(t\) — this is the economic value (unrealized gain or loss) of an already-open contract, relative to the price initially agreed



Initial strike price \(K\)
When the contract is opened, the delivery price \(K\) is set equal to the market price \(F_0\). At that moment, the value of the contract is zero: \(f_0 = 0\).
Over time, the market price \(F_t\) evolves (supply/demand, new information), while \(K\) remains fixed. A gap appears between \(F_t\) and \(K\), giving the contract a non-zero value.


Valuation formula
The value of a futures contract at date \(t\), for a contract whose strike price is \(K\) and maturity is \(T\), is written:
\[f_t = (F_t - K) \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\]
This is simply the discounting of the expected gain or loss at maturity (cash flow at \(T\): \(F_t - K\)), brought back to date \(t\) by discounting at the risk-free rate.






TipIntuition



If the market price \(F_t\) is higher than the agreed price \(K\), the futures buyer is in a winning position: he has locked in an advantageous purchase price. The value \(f_t\) is therefore positive. Conversely, if \(F_t < K\), the buyer is in a losing position and \(f_t\) is negative.




Value in the absence of dividend or yield
By substituting the price formula \(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\) into the expression for \(f_t\):
\[f_t = \left(S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)} - K\right) \cdot e^{-r(T-t)} = S_t - K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\]
This formula reveals three sources of exposure for the holder of a futures contract:

Exposure to the underlying: \(S_t\) directly influences \(f_t\). Holding a futures contract means being partially exposed to the underlying itself.
Exposure to expectations on \(S_T\): \(F_t\) (and therefore \(f_t\)) reflects the market’s expectations of the future value of the underlying.
Exposure to the risk-free rate: The present value of \(K\), namely \(K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\), depends on \(r\). A rise in interest rates increases the value of the futures for the buyer (by reducing the present value of the price to be paid \(K\)).







WarningImportant point



At contract opening, \(K = F_0\) and therefore \(f_0 = S_0 - F_0 \cdot e^{-r(T-0)} = S_0 - S_0 = 0\). The initial value is indeed zero, which is consistent: neither party pays a premium to the other at opening.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards
text:
Contango and Backwardation

Definitions
The term structure of futures prices (the relationship between the futures price and maturity) can take two opposite forms.
Contango: The futures price \(F_t\) is higher than the expected spot price \(E[S_T]\). The futures price curve is upward sloping.
Backwardation (or normal backwardation): The futures price \(F_t\) is lower than the expected spot price \(E[S_T]\). The futures price curve is downward sloping.






TipIntuition



In contango, the market anticipates rising prices (or reflects a high carrying cost, such as storage or interest). In backwardation, the market anticipates falling prices or reflects a high convenience yield — that is, market participants place a high value on having physical possession of the asset right now.




Economic interpretation







Situation
Market signal




Contango
Expected prices rising; high carrying or interest cost; little immediate demand


Backwardation
Expected prices falling; strong immediate demand; high convenience yield



These two states are not permanent: a market can switch from contango to backwardation (and vice versa) during the life of a contract, depending on the evolution of expectations and supply/demand conditions.






WarningImportant point — Convergence at maturity



Whatever the initial structure (contango or backwardation), the futures price \(F_T\) must necessarily converge toward the spot price \(S_T\) as maturity approaches.
This convergence is a fundamental property: if \(F_T \neq S_T\) at maturity, there would be a trivial arbitrage opportunity (buy the cheaper, sell the dearer).




Graphical representation
The graph below (taken from the course) illustrates the two cases:





graph LR
    A["Today\n(F_0)"] -->|Contango : F_t > Expected Spot| B["Maturity\n(F_T = S_T)"]
    A -->|Backwardation : F_t < Expected Spot| B






In contango, the futures price curve descends toward \(S_T\) over time. In backwardation, the curve rises toward \(S_T\) over time.

title: Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards
text:
Key Takeaways

Global summary






NoteKey takeaway — Chapter synthesis




Forward contracts (Futures / Forwards) allow one to buy or sell an asset in the future at a price fixed today.
The commitment is obligatory (no choice as with options).
A roll-over mechanism allows exposure to be maintained without ever taking physical delivery.
Futures are regulated and standardized (organized exchanges); forwards are less regulated (OTC).
The margin mechanism protects both parties against counterparty risk.
The price of a futures contract is derived by a no-arbitrage argument: \(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\) (with no income or yield).
The value of a futures contract reflects market expectations and is \(f_t = S_t - K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\).
The term structure can be in contango or backwardation, but always converges to the spot at maturity.





Summary table of formulas







Context
Formula




No income, dividend, or yield
\(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\)


With discrete income or dividend \(I\)
\(F_t = (S_t - I) \cdot e^{r(T-t)}\)


With continuous yield or cost \(q\)
\(F_t = S_t \cdot e^{(r-q)(T-t)}\)


Value of an existing contract
\(f_t = (F_t - K) \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\)


Simplified value (no dividend)
\(f_t = S_t - K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}\)

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors — Oral Review
text:
Imagine a planetary flea market open 24/7, where millions of participants simultaneously shout their prices. Some think they know the true value of objects (the “efficientists”), others simply watch them sell faster and faster and conclude they should buy (the “chartists”). Suddenly, for no apparent reason, everyone panics and throws their belongings on the ground in 5 minutes — then comes to their senses and picks everything up. That’s the Flash Crash.
This chapter answers a simple question: are markets smart, or just restless?

text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Markets exist to exchange assets in an organized way (or not).
The EMH asserts that prices are always “fair” — but reality often says the opposite.
Markets are not random walks: they have repeatable structures called stylised facts.
Volatility clusters, tails are fat, seasonal patterns are stable.
Market events can come from inside (endogenous) or outside (exogenous).
Market size is staggering: FX trades ~5,000 bn USD per day.

Concept
One-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




EMH (Efficient Market Hypothesis)
Prices reflect all available information → impossible to beat the market sustainably
If it were 100% true, Buffett and Soros would just be lucky


Weak form (Forme faible)
Past prices do not predict the future → technical analysis is useless
Yesterday’s price says nothing about tomorrow’s price

All public information is already in the price → reading the news is useless
The market has already read the newspaper before you

Theoretically perfect, empirically absurd


Regulated market (Exchange)

Direct transactions between parties, without a central exchange
More flexible, but riskier


Market maker
Market maker who holds inventory and profits from the spread
They assume risk in exchange for the spread


Volatility clustering
Large variations followed by large variations, small by small
Volatility arrives in episodes, not at random


Fat tails (queues épaisses)
Extreme events are far more frequent than the normal law predicts
Crashes are “impossible” according to Gauss, but they happen all the time


Stylised facts (Faits stylisés)
Universal empirical regularities of financial markets
What every market has in common, regardless of the era


Seasonality (Saisonnalité)
Repeatable patterns over time (intraday, weekly, annual)
In FX: peak at the London–New York overlap


Endogenous event
Shock born from the market itself (e.g. lack of liquidity)
The market panics on its own


Exogenous event
Shock coming from outside (news, central bank…)
The real world knocks on the market’s door


Futures
Standardised contract to buy/sell an asset at a future date
Forward + exchange + clearing house


Option
Right (not obligation) to buy (call) or sell (put) at a fixed price
You pay a premium for the right to choose

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

The EMH does not say markets never make mistakes — it just says you cannot exploit them systematically.
The strong form is the least empirically accepted — insider trading exists and is profitable (if illegal).
It is not the NFP figure that moves the market, it is the surprise: published figure − expected consensus.
A futures ≠ Forward: the futures is standardised, cleared, with daily margin calls.
Forgetting the roll over of a futures = taking physical delivery (barrels of oil, tonnes of wheat…).
Fat tails ≠ bug: it is a structural property. Modelling returns with a normal law systematically underestimates extreme risks.
Volatility clustering ≠ predictability of direction: you can predict that volatility will be high, not whether the market will rise or fall.
OTC = less protection: without a clearing house, counterparty risk is real.

title: Financial Markets and Behaviors — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: What is the EMH and why is it controversial?
Short answer: Fama’s theory (1960) that prices reflect all available information. Controversial because speculative bubbles, the Flash Crash and the sustained performance of some managers contradict it empirically.

Q: What are the 3 forms of the EMH?
Short answer: Weak (past prices), semi-strong (all public information), strong (all information including private). The weakest is the most plausible, the strong form is empirically rejected.

Q: What is a stylised fact? Name 3.
Short answer: Universal empirical regularity in markets. Examples: volatility clustering, fat tails, intraday seasonality.

Q: Why is volatility clustering important in finance?
Short answer: It shows that volatility is not constant (heteroscedasticity). It is the basis of GARCH models, essential in risk management.

Q: What is the difference between a futures and a forward?
Short answer: Same principle (deferred buy/sell at a fixed price), but the futures is standardised, exchange-traded, and cleared by a clearing house. The forward is OTC and flexible.

Q: Why do Gaussian models underestimate risk?
Short answer: Real returns have fat tails: extreme events are much more frequent than a normal law predicts. Using Gauss is to ignore crashes.

Q: What is the difference between an endogenous and an exogenous event?
Short answer: Endogenous = born from the market itself (e.g. lack of liquidity, flash crash). Exogenous = external shock (scheduled news like NFP, or unscheduled like a surprise central bank decision).

Q: Why is the FX market so particular?
Short answer: It is the largest market in the world (~5,000 bn USD/day), open 24/7, fully decentralised (OTC), with seasonality driven by global sessions. EUR/USD alone represents 25% of volume.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Review
text:
Stationarity

Why it is necessary

Consistency of relationships over time
Reliable parameter estimation
Simplified analysis
Avoid spurious correlations (Spurious Results)



Sources of non-stationarity



Source
Description
Example




Trend
Drifting mean
Rising asset price


Seasonality
Periodic variations
January effect, temperatures


Heteroskedasticity
Non-constant volatility
Markets in crisis





Formal definitions
Strict Stationarity :
\[
F(X_{t_1+\tau}, \ldots, X_{t_n+\tau}) = F(X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_n}) \quad \forall\, \tau, n
\]
→ The entire joint distribution is invariant under time translation. Difficult to verify.
Weak Stationarity — used in practice :
\[
\text{a) } \mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mu = \text{cte} \quad \text{b) } \text{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+\tau}) = \gamma(\tau)
\]
→ Constant mean + autocovariance depending only on lag \(\tau\).


ADF Test (Augmented Dickey-Fuller)

\(H_0\) : unit root → non-stationary
\(H_1\) : stationary




p-value
Decision




> 0.05
Non-stationary — do not reject \(H_0\)


≤ 0.05
Stationary — reject \(H_0\)





How to make a series stationary



Method
Formula / Action




Differencing
\(\Delta X_t = X_t - X_{t-1}\)


Log returns
\(r_t = \ln(X_t / X_{t-1})\)


Simple returns
\(r_t = (X_t - X_{t-1})\,/\,X_{t-1}\)


Log transform
\(\ln(X_t)\) — attenuates heteroskedasticity


Decomposition
Remove trend and seasonality









NotePractical rule



Prices → non-stationary (p-value > 0.05) | Returns → stationary (p-value ≈ 0.00)
Systematically work with returns in finance.

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Review
text:
Autocorrelation

Definitions
Correlation :
\[
\text{Cor}(X, Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\,\text{Var}(Y)}}
\]
Autocorrelation at lag \(\tau\) (under stationarity) :
\[
\rho_\tau = \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X_t - \mu)(X_{t+\tau} - \mu)]}{\sigma^2}
\]
ACF (Autocorrelation Function) : \(\text{ACF}(\tau) = \rho_\tau\) — represented by a correlogram.


Reading the correlogram



ACF signal
Interpretation




Slow, positive decay
Trend


Alternating +/−
Counter-trend / Mean-reversion


Peaks at regular intervals
Seasonality


All within CIs
White Noise



95 % Confidence Intervals (CI) : \(\pm\, 1.96\,/\,\sqrt{n}\)






TipRule



Bar exceeding the CIs → statistically significant autocorrelation at this lag.

text:
Autoregressive Models

Three fundamental models
AR(p) — Autoregressive of order p :
\[
X_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \varphi_i\, X_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t
\]
MA(q) — Moving Average of order q :
\[
X_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\,\varepsilon_{t-1} + \cdots + \theta_q\,\varepsilon_{t-q}
\]
ARMA(p,q) :
\[
X_t = c + \varepsilon_t + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \varphi_i\, X_{t-i} + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \theta_i\, \varepsilon_{t-i}
\]


AR vs MA Comparison









AR(p)
MA(q)




Depends on
Past values \(X_{t-i}\)
Past errors \(\varepsilon_{t-i}\)


Memory
Infinite (if \(|\varphi| < 1\))
Finite (exactly \(q\) periods)


Estimation
Analytical for \(p=1\)
Numerical (MLE)

title: Time Series and Autoregressive Models — Review
text:
AR(1) Model — Analytical Results
Model :
\[
X_t = c + \varphi_1\, X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)
\]

Key formulas








Property
Formula
Key derivation




Mean
\(\mu = c\,/\,(1-\varphi_1)\)
\(\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mathbb{E}[X_{t-1}]\) under stationarity

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review
text: Imagine a Parisian nightclub on Saturday night. If everyone goes: impossible to dance, lousy evening. If no one goes: crypt-like atmosphere. The winning strategy? Be in the minority — go when others stay home. Financial markets are the same: buying when everyone sells (and vice versa) is often the real opportunity. ABMs model exactly this tension between individual behavior and collective outcome, starting from simple microscopic rules — like simulating each car to make traffic jams emerge.

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review
text:
🧠 Chapter’s Central Idea

Markets produce stylized facts (fat tails, volatility clustering) that classical Gaussian models fail to reproduce.
The bottom-up (ABM) approach: simple local rules → complex emergent macroscopic behavior.
Each ABM targets one or a few stylized facts — no model reproduces everything.
The three course models illustrate three philosophies: physics-herding, economics-heterogeneity, and analytical minority game.
The Minority Game is the richest model: it admits analytical results and a phase transition.

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review
section: ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally
text:
⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally








Concept
1-sentence oral explanation
Intuition




Stylized facts (Stylised Facts)
Universally observed statistical regularities on real markets.
Fat tails, volatility clustering — the market is not Gaussian.


ABM (Agent Based Model)
We simulate each agent with simple rules and observe what emerges collectively.
Stupid ants build an intelligent anthill.


Herding
Agents imitate each other, forming clusters that amplify price movements.
If everyone sells at the same time, the price collapses.


Fundamentalists
Agents who compare market price to fundamental value and trade the gap.
Stabilizers: they bring the price back to reality.


Chartists
Agents who follow the trend (or contradict it) without looking at fundamentals.
Destabilizers: they amplify bubbles and crashes.


Minority Game
Game where the one who chooses the least populated side wins.
Being in the minority = being right.


Parameter \(\alpha = P/N\)
Ratio available information / number of agents — governs the system regime.
Too many agents for little info → chaos; few agents → predictable order.


Phase transition
At threshold \(\alpha_c\), the system switches from symmetric to asymmetric regime.
Like water freezing: one variable, a sharp qualitative change.


Predictability \(H\)
Measure of whether certain historical patterns systematically predict the future.
\(H \approx 0\) → efficient market ; \(H > 0\) → exploitable signal.

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review
text:
🔗 Concept Mind Map

\(M\) (history length) → \(P = 2^M\) patterns → \(\alpha = P/N\)
\(N\) (agents, odd) → \(\alpha = P/N\)
\(S\) (strategies/agent) → \(\alpha_c(S)\)
\(\alpha\) vs \(\alpha_c\) → symmetric or asymmetric phase
Symmetric phase → \(H \approx 0\), \(\sigma^2/N > 1\) (herding, worse than random)
Asymmetric phase → \(H\) rises, \(\sigma^2/N < 1\) (effective diversification)
Optimal zone: just before \(\alpha_c\) (minimum of \(\sigma^2/N\))
\(A(t)\) (attendance) → \(r(t) = A(t)/\lambda\) → price dynamics \(P(t)\)
Cont-Bouchaud: \(a \ll 0.5\) → clusters → fat tails
Lux-Marchesi: fundamentalists ↔︎ chartists migration → endogenous dynamics

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review

📐 Essential Formulas








Formula

\(P = 2^M\)

\(\alpha = 2^M / N\)

\(A(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i^{\mu(t), s_i}\)
Aggregate presence (attendance)
\(>0\): buyer majority ; \(<0\): seller majority


\(U_{i,s}(t+1) = U_{i,s}(t) - a_{i,s}^{\mu(t)} \cdot \frac{A(t)}{\beta}\)

Score ↑ if the strategy was in the minority

\(\alpha_c(S) \approx 0.3374 + \frac{S-2}{2}\)

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review
text:
⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

\(N\) must be odd: otherwise one can have a tie — no strict minority.
\(2^M\) ≠ \(2^{2^M}\): \(P = 2^M\) is the number of patterns ; \(2^{2^M}\) is the total number of strategies (combinatorial explosion — we store bit vectors, not indices).
Virtual score ≠ real score: all strategies are evaluated every round, even those not played — this is virtual scoring.
Optimal zone ≠ asymmetric phase: the minimum of \(\sigma^2/N\) is in the symmetric phase, just before \(\alpha_c\).
\(\lambda \to \infty\) does not mean “irrational agents” — it is the most rational behavior (best score always chosen).
Cont-Bouchaud: \(a = 0.5\) gives a Gaussian, NOT fat tails. Fat tails appear for \(a \ll 0.5\).
Lux-Marchesi: do not forget that agents change type — this is the heart of the model, not just the coexistence of two types.
\(\sigma^2/N = 1\) is the random benchmark (independent agents) — reference value for judging system performance.

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review
text:
🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions
Q: Why model markets with ABMs rather than with global equations?
Short answer: ABMs allow emergent macroscopic properties (fat tails, herding) to arise from simple microscopic rules, without assuming them a priori.

Q: In Cont-Bouchaud, what mechanism produces fat tails?
Short answer: Agents group into clusters that decide collectively. Large clusters generate massive synchronized orders → more frequent extreme movements → fat tails.

Q: What is the fundamental difference between fundamentalists and chartists in Lux-Marchesi?
Short answer: Fundamentalists trade the price/fundamental-value gap (stabilizers) ; chartists follow the trend or their neighbors (destabilizers). Migration between the two creates the dynamics.

Q: Why must \(N\) be odd in the Minority Game?
Short answer: To guarantee that there is always a strict minority — if \(N\) is even, one can have \(N/2\) on each side: a draw, no winner.

Q: What is \(\alpha\) and why is it important?
Short answer: \(\alpha = 2^M/N\) measures the information/agents ratio. It determines the system phase — below \(\alpha_c\): herding and high volatility ; above: diversification and predictability.

Q: Describe the two phases of the Minority Game.
Short answer: Symmetric phase (\(\alpha < \alpha_c\)): \(H \approx 0\), unpredictable market, \(\sigma^2/N > 1\) — worse than random. Asymmetric phase (\(\alpha > \alpha_c\)): \(H\) non-zero, exploitable patterns, \(\sigma^2/N < 1\) — better than random.

Q: Where is the optimal zone and why?
Short answer: Just before \(\alpha_c\) (symmetric phase), where the variance \(\sigma^2/N\) is minimal — perfect balance between information richness and number of agents.

Q: How does the Minority Game connect to real prices?
Short answer: We set \(r(t) = A(t)/\lambda\) — excess buyers push prices up. This link makes it possible to generate time series comparable to real markets.

Q: What is the role of parameter \(\lambda\) in strategy selection?
Short answer: \(\lambda\) controls the rationality of agents. \(\lambda \to \infty\): the agent always chooses its best strategy (deterministic). Low \(\lambda\): quasi-random choice.

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM) — Oral Review
text:
🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

ABM = simple micro rules → complex emergent macro behaviors.
Cont-Bouchaud: herding clusters → fat tails if \(a \ll 0.5\).
Lux-Marchesi: fundamentalists (stabilizers) + chartists (destabilizers) + migration between types.
Minority Game: \(\alpha = 2^M/N\) is the key ; \(\alpha_c \approx 0.3374\) (\(S=2\)).
Symmetric phase (\(\alpha < \alpha_c\)): unpredictable, high vol., herding.
Asymmetric phase (\(\alpha > \alpha_c\)): predictable, low vol.
Optimal zone: just before \(\alpha_c\), minimum of \(\sigma^2/N\).
\(\sigma^2/N = 1\) = random benchmark.
Virtual score \(U\) evaluates all strategies every round.
No ABM reproduces all stylized facts — each model illuminates one aspect.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Modern financial markets rely on precise mechanisms that allow millions of participants to exchange assets in an organized, transparent, and efficient manner. This chapter explores the Limit Order Book (LOB), the central tool that structures the vast majority of trading on the world’s major stock exchanges.
Understanding the LOB means understanding:

how prices are formed at every instant,
how orders interact with one another,
why certain execution strategies are more effective than others.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Modern financial markets rely on precise mechanisms that allow millions of participants to exchange assets in an organized, transparent, and efficient manner. This chapter explores the Limit Order Book (LOB), the central tool that structures the vast majority of trading on the world’s major stock exchanges.
Understanding the LOB means understanding:

how prices are formed at every instant,
how orders interact with one another,
why certain execution strategies are more effective than others.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
With Whom Do We Trade?
Before addressing the LOB in detail, it is essential to understand the two major exchange models that coexist in financial markets.

The Market Maker — Over The Counter (OTC)

Definition
A market maker is a financial intermediary that commits to continuously buying and selling an asset, permanently publishing a bid price and an ask price.
Trades executed directly with a market maker, without going through an organized exchange, are referred to as Over The Counter (OTC) trades.


How It Works
The market maker:

holds an inventory (stock of assets it owns or owes),
takes a risk related to the price evolution of that inventory,
matches buyers and sellers as much as possible,
hedges periodically with other market makers when its exposure becomes too large.

💡 Intuition: Imagine a second-hand bookseller who buys used books and resells them. If too many people sell him the same book, he ends up with excess stock and a risk that the price of that book will drop. He must then offload that surplus.


Concrete Example
Consider a sequence of orders submitted by participants:
x = {+1, +1, −1, −1, −1, −1, −1, −1, −1, …}
From the market maker’s point of view, each participant’s order generates an opposite order:
Market maker: {−1, −1, +1, +1, +1, +1, +1, +1, +1, …}
Quickly, the market maker accumulates a net position of −5 (it is massively net short). Its exposure becomes too risky, and it must hedge by trading with another market maker.


The Market Maker’s Source of Profit
The market maker earns its revenue from the bid-ask spread: it buys cheaper (bid) than it sells (ask). Even without any price movement, it makes a profit on every round trip.
🧠 Key takeaway: The market maker takes an inventory risk in exchange for a profit on the spread. This model is typical of OTC markets such as the foreign exchange market (Forex).




The Limit Order Book (LOB)
The alternative to the OTC model is the limit order book, used on the vast majority of organized exchanges (NYSE, SIX Swiss Exchange, Euronext, etc.).
In this model, participants do not trade directly with a market maker. They place their orders in a centralized system that matches them automatically according to precise rules.
💡 Intuition: Think of an auction room where buyers and sellers display their offers on a board. The LOB is that board, managed by an algorithm.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
LOB Behaviour

Operating Principle
When an order \(x\) is submitted to the LOB, an algorithm immediately performs the following checks:

Can the order be matched immediately?

Example: a seller offers 100 units at 50 USD and a buyer is waiting to buy 100 units at 50 USD → immediate match.

If not, the order becomes active: it is recorded in the LOB and waits to be matched or cancelled.



Formal Definition
The LOB \(\mathcal{L}(t)\) is the set of active orders at time \(t\), that is, orders submitted but not yet executed or cancelled.


Why Study LOB Dynamics?
Understanding how the LOB evolves is crucial for several practical reasons:

Improve execution: choose the right moment and the right order type to minimize costs.
Minimize market impact: avoid moving prices too strongly with a large order.
Design better trading algorithms: automate execution decisions.
Assess market stability and liquidity: a deep LOB (with many orders) indicates a liquid market.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Formal Definitions

The Order
An order is defined by three characteristics:
\[x = (p_x,\ w_x,\ t_x)\]
where:

\(p_x\) : the price at which the order is submitted,
\(w_x\) : the size of the order, expressed in multiples of the minimum lot \(\sigma\) ; \(w_x \in \{\pm k\sigma \mid k = 1, 2, \ldots\}\),
\(t_x\) : the timestamp (time of order insertion).



The Price Tick
The tick \(\pi\) is the smallest possible price increment between two consecutive orders.
Example: If \(\pi = 0{,}00001\), then the price directly below \(1{,}00000\) is \(0{,}99999\).


The Bid and the Ask

Bid \(b(t)\) : the best active buy price, that is, the maximum price among all active buy orders:

\[b(t) = \max_{x \in B(t)} p_x\]
where \(B(t)\) is the set of active buy orders.

Ask \(a(t)\) : the best active sell price, that is, the minimum price among all active sell orders:

\[a(t) = \min_{x \in A(t)} p_x\]
where \(A(t)\) is the set of active sell orders.


The Bid-Ask Spread
\[s(t) = a(t) - b(t)\]
⚠️ The spread is always positive: the ask is always greater than or equal to the bid. If this were not the case, a match would have occurred.


The Mid-Price
\[m(t) = \frac{a(t) + b(t)}{2}\]
The mid-price is often used as a reference for the “true” price of the asset, as it is less sensitive to fluctuations in the individual bid or ask.


Relative Price
The relative price \(\delta^x\) measures the distance of an order from the best price on its side:
\[\delta^x = \begin{cases} b(t) - p_x & \text{if buy order} \\ p_x - a(t) & \text{if sell order} \end{cases}\]
💡 Intuition: A relative price \(\delta^x = 0\) means that the order is placed exactly at the best price (at the bid for a buy, at the ask for a sell). A \(\delta^x > 0\) means that the order is placed less aggressively (further from the market).


Depth of the LOB
The depth of the LOB measures the available volume at each price level:

Buy side (bid side):

\[N^b(p, t) = \sum_{\{x \in B(t) \mid \delta^x = p\}} w_x\]

Sell side (ask side):

\[N^a(p, t) = \sum_{\{x \in A(t) \mid \delta^x = p\}} w_x\]
🧠 Key takeaway: Depth indicates how much volume is available at each relative price level. A deep LOB offers more liquidity.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Order Types

Limit Order
A limit order is an order that cannot be executed immediately at the desired price. It enters the LOB and waits for a counterparty.

For a buy order: the proposed price is less than or equal to the current bid (\(p_x \leq b(t)\)), or between the bid and the ask (\(b(t) < p_x < a(t)\)).
For a sell order: symmetric logic.

⚠️ Associated risk: A limit order is never guaranteed to be executed. If the market does not return to the desired price, the order remains inactive. This is called opportunity risk.


Market Order
A market order is an order executed immediately at the best available price in the LOB.

For a buy order: the proposed price is greater than or equal to the ask (\(p_x \geq a(t)\)). The order is matched with the best active seller.

💡 Intuition: A market order says “I want to buy now, regardless of the exact price”. A limit order says “I want to buy, but only at this exact price”.
🧠 Key takeaway: There is a fundamental trade-off between the two order types:

Limit order → potentially better price, but risk of non-execution.
Market order → guaranteed execution, but less favorable price.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Evolution of the LOB

The Three Cases for a Buy Order
Let \(x = (p_x, w_x, t_x)\) be a buy order submitted to the LOB. Three situations are possible:

\(p_x \leq b(t)\) : the order is a limit order, placed below the bid. It enters the LOB without modifying the bid.
\(b(t) < p_x < a(t)\) : the order is a limit order, placed inside the spread. It enters the LOB and raises the bid to \(p_x\).
\(p_x \geq a(t)\) : the order is a market order, it is immediately matched with the best active seller at price \(a(t)\).

For sell orders, the logic is symmetric.


Detailed Numerical Example
Consider an initial LOB with:

Bid : \(b(t) = 1{,}50\)
Ask : \(a(t) = 1{,}53\)
Mid-price : \(m(t) = 1{,}515\)
Spread : \(s(t) = 0{,}03\)

Important Remarks
