⚠️ Why not always use limit orders? Because in a fast-moving market, waiting for the desired price can mean missing an opportunity or worse, leaving a losing position open.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Priority Management

The Problem
When several orders arrive at the same price, or when orders at the same price level coexist, a priority policy is needed to decide which one will be executed first.


The Three Main Rules

Price-Time Priority

First criterion: the best price is served first.
In case of price tie: first come, first served (FIFO — First In, First Out).

✅ Advantage: Favors those who post their orders early. Encourages rapid order submission.


Pro-Rata Priority

First criterion: the best price.
In case of tie: the executed quantity is distributed proportionally to the order sizes (\(w / \sum w\)).

✅ Advantage: Favors large-size orders.


Price-Size Priority

First criterion: the best price.
In case of tie: the largest order is served first.

✅ Advantage: Rewards participants who take the most size risk.



Illustrative Example (pro-rata rule)
Suppose three orders at the same price \(p_0\):

\(w_0 = 4\), \(w_1 = 2\), \(w_2 = 4\) (with \(w_0 = 2w_1 = w_2\))

An order \(w = -2\) arrives. Under the pro-rata rule:

Share of \(w_0\) : \(2 \times \frac{4}{10} = 0{,}8\) → about half of \(w_0\)
Share of \(w_1\) : \(2 \times \frac{2}{10} = 0{,}4\) → about half of \(w_1\)
Share of \(w_2\) : \(2 \times \frac{4}{10} = 0{,}8\) → about half of \(w_2\)

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Visibility

The General Principle
Most organized exchanges publish their LOB in real time (or with a slight delay), offering all participants visibility on active orders, not just on the bid and ask.


Complexities and Exceptions
Not all orders are visible. Several mechanisms reduce transparency:

Iceberg Orders
An iceberg order displays only a portion of its true size in the LOB. The visible portion is executed, then a new tranche is revealed.
💡 Intuition: Like an iceberg, only the emerged part is visible. Large players use this mechanism to avoid revealing the extent of their intentions.


Dark Pools
Dark pools are alternative trading systems where all active orders are hidden.

Only partial information on executions is disclosed.
They allow large institutional investors to exchange large volumes without visibly impacting the market.

⚠️ Limitations: Dark pools are not always as efficient as advertised. Scandals have emerged (e.g. Goldman Sachs fined 800,000 USD by US regulators for failing best-execution obligations in its dark pool).



What the LOB Reveals
With a transparent LOB, one has access to:

The bid \(b(t)\) and the ask \(a(t)\),
The depth at each price level,
The history of submitted, executed, and cancelled orders,
Information on participants’ intentions.

🧠 Key takeaway: Despite the richness of this data, we still know very little about how to fully read and interpret LOB dynamics. This is an active research area.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Empirical Facts
Numerous empirical studies have analyzed the statistical properties of LOBs across different markets and assets. Although some results vary by context (commodities do not behave like stocks, and the NYSE may differ from the SIX Swiss Exchange), several robust properties emerge consistently.

a) Order Size
Observation:

Order sizes are uniformly distributed at large scale.
They tend to cluster around round values (100, 500, 1000 units…).

💡 Intuition: Traders have a natural preference for round numbers, creating concentrations at these levels.


b) Relative Price (\(\delta\))
Observation:

The distribution of relative prices follows a scaling law, with fat tails.
This implies that a non-negligible number of orders is placed very far from the current bid/ask.

⚠️ Implication: Contrary to what a normal distribution would predict, extremely distant orders from the current price are much more frequent than expected.


c) Order Cancellation
Observation:

70% to 80% of orders are cancelled before being executed.

🧠 Key takeaway: The vast majority of orders submitted to the LOB never lead to a transaction. This reflects price exploration strategies, algorithmic orders that constantly adjust, and changes in participants’ intentions.


d) Depth of the Book
Observation:

LOB depth is also distributed with fat tails.
The exact shape of the distribution varies by market (variable \(\Delta p\) parameter).

💡 Intuition: Close to the best price, many orders accumulate. But one also finds — more rarely — significant concentrations at prices far from the market.


e) Market and Price Impact

Definitions

Price impact: modification of \(a(t)\) and \(b(t)\) caused by an order (may be temporary).
Market impact: deeper modification of the LOB, potentially triggering a cascade of other orders.
Instantaneous impact: immediate effect on the price.
Permanent impact: durable effect on the price, even after the order has been executed.



Why a Permanent Impact?
An order can have a durable impact for two main reasons:

Information transmission: a large buy order may signal that the buyer has positive information on the asset. Other traders adjust their prices accordingly.
Cascade of actions: an order may trigger stop orders, algorithms, or reactions from other participants.



Shape of the Instantaneous Impact
Empirical observation (Lillo et al.):

The instantaneous impact \(I(|w|)\) is a concave function of the order size \(|w|\):

\[I(|w|) \text{ concave in } |w|\]
💡 Intuition: Doubling the size of an order does not double the price impact. The impact increases, but at a decreasing rate. This phenomenon is explained by the increasing depth of the book: as a large order “consumes” liquidity, it must reach orders increasingly far from the best price.


The Master Curve
Lillo et al. showed that by normalizing the impact by the company’s market capitalization, one obtains a universal master curve for all capitalization groups.
This curve follows a power law, suggesting that identical statistical mechanisms govern market impact for very different assets.
⚠️ Practical implication: This universality is crucial for designing optimal execution algorithms, regardless of the traded asset.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
LOB Modelling

Two Major Approaches
LOB modelling is a domain where two major scientific traditions compete:









Approach
School
Assumptions
Strengths




Economists
Financial microstructure
Rational traders, utility functions
Strong theoretical foundations


Physicists
Econophysics
Simplified models, physics inspiration
Captures emergent properties



In practice, the choice depends on the objective:

To understand fundamental mechanisms → physical approach.
For policy recommendations or price theory → economic approach.
For algorithmic execution → both, combined with agent models.



The Maslov Model

Presentation
The model proposed by physicist Sergei Maslov [7] is one of the simplest, and yet one of the richest, for simulating LOB dynamics.


Algorithm
At each time step, a single trader arrives on the market. The process is as follows:

Side: with probability 0.5, the trader is a buyer; otherwise, a seller.
Order type:

With probability \(1 - r\) : market order \(x = (\text{bid/ask},\ \sigma,\ t_x)\).
With probability \(r\) : limit order \(x = (p_x,\ \sigma,\ t_x)\), with:

For a buyer: \(p_x = p' - k\) (below the last price)
For a seller: \(p_x = p' + k\) (above the last price)
\(p'\) is the last transaction price.
\(k\) is a random variable following a given distribution.


No cancellation in the basic version.



Simple Example
With 1000 iterations, \(r = 0{,}5\), and \(k = 1\) with probability 1, the model generates:

A fat-tailed distribution of price changes.
A negative anti-correlation of short-term price changes.

🧠 Key takeaway: These properties, observed in real markets, emerge from an extremely simple model. This is the power of the physical approach: reproducing complex behaviors from elementary rules.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Results of the Maslov Model

Price Dynamics
The model generates a price trajectory very different from an ordinary random walk:

Large price increments are clustered in regions of high volatility, separated by relatively calm periods.
This phenomenon is called volatility clustering and is well documented in real markets.



The Hurst Exponent
The model produces a Hurst exponent measured at 1/4, far from the value 1/2 expected for a random walk.
The Hurst exponent \(H\) is a measure of the long-term memory of a time series:

\(H = 0{,}5\) → no memory (random walk).
\(H > 0{,}5\) → persistent trend (trending).
\(H < 0{,}5\) → anti-persistence (mean-reverting), as here.

⚠️ This result implies that price changes in the Maslov model are anti-persistent: an uptick tends to be followed by a downtick, and vice versa.


Distribution of Price Increments
The model produces strongly non-Gaussian distributions of price increments \(p(t + \delta t) - p(t)\):

For short time lags (\(\delta t = 1, 10, 100\)), the distribution is tent-shaped (Laplace-like), with tails much fatter than the normal law.
As the lag \(\delta t\) increases, the central peak gradually softens, but the wings remain non-Gaussian.

💡 Intuition: This behavior is directly observed in real markets. The Maslov model, despite its simplicity, reproduces it remarkably well.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Extensions: Agent-Based Models
The Maslov model assumes that all traders are identical (homogeneous). To introduce heterogeneity (traders with different strategies, time horizons, and information), one uses Agent-Based Models (ABM).
These models are addressed in a dedicated chapter. The key idea is that complex collective behaviors (bubbles, crashes, asymmetric liquidity) can emerge from the interaction of simple but heterogeneous agents.

title: The Limit Order Book
text:
Key Takeaways

Structured Summary
🧠 What to remember from this chapter:
On exchange mechanisms:

Trading occurs either with a market maker (OTC), or via an LOB (organized exchanges).
The market maker earns revenue via the spread, but takes an inventory risk.
The LOB is the dominant exchange mechanism on major stock exchanges.

On LOB structure:

An LOB is the set of active orders at a given instant.
Limit orders wait for a counterparty; market orders execute immediately.
Depth, spread, bid, and ask summarize the instantaneous state of the LOB.

On empirical facts:

Order sizes are uniform and concentrated on round values.
Relative prices follow a fat-tailed scaling law.
70–80% of orders are cancelled before execution.
Price impact is a concave function of order size.

On modelling:

A very simple model (Maslov) reproduces key statistical properties of real markets.
The distribution of price increments is strongly non-Gaussian.
The measured Hurst exponent (\(H \approx 1/4\)) indicates marked anti-persistence.

On current limitations:

The LOB contains much more information than just the bid/ask, but we do not yet fully know how to exploit it.
This is a very active research area, at the intersection of finance, statistical physics, and computer science.

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
In modern financial markets, large orders cannot be executed all at once without significant consequences on prices. Algorithmic Execution refers to the use of automated computer programs to slice and execute orders in an optimized manner, taking into account price, volume, time, and other market parameters.
💡 The fundamental idea is simple: do not disturb the market with your own transactions.



Imagine that investor A wishes to acquire 10,000 shares of company XYZ, whose average daily volume is precisely 10,000 shares.
This situation immediately raises several problems:

Market impact: If A buys everything at once, his own order will drive the price up.
Execution timing: If he splits the order, when should he buy?
Delay: The longer the execution takes, the more the initial investment signal risks becoming obsolete.
Opportunity cost: Can he really obtain the right number of shares at the right price?

⚠️ In this example, the investor represents 100% of the daily volume on his own. Any massive and immediate purchase would have a considerable impact on the price.



The reference book for this field is:

Algorithmic Trading and DMA, Barry Johnson [8]

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
In modern financial markets, large orders cannot be executed all at once without significant consequences on prices. Algorithmic Execution refers to the use of automated computer programs to slice and execute orders in an optimized manner, taking into account price, volume, time, and other market parameters.
💡 The fundamental idea is simple: do not disturb the market with your own transactions.



Imagine that investor A wishes to acquire 10,000 shares of company XYZ, whose average daily volume is precisely 10,000 shares.
This situation immediately raises several problems:

Market impact: If A buys everything at once, his own order will drive the price up.
Execution timing: If he splits the order, when should he buy?
Delay: The longer the execution takes, the more the initial investment signal risks becoming obsolete.
Opportunity cost: Can he really obtain the right number of shares at the right price?

⚠️ In this example, the investor represents 100% of the daily volume on his own. Any massive and immediate purchase would have a considerable impact on the price.



The reference book for this field is:

Algorithmic Trading and DMA, Barry Johnson [8]

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
Market Impact

Definition
Market Impact is the price change caused by the execution of an order. The larger an order is relative to the available volume, the higher its potential impact.
The impact decomposes into two components:
\[\text{Market Impact} = \text{Temporary Impact} + \text{Permanent Impact}\]


Temporary Market Impact
Temporary impact corresponds to the transient price disturbance caused by the order. Once the order is executed and absorbed by the market, the price gradually returns to its normal level.
💡 Intuition: it is like momentarily pressing on a spring — the price rises during the purchase, then falls back down.


Permanent Market Impact
Permanent impact corresponds to the definitive price shift induced by the order. Even after the execution ends, the price remains at a higher level because the market has received an informative signal (someone really wants to buy these shares).
💡 Intuition: the presence of a large buyer reveals information to the market, which durably revalues the price upward.


Difficulty of Measurement
Impact is difficult to measure precisely because one must compare the price evolution with and without the trade. In practice, one analyzes jointly:

The price evolution over the period
The evolution of the order book

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
The Actors Around Trading

Overview
The process that leads from an investment idea to an actual execution involves many actors:

Analyst: generates buy/sell ideas based on his research
Portfolio Manager: optimizes the portfolio and controls risks
In-house Trader: performs pre-trade analysis, selects brokers, and executes
Salesperson (Sell-side): analyzes, monitors, and produces reports



Execution Methods
Several execution channels exist (denoted A, B, C, D, E in the reference figure [8]):

A — Manual trader: execution via a human trader
B — Direct Market Access (DMA): the client sends his orders directly to the market
C — Algorithmic Trading: automated execution by algorithms
D — Combination: mix between trader and algo
E — Sponsored Access: ultra-fast direct access for qualified clients

🧠 Key takeaway: the buy-side makes the investment decisions. The sell-side provides execution and research services.

Overview of Algorithms

Execution algorithms can be grouped according to their main objective:

General Principles

These algorithms are generic — each broker has its own implementations.
The concepts of one algorithm can be combined with those of another (mix and match approach).
The common objective remains to minimize market impact, whether temporary or permanent.

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
TWAP — Time Weighted Average Price

Definition
TWAP (Time Weighted Average Price) is the simplest execution algorithm. It consists in dividing an order into equal slices distributed uniformly over time.
The input parameters are:

\(t_0\) : start time
\(t_1\) : end time
\(\Delta t\) : time interval between slices
\(w\) : total quantity to execute

The number of slices is:
\[n = \frac{t_1 - t_0}{\Delta t} + 1\]
Each slice represents \(\frac{w}{n}\) shares.


Numerical Example
Parameters:

\(w = 10\,000\) shares
\(t_0 =\) now, \(t_1 = t_0 + 1h\), \(\Delta t = 15\) minutes → 5 slices

Execution schedule:



Time
Quantity




\(t_0\)
2,000 shares


\(t_0 + 15\) min
2,000 shares


\(t_0 + 30\) min
2,000 shares


\(t_0 + 45\) min
2,000 shares


\(t_0 + 60\) min
2,000 shares





Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages:

Extremely simple to implement
Predictable behavior and easy to audit
Guarantees complete order execution

Disadvantages:

Uses no market information (neither price nor volume)
Very predictable: a competitor can anticipate the orders and exploit them (front-running)
May execute at unfavorable prices if the market is particularly active or quiet at certain times

⚠️ Predictability is a major risk: if a malicious actor knows that a TWAP algorithm will buy at regular intervals, he can buy just before and resell just after.


Common Variants

Adding Noise (Randomisation)
To reduce predictability, one can add random noise:

On time intervals: \(t_i = t_{i-1} + \Delta t + \varepsilon\)
On slice sizes: the quantity per slice varies randomly around \(w/n\)



Aggressive or Passive Profile
One can introduce an urgency factor to modulate the execution pace:

Aggressive profile: more execution early in the period (useful if one wants to reduce timing risk)
Passive profile: more execution late in the period (useful if one anticipates favorable conditions later)



Price-Adaptive TWAP
A variant incorporates dynamic adjustments based on the evolution of the market price, bringing it closer to the PI (Price Inline) algorithm.

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
VWAP — Volume Weighted Average Price

The VWAP Benchmark
VWAP (Volume Weighted Average Price) is both a benchmark and an execution algorithm.
The VWAP benchmark is defined as:
\[\text{VWAP} = \frac{\sum_i p_i v_i}{\sum_i v_i}\]
where \(i\) indexes the transactions between \(t_0\) and \(t_1\) (typically the beginning and end of a day), \(p_i\) are the prices and \(v_i\) the volumes.
💡 Intuition: VWAP gives a measure of average market conditions over the day, weighted by actual activity. Large transactions weigh more than small ones.


Principle of the Algorithm
The objective is to track the VWAP benchmark: if one buys below the day’s VWAP, it is a good execution.
🧠 Key takeaway: a broker can contractually guarantee a VWAP price to his client, for a commission. He then assumes the execution risk.


The Problem of Unknown Volume
The total \(\sum_i v_i\) is only known at the end of the day, which poses an operational problem: how to build the algorithm in real time?
The solution is to use historical data to estimate the intraday volume profile.


Numerical Example
Parameters:

\(w = 10\,000\) shares to buy
\(t_0 = 8\):00, \(t_1 = 16\):30
\(H = 50\,000\) shares (estimated total historical volume)










Time
Historical volume \(h_i\)
Proportion \(h_i/H\)
Quantity to trade \(h_i/H \times w\)




8:00
2,600
5.2 %
520 shares


8:15
2,500
5.0 %
500 shares


8:30
2,700
5.4 %
540 shares


…
…
…
…





Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages:

Simple to implement with historical data
Guarantees complete order execution (\(100\%\) of \(w\))
Good average behavior on stable markets

Disadvantages:

The execution price is not guaranteed: the algo follows the estimated volume, not the actual price
Actual volumes can deviate significantly from historical data
The algo does not react to current market conditions in real time



Variant: Integration of Real-Time Conditions
To reduce dependence on historical data (a significant source of deviation), a variant monitors and incorporates current market conditions, dynamically adjusting the execution profile.

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
POV — Percentage of Volume

Definition
POV (Percentage of Volume) is a natural evolution of VWAP. Instead of relying on a historical volume profile, it adapts the size of each slice to the real observed volume in real time.
The formula is:
\[w_i = \alpha \cdot v_i\]
where:

\(v_i\) is the volume traded during interval \(i\)
\(\alpha\) is a fixed participation rate (typically between \(1\%\) and \(20\%\))

💡 Intuition: we buy proportionally to what the market trades. When the market is active, we buy more; when it is quiet, we buy less.


Numerical Example
Parameters:

\(w = 10\,000\) shares in total
\(\alpha = 5\%\)
Start: 8:00, optional end at 16:00









Interval
Observed volume \(v_i\)
Quantity bought \(w_i = 0.05 \times v_i\)




8:00–8:15
3,000
150 shares


8:15–8:30
2,700
135 shares


…
…
…



The algorithm ends either when the 10,000 shares have been bought, or at \(t_1\) if set.


Correction for Own Participation
When \(\alpha\) is high, the algorithm’s own orders influence the observed volume \(v_i\). To correct for this, one computes an adjusted participation rate \(\tilde{\alpha}\):
\[\tilde{\alpha} = \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \alpha}\]
Example with \(\alpha = 5\%\):
\[\tilde{\alpha} = 0.05 \times \frac{1}{1 - 0.05} = 5.3\%\]


Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages:

Dynamically adapts to real market conditions
Similar to VWAP but without dependence on historical data
Natural impact control (we never represent more than \(\alpha\%\) of the market)

Disadvantages:

Still predictable (same proportional rhythm)
No price sensitivity
Execution can be very slow if the market is inactive



Common Variants

Integration of volume forecasts: anticipate upcoming liquidity spikes
Price-adaptive versions: adjust \(\alpha\) based on the current price relative to a benchmark

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
MI — Minimal Impact

Definition and Philosophy
The MI (Minimal Impact) algorithm constitutes the logical progression from VWAP and POV. Its main objective is to minimize market impact, rather than following a volume or time profile.


Use of Dark Pools
MI relies on dark pools (opaque markets) and hidden order types to reduce the risk of impact.
Dark pools:

Are non-transparent markets (see the course on the Limit Order Book)
Allow execution at mid prices (between bid and ask)
Reduce the visibility of orders to other participants

⚠️ The trade-off is a high risk of low completion rate: if no one is selling in the dark pool, the order is not executed.


Hybrid Structure
To mitigate the risk of non-execution, a portion of the order (typically \(20\%\)) can be executed via a passive VWAP or POV algorithm on the public market.


Common Variants

Estimation of the probability of being filled in the dark pool
Estimation of a cost of impact model used as a reference benchmark

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
IS — Implementation Shortfall

Definition
IS (Implementation Shortfall) focuses on minimizing the gap between:

The decision price: the price at the moment the investor decides to buy
The execution price: the price actually obtained in the trade



The Fundamental Trade-Off
IS seeks the optimal balance between two opposing forces:

Market impact: the faster we execute, the more we disturb the market and the price rises
Timing risk: the longer we wait, the more the price may evolve unfavorably






graph LR
    A[Buy decision] --> B{IS trade-off}
    B --> C[Fast execution\nHigh impact cost\nLow timing risk]
    B --> D[Slow execution\nLow impact cost\nHigh timing risk]








Characteristics

Often implemented as an enriched VWAP or POV that favors trading early in the session (to quickly capture the investment signal)
The key parameters are volatility and the asset type
The investor’s risk aversion is an important input: a more risk-averse investor will accept a higher impact cost to reduce timing risk



Common Variants

Use of short-term volatility
Use of implied volatility (see the course on Options)

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
AS — Adaptive Shortfall

Definition
AS (Adaptive Shortfall) is derived from IS with adaptive behavior: the algorithm reacts in real time to the evolution of the market price.


Two Antagonistic Strategies
AS comes in two approaches (the terminology is borrowed from options):

AIM — Aggressive In-the-Money

Behavior: trades more aggressively when prices are favorable, less aggressively when they are unfavorable
Underlying hypothesis: short-term trends are ephemeral and will soon reverse (mean-reversion hypothesis)

💡 Example: the price falls (favorable for the buyer) → the algo buys faster because it anticipates a quick rebound.


PIM — Passive In-the-Money

Behavior: trades less aggressively when prices are favorable, more aggressively when they are unfavorable
Underlying hypothesis: trends persist — if the price moves unfavorably, one must act quickly to avoid larger losses

💡 Example: the price rises (unfavorable for the buyer) → the algo buys faster because it fears it will continue to rise.



Common Variants

Reaction to order book depth
Integration of any available liquidity measure

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
MC — Market Close

Definition and Context
The MC (Market Close) algorithm targets the closing price as the reference price.
The market close is a widely used reference price by institutional investors for:

Valuing their portfolios (NAV — Net Asset Value)
Evaluating manager performance
Calculating stock indices



The Timing Dilemma
Execution around the close is delicate:

Starting too early: significant timing risk (the price may evolve before the close)
Starting too late: significant market impact (everyone trades at the same time)

The optimal time horizon can be estimated from:

The asset volatility (possibly via a model)
The usual trading volume around the close



Common Variants

Possibility of targeting any time of day as a reference (example: the noon price)

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
PI — Price Inline

Definition
The PI (Price Inline) algorithm adapts its trading activity to the evolution of the market price, in a manner similar to POV but on the price dimension rather than volume.


How It Works
A reference price (benchmark price) is defined. The algorithm adjusts its activity based on the deviation between the current price and this benchmark.


Available Strategies
Two orientations are possible:

Strategy A (counter-trend): more aggressive when prices are favorable, anticipating mean reversion
Strategy P (trend-following): less aggressive when prices are unfavorable, following the trend

PI is generally expected in strategy A (counter-trend) mode, which allows it to capture price opportunities.


Common Variants

Use of prices of other assets to drive the algorithm (cross-asset strategies)

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
LIQ — Liquidity Driven

Definition
The LIQ (Liquidity Driven) algorithm trades only when two conditions are simultaneously met:

There is sufficient liquidity
The price is favorable

💡 Intuition: highly liquid phases are associated with reduced transaction costs (tighter spread). Finding liquidity is therefore a major lever for cost reduction.


Implementation Complexities
Implementation is more complex than other algorithms because:

Markets are increasingly fragmented (multiple venues, dark pools, ECNs)
Hidden orders and cancellations make it difficult to assess real liquidity
An error on an illiquid asset can move the price significantly



Sources of Information

Historical data on intraday liquidity profiles
Stylized facts of markets (see the course Markets and Behaviours)



Common Variants

Specifying particular venues to trade on preferentially
Categorizing one’s own orders as hidden to avoid signaling intentions

Detail of Categories

Explicit Costs
Explicit costs are directly visible and measurable:

Taxes: financial transaction taxes (e.g. FTT in France)
Broker commissions: broker’s remuneration for the execution service
Market fees: fees charged by trading platforms



Implicit Costs
Implicit costs are more difficult to measure but often more important:

Spreads: difference between the ask price and the bid price. We buy at the ask, we sell at the bid — the spread is a cost.
Market impact: price displacement caused by one’s own order
Price trend: unfavorable price evolution during execution
Timing risk: uncertainty about the final price due to execution duration
Opportunity cost: cost related to the incomplete execution of the order



Delay Cost
Delay cost occurs between the moment of the investment decision and the receipt of the order by the broker. The price may have moved in the interval.
⚠️ This cost is often underestimated but can be very significant.

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
Efficient Frontier

Concept
Faced with the diversity of available algorithms, how to choose the right one? The answer lies in the concept of efficient frontier, borrowed from modern portfolio theory.
On a cost vs risk graph, each algorithm occupies a specific position.





graph LR
    subgraph "Space of possible algorithms"
    MC --> IS
    IS --> AS
    AS --> POV
    POV --> PI
    PI --> VWAP
    VWAP --> LIQ
    LIQ --> MI
    end








Definitions on the Frontier

The cost axis represents transaction costs as defined above
The risk axis represents the variation of costs (essentially timing risk)

The efficient frontier groups the algorithms that minimize cost for a given level of risk. Algorithms outside the frontier (above) are inefficient: there exist others that are less costly at the same level of risk.


Positioning of Algorithms

MC (Market Close): low risk (the close is a precise target), but high cost to reach it
MI (Minimal Impact): high risk of execution price variation, but low impact (cost)
TWAP: often found outside the efficient frontier — there exist cheaper algorithms for the same risk

⚠️ TWAP is therefore suboptimal in most cases. Its only virtue is its simplicity.


Algorithms on the Frontier (from most costly/least risky to least costly/most risky)
According to the reference figure [8]:
\[MC \rightarrow IS \rightarrow AS \rightarrow POV \rightarrow PI \rightarrow VWAP \rightarrow LIQ \rightarrow MI\]

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
Risk Aversion

Formal Definition
Risk aversion \(\lambda\) is defined as the ratio between cost and risk:
\[\lambda = \frac{\text{cost}}{\text{risk}}\]
This parameter represents the slope of the tangent line to the efficient frontier from the origin. The tangency point indicates the optimal algorithm for that investor.


Interpretation

High \(\lambda\) (high aversion): the investor prefers to pay more to reduce risk → one selects an algorithm with low risk and higher cost (e.g. MC or IS)
Low \(\lambda\) (low aversion): the investor accepts more risk to reduce costs → one selects an algorithm with low cost and higher risk (e.g. MI or LIQ)

💡 Geometric intuition: \(\lambda\) is the slope of a line passing through the origin. The larger \(\lambda\), the more vertical the line (cost rises quickly per unit of risk). The optimal algorithm is the point where this line is tangent to the efficient frontier.


Factors Influencing Risk Aversion
An investor’s risk aversion depends on:

The nature of the investor (hedge fund vs pension fund)
The urgency of the investment signal (short-lived alpha → high aversion)
The size of the position relative to the portfolio
Regulatory or contractual constraints

🧠 Key takeaway: for a given level of risk, one must choose the algorithm on the efficient frontier whose position corresponds to the desired cost/risk ratio.

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
Portfolio Trading

Beyond the Single Security
Until now, we have considered the execution of an order on a single asset. In practice, portfolio management involves dozens, even hundreds of assets simultaneously.


The Diversification-in-Alignment Problem
When a portfolio must be realigned — for example during a rebalancing — many orders must be executed simultaneously in order to:

Preserve the diversification of the portfolio during execution
Maintain benchmark exposure throughout the process
Limit the trading risk related to partially executed positions

⚠️ If orders are executed sequentially, the portfolio may be temporarily poorly exposed.


Available Solutions

In-house Execution
Sophisticated managers integrate portfolio risk measures directly into their execution algorithms. This may require algorithms of algorithms (meta-algorithms) to orchestrate the whole.


Outsourcing to a Broker (Portfolio trading)
One can entrust the complete realignment of the portfolio to a specialized broker. The latter receives information on the current and target portfolio, and handles optimal execution.
⚠️ Confidentiality risk: sharing complete information on one’s portfolio with a broker exposes the investor to the risk that the broker (or one of its traders) exploits this information.

title: Algorithmic Execution
text:
Synthesis and Key Points

What to Remember
The essential points of this chapter on algorithmic execution are:
Market impact:

A large market impact must absolutely be avoided
Large orders require particular attention to minimize permanent impact

Diversity of algorithms:

There exist many algorithms exploiting different variables: time (TWAP), volume (VWAP, POV), price (PI, AS), liquidity (LIQ, MI)
Each algorithm targets a different objective: simplicity, average price, minimal impact, cost/risk optimization

Efficient frontier:

An efficient frontier exists for these algorithms
It identifies the algorithms of minimal cost for a given level of risk
TWAP is generally outside this frontier → inefficient

Risk aversion:

The risk aversion parameter \(\lambda\) allows identifying the appropriate algorithm based on the investor’s profile
High \(\lambda\) → low-risk algorithms (MC, IS)
Low \(\lambda\) → low-cost algorithms (MI, LIQ)

Portfolio trading:

Multi-asset portfolios require a specific approach to maintain diversification during execution
The choice between in-house execution and outsourcing depends on the investor’s sophistication and confidentiality stakes

title: Agent Based Models
text:
Financial markets are not purely random phenomena. They result from complex interactions between many participants with varied behaviors. These interactions produce stylised facts — statistical regularities observed empirically on almost all markets — such as fat-tailed distributions, volatility clustering, or autocorrelation of absolute returns.
Faced with these observations, several fundamental questions arise:

How to explain the emergence of these phenomena?
How to model them realistically?
How to predict market evolution?




There are two opposing philosophies for approaching market modelling:
Top-Down Approach
One starts from equations describing the global dynamics of the system. These models are often analytically tractable but may mask the underlying mechanisms.
Bottom-Up Approach
One defines simple local rules for each participant (agent), and observes how their collective interaction produces a complex global dynamics. This is the approach of Agent Based Models (ABM).






TipIntuition



The key idea is that simple microscopic behavior can generate macroscopic complexity that is difficult to model otherwise. The classic example is urban traffic: simulating each car with simple rules (accelerate, brake, change lane) allows reproducing traffic jams, congestion waves, and other phenomena that global equations struggle to capture.








NoteKey takeaway



ABMs do not necessarily claim to reproduce all stylized facts with a single model. Each model targets one or more particular properties of the market.

title: Agent Based Models
text:
Overview of Three Famous ABMs
This chapter presents three representative ABMs, each with a different philosophy.


The Cont-Bouchaud Model

Context and Objective
The Cont and Bouchaud model [11] comes from statistical physics. Its main objective is to reproduce the fat-tailed distributions of financial returns from a mechanism of herding behaviour.


Central Mechanism: Cluster Formation
In this model, agents do not decide individually and independently. They group into random clusters. Each cluster makes a collective decision:

Sell with probability \(a\)
Buy with probability \(a\)
Do nothing with probability \(1 - 2a\)

The constraint \(a \leq 0.5\) is imposed to guarantee the coherence of the model.


Key Results According to the Value of \(a\)
The parameter \(a\) entirely controls the nature of the return distribution:

When \(a = 0.5\) → the return distribution is Gaussian, as in a perfectly random market.
When \(a \ll 0.5\) → the distribution becomes fat-tailed, close to what is observed in real markets.







TipIntuition



When agents group into large clusters (herding phenomenon), massive buy or sell orders can appear simultaneously. These episodes create extreme price movements much more frequent than a normal law would predict — hence the fat tails.




Extensibility of the Model
One of the strengths of the Cont-Bouchaud model is its modularity: extensions can be grafted to study additional policies or mechanisms, such as adding a Tobin Tax on financial transactions.






NoteKey takeaway



A simple herding mechanism suffices to reproduce fat-tailed return distributions — a fundamental property of real markets absent from classical Gaussian models.






The Lux-Marchesi Model

Context and Objective
The Lux and Marchesi model [12] adopts a more economic perspective. It seeks to reproduce market properties by simulating the interaction between two types of participants with radically different behaviors.


The Two Types of Agents
The Fundamentalists
These agents compare the current market price to what they estimate to be the true price of the asset:

If the price is too low relative to the fundamental value → they buy (they anticipate a return to intrinsic value).
If the price is too high → they sell.

Their behavior is stabilizing and anchored on economic fundamentals.
The Chartists
These agents are not interested in fundamentals. They observe the recent price evolution and the actions of their neighbors. Among them, two sub-categories coexist:

The optimists: they follow the trend (Trend Followers). If the market rises, they buy.
The pessimists: they go against the trend (Counter-Trend). They anticipate a reversal.



Dynamics and Category Change
A crucial element of the model is that agents can change category depending on market conditions. A chartist agent can become a fundamentalist, and vice versa.






TipIntuition



This migration mechanism between categories creates a realistic endogenous dynamic: during a bubble, many agents become optimistic chartists and amplify the rise; when the market crashes, the fundamentalists regain the upper hand and anchor the price.




Model Results
The model uses a parameter \(\tau\) representing the price time-lag:

Low values of \(\tau\) correspond to short horizons (order of days).
High values of \(\tau\) correspond to long horizons (order of months).

The results show that the diversity of market participants allows reproducing fat-tailed distributions, and that the model behavior is partially in contradiction with the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), notably concerning the reaction to incoming news.






NoteKey takeaway



The Lux-Marchesi model illustrates how the coexistence of heterogeneous strategies — stabilizing fundamentalists and destabilizing chartists — naturally produces complex market behaviors, including fat tails and volatility clustering.

title: Agent Based Models
text:
The Minority Game: In-Depth Exploration

The El Farol Bar Problem

Presentation of the Problem
The Minority Game (MG) is directly inspired by the El Farol Bar problem, proposed by economist W. Brian Arthur. The scenario is as follows:

A finite population of \(N\) people wants to go to the only bar in town: the El Farol Bar.
If less than 60% of the population goes there → the evening is better than at home.
If more than 60% go there → the crowd is too dense and the evening is less pleasant than at home.
Each individual must decide in advance and simultaneously, without direct coordination.



The Tension Between Individual and Collective Interest
This problem highlights a fundamental tension between two levels of optimization:
At the individual level: each agent seeks to maximize his personal pleasure. The best strategy depends on what the others do — a problem of circular anticipation.
At the collective level: the global objective is to reach a frequency of exactly 60%. Any deviation — too many people or too few — generates dissatisfaction.






TipIntuition



This problem captures the essence of financial markets: if everyone anticipates a rise and buys, the price rises too much — and no one really benefits from the opportunity. Being in the minority (buying when others sell, and vice versa) is often the winning strategy.




The Dynamics of Fluctuations
In practice, attendance oscillates around the 60% threshold without ever stabilizing perfectly. These fluctuations produce alternately:

Periods where too many people come (above 60%) → dissatisfied participants.
Periods where too few come (below 60%) → some agents could have enjoyed the evening.

This oscillating dynamic is a direct reflection of the market cycles observed in finance.




Formal Definitions of the Minority Game

Proposed by Challet and Zhang
The Minority Game was formalized by Challet and Zhang [13] (University of Fribourg). Since the seminal paper, very many variants have been developed.


Fundamental Parameters
The model relies on four essential parameters:

\(N\) : the number of agents (always odd to guarantee the existence of a strict minority at each turn).
\(M\) : the length of the history \(\mu(t)\), coded in bits (0 and 1).
\(S\) : the number of strategies per agent.
\(P = 2^M\) : the number of possible history patterns.



The Strategy Space
The total number of available strategies is \(2^{2^M}\), which grows extremely rapidly:



\(M\)
Number of strategies \(2^{2^M}\)




2
16


3
256


4
65,536


5
4,294,967,296









WarningAttention: combinatorial explosion



As soon as \(M = 5\), the number of strategies exceeds 4 billion. In practice, strategies are not stored as numbers, but as vectors of \(2^M\) bits chosen randomly.


A strategy can be seen as a lookup table: to each history \(\mu \in \{0, 1, \ldots, 2^M - 1\}\), it associates an action (+1 or -1).




Strategy Selection

The Probabilistic Choice Mechanism
At each period \(t\), each agent \(i\) has \(S\) strategies. He chooses his strategy \(s_j\) with a probability given by the Boltzmann distribution (Softmax):
\[P(s_j^t) = \frac{\exp(\lambda \, U_{s_j}(t))}{\sum_{k=1}^{S} \exp(\lambda \, U_{s_k}(t))}, \quad 1 \leq j \leq S, \quad \lambda > 0\]
where \(U_{s_j}(t)\) is the utility function (virtual score) of strategy \(s_j\) at time \(t\).






TipIntuition



The parameter \(\lambda\) controls the degree of rationality of the agents:

If \(\lambda \to \infty\) → the agent always chooses the strategy with the highest score (deterministic and rational behavior).
If \(\lambda\) is low → the choice is more random, underperforming strategies still have a chance of being selected.





Definition of the History \(\mu(t)\)
The history can be constructed in three different ways:
Random history: at each step, a random number \(\pi\) is drawn:

If \(\pi < 0.5\) → bit = 0
If \(\pi \geq 0.5\) → bit = 1

Endogenous history: generated by the model’s own dynamics (the game result determines the next bit).
Empirical history: built from observed real prices:

If the return is negative → bit = 0
If the return is positive → bit = 1





Actions and Aggregate Attendance

Individual Action
For each agent \(i\), the current strategy \(s_i\) and the history \(\mu(t)\) determine his action:
\[a_{i, s_i(t)}^{\mu(t)} = a_i(t) \in \{+1, -1\}\]
where \(+1\) corresponds to buy and \(-1\) to sell.
Concrete example (M=2, 2-bit history):
Suppose a strategy defined by the table:



History \(\mu\)
Action




00
0


01
1


10
-1


11
0



If the current history is \(\mu(t) = 01\) → the agent chooses \(a_i(t) = +1\) (buy).
If \(\mu(t) = 10\) → the agent chooses \(a_i(t) = -1\) (sell).


Aggregate Attendance
The aggregate attendance \(A(t)\) is the sum of the actions of all agents:
\[A(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i^{\mu(t), s_i}\]
\(A(t) > 0\) means a majority of buyers, \(A(t) < 0\) a majority of sellers. The agents in the minority are those whose action has the opposite sign to \(A(t)\) — they are the winners of the turn.




Utility Function and Predictability

Strategic Score Update
The virtual score of strategy \(s\) of agent \(i\) is updated after each turn according to:
\[U_{i,s}(t+1) = U_{i,s}(t) - a_{i,s}^{\mu(t)} \cdot \frac{A(t)}{\beta}\]
where \(\beta\) is a normalization factor that can take the values:

\(\beta = 1\) (no normalization)
\(\beta = N\) (normalization by the number of agents)
\(\beta = 2^M\) (normalization by the number of patterns)







TipIntuition



This update rule is intuitive: if the action prescribed by strategy \(s\) is of opposite sign to \(A(t)\), it means that the strategy was in the minority — it won. Its score increases. Conversely, a strategy that prescribed the majority action sees its score decrease.




The Control Parameter \(\alpha\)
A key parameter for analyzing the model behavior is defined as:
\[\alpha = \frac{P}{N} = \frac{2^M}{N}\]
This ratio measures the information complexity available relative to the number of agents. It plays a central role in characterizing the phases of the system.


Predictability \(H\)
Predictability is defined as the quadratic mean of the conditional attendance:
\[H = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{\mu=0}^{2^M - 1} \langle A | \mu \rangle^2\]
where \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) denotes the time average.

If \(\langle A | \mu \rangle \approx 0\) for all \(\mu\) → history brings no information on the next movement → unpredictable market.
If \(\langle A | \mu \rangle \neq 0\) for some \(\mu\) → some historical patterns systematically predict a movement in one direction → partially predictable market.





The Two Phases of the Minority Game

Symmetric Phase vs Asymmetric Phase
The analysis of the Minority Game reveals the existence of two distinct regimes, separated by a critical value \(\alpha_c\):
Symmetric Phase — regime \(\alpha < \alpha_c\)
In this phase:

The predictability \(H\) is close to zero.
For each history \(\mu\), the probability \(P(1|\mu)\) that the winning action is \(+1\) is close to 0.5 for all \(\mu\).
The market is essentially unpredictable: history does not allow predicting the next movement.
One is in a regime of high volatility (agents step too much on each other’s toes).

Asymmetric Phase — regime \(\alpha > \alpha_c\)
In this phase:

The predictability \(H\) increases significantly.
The probabilities \(P(1|\mu)\) vary strongly depending on \(\mu\): some patterns systematically predict a movement in one direction.
The market exhibits predictable structures that can be exploited.
Volatility is lower than in the random reference case.







TipIntuition



The phase transition resembles a phase transition in statistical physics. Below \(\alpha_c\), agents are too numerous relative to the available information: they involuntarily coordinate and create erratic movements. Above \(\alpha_c\), information is sufficiently rich for strategies to diversify effectively.








NoteKey takeaway



For \(S = 2\), the critical value is \(\alpha_c \approx 0.3374\).
For a general number of strategies \(S\), one has the approximation:
\[\alpha_c(S) \approx \alpha_{c, S=2} + \frac{S-2}{2}\]
Master curves appear: for a given \(S\), the curves obtained for different values of \(N\) superimpose when plotted as a function of \(\alpha\).






Volatility of Attendance

Calculation of the Variance of \(A\)
The variance (volatility) of the aggregate attendance \(A\) is defined as:
\[\sigma^2 = \text{Var}(A) = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=0}^{T} A(t)^2\]
The simplification \(\langle A(t) \rangle = 0\) is used (the time average of \(A\) is zero by symmetry).


Reference: Random and Independent Agents
If all agents choose their action randomly and independently, with probability 1/2 of choosing \(+1\) or \(-1\), then:

\(\mathbb{E}[a_i(t)] = 0.5 \cdot 1 + 0.5 \cdot (-1) = 0\)
\(\text{Var}(a_i(t)) = 0.5 \cdot 1^2 + 0.5 \cdot (-1)^2 = 1\)
By independence: \(\text{Var}(A(t)) = \sum_{i=1}^N \text{Var}(a_i) = N\)

Thus, the random benchmark gives \(\sigma^2 / N = 1\).


The Four Zones of Behavior
By plotting \(\sigma^2/N\) as a function of \(\alpha\), one distinguishes four remarkable zones:
Zone 1 — Symmetric, worse than random (\(\alpha < \alpha_c\), \(\sigma^2/N > 1\)):
Too many agents for little information. Herding behavior amplifies fluctuations beyond the random level.
Zone 2 — Symmetric, better than random (\(\alpha\) close to \(\alpha_c\) from below):
The optimal zone: variance is minimized just before the phase transition. Agents effectively exploit the available information without excess coordination.
Zone 3 — Asymmetric, better than random (\(\alpha\) slightly above \(\alpha_c\)):
Volatility remains below the random level. Strategies diversify naturally.
Zone 4 — Asymmetric, close to random (\(\alpha \gg \alpha_c\)):
Too few agents relative to the strategy space. Each agent plays practically alone — behavior close to pure randomness.






TipIntuition



The optimal zone corresponds to the point where the number of agents and the richness of information are in perfect balance. It is there that collective coordination is most effective — a lesson potentially applicable to market design.






Connection with Financial Markets

From the Minority Game to Asset Prices
The link between the model and real financial markets is established via the relation between the aggregate attendance \(A(t)\) and price returns:
\[r(t) = \ln\frac{P(t)}{P(t-1)} = \frac{A(t)}{\lambda}\]
which implies a price dynamics:
\[P(t) = P(t-1) \cdot \exp\!\left(\frac{A(t)}{\gamma}\right)\]
where \(\gamma\) is typically a multiple of \(N\) (market liquidity parameter).






TipIntuition



An excess of buyers (\(A(t) > 0\)) pushes the price up, and an excess of sellers (\(A(t) < 0\)) makes it fall. This mechanism is analogous to the real functioning of an order book.




Extensions to Enrich the Model
Several extensions allow bringing the Minority Game closer to real empirical data:

Contrarian vs trend-following agents: modify the utility function to produce two different types of behaviors.
Autocorrelation: introduce terms in the utility that generate temporal dependencies.
Selective participation: allow agents to abstain from playing when their strategies are poorly performing. This extension is particularly important because it allows reproducing properties of the return distribution close to those observed in real markets.





Minority Game Algorithm

Description of the Implementation
The basic Minority Game algorithm proceeds as follows:
Initialization:

Define \(N\), \(M\), \(S\) and \(\gamma\).
Choose an initial random history \(\mu\) (ex.: \(\mu = 00101\) for \(M = 5\)).
Create \(N\) agents, each with \(S\) strategies. Each strategy is represented as a vector of \(2^M\) bits drawn randomly (avoid storing strategies by their numerical index given the combinatorial explosion).

Main loop (T iterations):
For t = 1 to T:
    1. Calculate A = sum of agents' actions
    2. Update scores: U(t+1) = U(t) - a * A / beta
    3. Select the active strategy of each agent
    4. Add a new bit to history mu (possibly delete the oldest)
    5. Update price: p = p * exp(A / gamma)






NoteKey takeaway



The history update is crucial: it ensures that the informational context evolves over time, allowing the model to generate a non-trivial dynamic. It is the memory of the system.






Conclusions on the Minority Game

Richness of a Minimalist Model
The Minority Game is remarkable for its economy of means: with only a few parameters (\(N\), \(M\), \(S\)), it generates a very rich phenomenology.
The essential properties of the model can be summarized as follows:
At each turn:

Agents choose between two decisions (+1 or -1) according to their current best strategy.
The minority wins the turn.
Strategies that predicted the winning side are rewarded.
The attendance history guides the evolution of strategies.

The remarkable emergent behaviors include:

Herding behaviour — visible in the symmetric phase.
A price return distribution close to what is observed in reality.
Analytical results derivable thanks to the mathematical structure of the model.
An extensible framework allowing many variants to be derived.







TipIntuition



The Minority Game is a microcosm of the market: heterogeneous agents, limited and shared information, competition to be in the minority. The richness of emergent behaviors — phase transition, master curves, predictability — shows that minimalist modelling can capture the essence of complex dynamics.

title: Agent Based Models
text:
Key Takeaways

What ABMs Teach Us
Bottom-Up modelling offers a complementary perspective to classical approaches in finance:

Complex macroscopic market behaviors can emerge from simple microscopic rules.
Stylized facts — fat-tailed distributions, volatility clustering — are reproducible from simple individual behaviors.
ABMs allow exploring the impact of policies (e.g. Tobin tax) or structural changes on market dynamics.



The Three Models in Brief
The three models presented each illustrate a different facet of markets:
Cont-Bouchaud — Physicists’ model focusing on herding behaviour. A simple clustering mechanism reproduces fat-tailed distributions.
Lux-Marchesi — Economists’ model simulating the interaction between fundamentalists and chartists. The diversity of participants produces realistic dynamics.
Minority Game (Challet-Zhang) — Physicists’ model where agents seek to be in the minority to win. Allows analytical results and many extensions towards real markets.






ImportantCentral message



There is no single ABM capable of reproducing all stylized facts simultaneously. Each model illuminates a particular dimension of market behavior. The value of these approaches lies in their ability to link microscopic mechanisms and macroscopic properties observed empirically.
